The study of anisotropies in ultra-high energy cosmic rays reveals intriguing patterns in cosmic ray development.  Using data collected by the Pierre Auger Observatory over a 9-year period, researchers discovered significant dips in cosmic ray arrivals on the Earth's surface, featuring two distinct components: one minor and one major, originating from different parts of the Northern Hemisphere.  These anisotropy patterns were discovered within two groups of extremely energetic cosmic rays: those with energies exceeding 4 EeV and those with energies ranging from 4 to 20 EeV.  Interestingly, the major component's amplitude exhibits an energy dependence, increasing by approximately two orders of magnitude between the two energy ranges, while the anisotropy's shape and orientation remain relatively constant.  In contrast, the minor component's characteristics remain consistent across the studied energy ranges, holding the same amplitude, shape, and orientation regardless of energy variations.  These findings were verified through various checks and analyses, reinforcing the results.  Two separate interpretations of the anisotropy patterns were considered: one assuming the anisotropy's dipole is accurate and the other allowing a more comprehensive description of the four-dimensional anisotropy surface.  In the second scenario, researchers discovered that the anisotropy patterns become less pronounced as the anisotropy order increases, exhibiting significant decreases in amplitude for quadrupoles and octupoles, while the anisotropy patterns' orientation and shape show less dependence on the order.  In the lowest energy range of 4 to 14 EeV, the quadrupole and octupole amplitudes were discovered to be approximately 0.15 and 0.02, respectively, in comparison to the dominant dipole amplitude of 0.20, oriented in the same direction.  In the highest energy range of 13 to 56 EeV, the octupole amplitude was discovered to be significantly reduced to 0.01, while the quadrupole amplitude remained steady at 0.15, while the dipole amplitude showed notable increases to 0.22.  These findings were also verified through various checks and analyses, reinforcing the results.  These discoveries are a crucial step in comprehending the complex nature of cosmic ray development.  Future updates with freshly collected data are anticipated to provide further insights and enlightenment.  This research is part of a collaborative project between the Pierre Auger Collaboration and the Astronomy and Astrophysics sector of the Ministry of Science and Technology in Argentina.

The shift in cancer research towards integrated, multi-dimensional data requires updated methods for digitizing and analyzing tissue sections while preserving precious sample material. This has prompted the development of a new, fully digital approach for scoring tumor cells using immunohistochemistry-stained tissue sections. This approach, using a custom-designed system that combines a light source and a high-resolution camera, enables live scoring of TILs during microscopic examination, thus facilitating rapid assessment of tumor tissue samples. By comparing traditional histological whole slides with measurements from this scoring system, we have found that they are essentially equivalent, indicating that the digital platform can replace traditional methods for TIL scoring, making it more efficient and sample-conserving. Furthermore, our system enables the extension of scoring parameters to capture additional information about lymphocyte subsets, enabling the generation of more comprehensive data. This new platform has been validated and shown to provide reliable results for the analysis of TILs in melanoma samples, thus demonstrating its effectiveness and utility in clinical settings. Additionally, we have found that the mechanical movement of the sampling frame allows for the selection of areas for staining, thereby improving the efficiency of both scoring and staining procedures. This innovative, digital tool has the potential to streamline clinical workflows, enhance the availability of digital data, and accelerate the development of predictive models in oncology. In addition to its scientific benefits, this technology also has the potential to benefit researchers, clinicians, and industry professionals. In fact, we believe that the development of similar digital tools will be crucial for making significant progress in the field of oncology, thus necessitating updated ethical guidelines that take into account the new requirements of precision medicine. Precisely, our proposed guidelines for digital pathology research can serve as a model for navigating the complexities of digital research, while more broadly, these guidelines can inform the broader biomedical research community on how to ethically conduct digital research. This work presents a reinforcement learning solution for generating adaptive gaits in quadrupedal robots. Underlying this approach is a novel multibody dynamics model that efficiently simulates dynamic movements with minimal computation. To create practical control policies, this research adopts a continuous action space strategy, eliminating the need for high-resolution trajectory planning. Furthermore, a realistic reinforcement learning-based training environment is established using simulated quadrupedal robots in challenging terrain and conditions. Achieving optimal gait control requires substantial training, so an experience replay and incremental learning technique are implemented to accelerate the process. The outcome of this research is a quadrupedal robot capable of learning gait patterns through reinforcement learning, paving the way for adaptive locomotion in real-world applications. Experimental tests conducted on the Meta Quadruped Robot demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in generating robust gaits for navigating complex terrain and recovering from initial disturbances. Specifically, the robot successfully navigated a steep ramp while carrying a heavy load, recovering from a significant tilt of 54.7 degrees, and quickly achieved a stable gait with a reduced impact of 43.2 and recovered 84.5% compared to the initial tilt. Furthermore, these results show that the robot could extract useful knowledge from previous experiences, enabling the acceleration of reinforcement learning by up to 75% through the transfer of knowledge. Comprehensive high-fidelity simulations were also conducted to validate the model's accuracy across a range of dynamics, gaits, and loads, further emphasizing the efficiency of the multibody dynamics model used in this research. Specifically, the model exhibited a speed of execution of 45-70 milliseconds, compared to 200-300 milliseconds required by other models. High-fidelity simulations of the Meta Quadruped Robot in various poses confirmed the model's precision across multiple situations, including static positions, dynamic movements, and impacts, demonstrating the effectiveness of this model for simulating real-world quadrupedal robot movements. Furthermore, the model successfully predicted the robot's motion in real-time with a level of accuracy of less than 10 cm in terms of squared error, compared to other models used in the research, which is seen as an area of improvement. Overall, the model, model structure, and simulation strategy presented in this research are suitable for generating adaptive gaits through reinforcement learning in quadrupedal robots. The integration of this model with a novel multibody dynamics model, realistic simulation environment, reinforcement learning technique, and high-fidelity simulation validation enables the efficient development of such control strategies. A semi-analytical model of galaxy evolution is presented, which incorporates high-energy output from local active galactic nuclei (AGN) to demonstrate how a feedback mechanism operates across entire galaxies. This is achieved by combining a hydrodynamic model of the galaxy's interstellar medium, a AGN black hole feedback mechanism, and a network of nearby galaxies to supply fuel for the central black holes. This framework is then used to investigate how a feedback mechanism of this type influences the evolution of galaxies. Specifically, the model's findings indicate that when the AGN output is heightened in less luminous centres, a feedback loop is triggered, which regulates the mass of the central black hole. This results in a uniform distribution of black hole masses, with little variation, while prolonged increased energy output eventually leads to a loss of interstellar medium mass. This phenomenon is observed in close pairs of galaxies that are likely to merge, as their hot winds interact and cause gas loss. This hot wind feedback mechanism plays a significant role in shaping the evolution of galaxies, particularly through the regulation of black hole growth and the influence of high-energy output on the interstellar medium. In the field of process control, a significant challenge lies in the reinforcement learning (RL) process's prolonged transient period, where little to no practical value is gained from the experience accumulated through trial and error. The author of this research offers a model-free approach to designing an optimal controller for RL-based optimal regulator redesign, aiming to enhance transient performance. By leveraging data collected during the initial stages of the transient period, the Author develops a new method to create a positive definite Lyapunov function and proves its connection to optimal control performance. Furthermore, it is established that this positive definite Lyapunov function remains within specified bounds throughout the transient period, ensuring the stability of the system. The Author also implements this approach to a pair of simulated processes, specifically a non-linear process and a linear time-varying process, and provides comparative analyses with conventional PPO and POFO methods. The results indicate that the proposed model-free design technique yields superior transient performance while matching the efficiency of PPO and outperforming POFO in terms of efficiency. The research offers evidence that a more efficient transient period can be achieved through the ongoing collection of experience during the transient period. Ultimately, the research shows that the technique is functional in processes with significant variations in mass flow and reaction rates. The research indicates that the use of prior knowledge of the process can accelerate the transition to the steady-state period. A new generation of extremely powerful lasers has enabled researchers to create an unprecedented level of metallicity and chemical diversity of elements within a material through a process known as laser-induced material design. This has allowed researchers to replicate, for the first time, the complex composition of a high-metallicity star found in a specific type of galaxy outside of the Milky Way. This breakthrough has been used to explain the structure of an X-shaped star cluster within the galaxy and its unique characteristics. This research used a combination of computational models and experimental data to create a database of chemical compositions that matches the levels of metallicity and chemical diversity found in a high-metallicity star. This was achieved by subjecting a material to an extremely high temperature and pressure created by a high-powered laser, while also varying the temperature and pressure to replicate the different chemical properties found in the star. The results showed agreement with the star's composition for eight elements, while also accurately predicting the relative abundances of the remaining elements. This research has been successful in creating a high-metallicity material, with a unique composition that mimics the conditions found in a high-metallicity star. While the experimentally determined composition was found to differ from the star's composition for some elements, the variations were found to be much lower than the uncertainties associated with the star's composition measurements. A unique feature of the material designed is the creation of an iron-rich alloy that is not typically found in the star or X-shaped cluster. Despite the differences, the material designed, with a metallicity of approximately one-thousandth that of the star, was found to exhibit similar properties in terms of its stellar composition, including the ratios of elements such as nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine. This research has taken a novel approach to designing materials, not through the typical exploration of a continuous variable space, but by targeting a specific, complex composition, underscoring the power of laser-induced design and highlighting its potential to expand the palette of materials available. The material designed, with a high metallicity and unique chemical composition, demonstrates the ability of laser-induced design to create materials with properties similar to those found in high-metallicity stars. While the experimentally determined composition, with a lower metallicity, differed from the star's composition, the results show that high-powered laser material design can accurately replicate the complex composition of a high-metallicity star, with the added benefit of designing materials with properties not previously found in nature. The research presents a new approach to designing materials, targeting a specific, complex composition, and highlights the potential of laser-induced design

Despite significant research on active nematics, there remains a significant knowledge gap regarding their dynamic behavior, particularly how it compares to equilibrium systems. This study employs two powerful theoretical methods to investigate the dynamics of two-dimensional active nematics: a generalized hydrodynamical framework and a stochastic model. These approaches enable the examination of the system's orientational order, fluctuations, and the relationship between fluctuations and dissipation. The results show that the fluctuations in the two-dimensional active nematics follow a power-law decay over all wavenumbers, a characteristic distinct from equilibrium systems, where a exponential decay is observed. Furthermore, the fluctuations in the two-dimensional active nematics are found to be in equilibrium with their own dissipation, a phenomenon not observed in equilibrium systems. Additionally, the general hydrodynamical framework allows for the calculation of the dynamic structure factor, a quantity crucial for understanding the system's behavior. Finally, the stochastic model is used to investigate the time-dependent behavior of the fluctuations in the two-dimensional active nematics, a quantity expected to be observed in future experiments. The findings of this study provide a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic behavior of two-dimensional active nematics, a knowledge gap that has hindered researchers in the field. This work lays the foundational knowledge that will guide future experiments and investigations in this area. Moreover, the results of this study are universally applicable to a wide range of two-dimensional active nematic systems, a class of smart materials capable of self-directed behavior. This work aims to contribute to the development of smart materials with the ability to respond to external stimuli in a directed manner. Furthermore, the findings of this research may be applied to a variety of real-world two-dimensional systems, such as cytoskeletal filaments and polarized droplets. Finally, the results of this study have implications for the development of new two-dimensional active nematic materials capable of displaying unique and stable polar orders, a property not commonly observed in materials of this type. The researchers speculate that the pressure of the droplets could be reduced to a critical value, where the material transitions to a disordered state characterized by the presence of both clockwise and counterclockwise rotations. This theoretical model provides a framework for understanding the droplets' behavior under varying pressures and may be applied to the development of new two-dimensional active nematic materials capable of displaying a permanent polar order, a property not commonly observed in materials of this type. This research develops an innovative method of obtaining the vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD) at infrared wavelengths using wide-field photometry and color information, eliminating the need for absolute photometric calibration. The approach relies on comparing the observed brightness of the zodiacal light (ZL) lung region to a reference AOD value, with variations accounted for using a diurnal temperature curve model and an atmospheric extinction model. In order to determine the reference AOD, the program uses observations from multiple wide-field surveys, incorporating data from the VLA radio observations to adjust for variations. This analysis utilizes wide-field photometry from the VST-ATLAS and Gaia missions, along with the VLA radio AOD dataset, to generate a vertical map of zodiacal AOD from 1.25 to 2.4 $\mu m$. The results of this study indicate that the VST-ATLAS and Gaia datasets provide AOD accuracy comparable to that obtained through the VLA mission, with the Gaia data exhibiting slightly higher uncertainties due to noise limitations. This wide-field photometry mission data proves capable of supplying essential infrared zodiacal light maps for future wide-field mission planning, with implications for future missions to study the space environment. Additionally, the program demonstrates that Gaia data on the zodiacal light is limited by noise, highlighting the necessity of improving the signal-to-noise ratio in the long-wavelength bands of the mission for accurate wide-field infrared zodiacal light mapping. The research also addresses issues with noise in the long-wavelength bands of the Gaia mission that restricts the utility of this dataset for wide-field infrared zodiacal light mapping. Building upon regularized Anderson acceleration for fixed points, the DWIFOB algorithm was developed to enhance robustness while minimizing computational costs. In this study, we examine how altering key components of the DWIFOB approach affects its robustness and computational efficiency using a variety of numerical examples. These investigations manifest from observations made during a previous large-scale study on acceleration techniques for nonlinear equations, which prompted this in-depth analysis to further clarify the relationships between algorithmic parameters and performance. Specifically, we found that varying the robustness of the DWIFOB algorithm relative to its regularized counterpart follows a predictable pattern. Although experiments were conducted using nonlinear systems, the findings are also applicable to nonlinear optimization problems, as demonstrated through additional examples. Furthermore, we found that scaling the penalty parameter in the DWIFOB algorithm can be analogous to adjusting the regularization parameters in Anderson acceleration. If the penalty parameter approaches zero, the algorithms converge to simple extrapolation methods, whereas increasing it yields optimal results. While intermediate values of the penalty parameter can still yield accurate outcomes, the optimal scaling factor varies across problems, rendering it difficult to prescribe a specific value without conducting preliminary experiments. Consequently, a recursive approach may be necessary to determine the most effective scaling factor for a given problem. Conversely, the computational costs associated with determining the optimal scaling factor are relatively low, specifically quadratic for the studied problems in this work. Moreover, we discovered that the robustness of the DWIFOB algorithm can be substantially improved by approximating the optimal scaling factor using data from previous iterations, which can also reduce computational costs by limiting the scope of these searches. While these estimates are only approximate, they are close enough to enable the robustness of the DWIFOB algorithm to approach that of the regularized Anderson acceleration method. In fact, the robustness of the DWIFOB algorithm is at least 90% of its potential maximum, as indicated by the studied problems in this work. Finally, the optimal scaling factors for the studied problems in this work are mostly integer values, primarily due to the underlying properties of the nonlinear systems examined, which may also apply to other classes of nonlinear optimization problems. Nonetheless, the robustness of the DWIFOB algorithm can still be substantially improved by limiting these optimal scaling factors to a more manageable range, specifically a symmetric interval. By doing so, the robustness of the DWIFOB algorithm can increase by at least 150%, as demonstrated through additional examples. This research focuses on two non-linear wave equations defined on a specific type of metric graph, specifically those with non-uniform slope conditions in an exponential potential. We investigate whether these equations exhibit exponential stability, considering both necessary and sufficient conditions under which exponential stability is achieved, taking into account the presence or absence of elastic forces at the edges. If elastic forces are absent, we demonstrate that exponential stability is possible if the graph's vertices form a convex subset of the Euclidean space, whereas if elastic forces are present, we find that exponential stability is ensured if the graph's vertices constitute a subset of the Euclidean space's closed interior. Furthermore, we develop an applicable stability criterion for a specific type of star-shaped graph, showing that exponential stability is only possible if the convex hull of its edges contains the origin. Ultimately, we provide numerical examples to verify our findings. Additionally, this study offers an innovative approach to addressing stability in non-linear wave equations defined on general metric graphs, assuming the equations' data possess certain monotonic properties. As a result, this research may be of interest to researchers working on monotone systems. We take advantage of the monotonicity of solutions, allowing us to draw inspiration from recent results for monotone systems, though our findings differ due to the unique properties of wave equations and metric graphs. In particular, the proof of exponential stability relies on the use of an energy function that differs from those previously proposed in the literature, as well as the introduction of a new concept involving 'energy reservoirs' at the edges of the graphs. We believe these observations to be noteworthy. Finally, the text is accompanied by an extensive appendix that complements the main findings. Additionally, section 9 provides a summary of future research directions that are worthy of exploration. We hope that our study may serve as a useful guide for researchers working in this domain. By incorporating local symmetry breaking into our analysis, we reveal an instability in the $ (u\dag v + v^\dagger u) $ channel and an absence of instability in the other channels. Our results also show that the inhomogeneous phase may only manifest in systems with first-order phase transitions, and we outline the conditions for inhomogeneous bubbles to occur, explaining why such a transition might not be realized in nature due to the difficulty of undergoing a first-order transition in the pure QCD phase transition. Moreover, our study in the $ (u\dag v + v^\dagger u) $ channel reveals that the inhomogeneous matter could exhibit different behavior depending on the number of flavors present. Finally, we provide an overview of the potential implications of our findings for the quark star scenario, highlighting the possibility of inhomogeneous matter forming within the core of such stars. Additionally, our work contributes to ongoing research in this area, which is also influenced by other recent theories such as the baryonic liquid drop model and the color superconducting liquid drop model. Furthermore, the quark star provides an ideal setting to examine the possible formation of condensed matter at the surface, through the phenomenon of neutron star heating. In this research, we introduce a utility function learning approach that uses expert knowledge to create a comprehensive utility function offline, allowing for enhanced optimization decision-making.
Our utility learning method diverges from the conventional pairwise result preference technique, which only considers relative rankings of outcomes, and instead strives to achieve more precise preferences.
To validate our approach, we conducted experiments on a light bulb scheduling problem from the Netfleet dataset and our results show that offline utility learning, combined with pairwise result preferences, yields better performance and increased robustness in comparison to pairwise result preferences alone.
Additionally, we found that offline utility learning is capable of incorporating expert knowledge more effectively, resulting in solutions closer to the optimal value.
Our study also reveals that the structure of the optimization problem and the distribution of outcomes significantly impact the performance and robustness gained through offline utility learning.
In conclusion, our findings indicate that offline utility learning is a valuable technique, offering enhanced performance and robustness in optimization decision-making. Further research is necessary to investigate the limitations and constraints of our approach in various optimization problems. Significant advancements have been made in generating coherent future scenarios in both real-world and simulated environments. Building upon sequence-to-sequence models that leverage expert knowledge, researchers have used various approaches, including adding a future penalty to the reward system and employing conditional generation methods. Recent studies have applied pre-trained transformer models to achieve state and action predictions from sequential data. Although these models perform well, they often struggle with generalizing to novel scenarios. In an effort to improve performance in unseen situations, some experts propose using a module that generates and evaluates future scenarios before taking the next action. In this study, a distinct scenario generation module is proposed, and it is demonstrated that it can be trained independently using sequence-to-sequence models, without requiring interaction with the reward system. Furthermore, a two-stage training process is suggested, where the module is initially trained using expert data and then refined through self-improvement using online prediction errors. In addition, these modules can be used in conjunction with existing methods to generate more plausible future scenarios. The study presents experimental evidence of improved future generation capabilities when these modules are integrated into leading sequence-based models, and it highlights the benefits of independent training of the generator and evaluator, leading to more realistic predictions, particularly in the long term. This chiral characteristic enables us to define an invariant quantity that measures the system's non-local connectivity structure within the lattice. By introducing specific perturbations to the Hamiltonian, we can alter the lattice's properties, effectively changing its chiral nature. This variation can be achieved through different methods such as adding impurities or asymmetrical external influences. Our research focuses on the ground state properties of this system, specifically its non-reciprocal energy gaps, non-local connectivity structure invariants, and wave function localization patterns. Furthermore, we can map the herringbone model to a well-known one-dimensional system, utilizing a localized Wannier basis, which enables us to explore the spectral properties of the model. Our study also finds that the wave functions of these excited states exhibit localized patterns, which become more concentrated as the wave number increases. These findings are comparable to the results obtained using the effective mass approach, highlighting the effectiveness of this method in calculating key properties of the system. Experimental validation of our findings on multiple game environments confirms that RNDQ-RR* exhibits superior performance compared to prior methods. This work showcases the value of combining conceptual theoretical analysis with innovative algorithmic design to reveal previously unseen connections. In modern distributed machine learning, communication overhead is a major factor that determines total execution time. Current methods focus on reducing the amount of data that needs to be transmitted during training, yet they fail to address a crucial question: what should be done with data that isn't used in a model's current state? Traditional approaches resort to linear aggregation or parameter averaging, which ultimately discard information. By introducing the weighted power-mean (WPM) aggregation function, our research shows that one can engage dormant information and improve model performance when reactivating it under certain conditions. Building on this idea, we develop a novel active learning scheme for distributed neural networks, where the trainer acts as a controller that decides when to "wake up" and update specific network parameters. Our approach is implemented in a neural network called SNLI, which outperforms standard models and demonstrates the effectiveness of our strategy. Moreover, our research uncovers statistical properties of WPM that could be useful for future applications. Finally, our findings show that WPM and other efficient aggregation functions like geometric mean possess similar statistical characteristics, albeit at different speeds. This discovery allows these functions to be used reliably in various distributed machine learning contexts. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused a significant shortage of mechanical ventilators, forcing healthcare workers to share a single device among multiple patients. However, managing this shared resource poses a significant challenge, as each patient requires a set tidal volume to ensure adequate ventilation. To complicate matters, accurately measuring volumes is crucial, and reliable, transportable ventilators often lack these capabilities, making it difficult to ensure each patient receives their desired tidal volume. To address this issue, we have developed an innovative solution, drawing on principles from control theory, to allow a single ventilator to serve each patient's unique needs. Specifically, we have created an adjustable pressure limiting (APL) feature that allows the ventilator to maintain a set pressure, enabling patients to receive their desired tidal volumes. By modeling the ventilator system and developing an optimal controller, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed APL algorithm, which can accurately provide each patient's required tidal volume, even in the presence of uncertainties. To ensure safe and reliable operation, the algorithm incorporates safety protocols and employs robust control techniques, such as integral summer and exponential weighting, to mitigate errors and maintain stable ventilation. Our approach has been successfully tested using real patient data, as presented in a companion video. Experimental trials are planned to validate the solution further in a clinical setting. This study investigates the posterior contraction rates in Bayesian linear regression under a sparse prior, considering a range of error variances from a single uniform distribution to multiple uniform distributions along different coordinates. We demonstrate that incorporating unknown error variance leads to faster posterior contraction rates than models assuming a single error variance. The results are further extended to high-dimensional settings, where we find that using separate priors for coefficients and error variance yields faster contraction rates than a single-prior approach. Finally, we use a control-theory approach to establish a fundamental bound on the contraction rate, showing that the prior-induced risk limits the achievable contraction rate. This bound is applicable to a broad class of Bayesian models and can be expressed as a function of the Fenchel-Lagrange saddle point problem. A companion technical report provides additional proofs. Experimental validation of our findings is presented in a supplementary document. Joint work with Y. Chu, A. Candall, and J. N. Fan. The behavior of thermal fluctuations in many-body quantum systems is generally assessed based on how they impact the analysis of order parameters. However, in systems where multiple particles interact, thermal fluctuations can significantly impact higher-order correlations, making it challenging to interpret them. This difficulty is demonstrated in the context of the two-Yang-Baxter model, a theoretically significant system that interacts particles in three-dimensional space and exhibits quantum order characterized by multiple correlation functions. By investigating the impact of thermal fluctuations on these correlations, we show that the system's correlation functions, initially indicating ordered phases, display fluctuations that suggest disordered states at temperatures below their critical point. This finding indicates that the system's order is obscured by thermal fluctuations, making it necessary to consider more complex correlation functions to determine the system's phase structure. This discovery is relevant to experiments observing the system's properties and highlights the importance of accounting for thermal fluctuations in higher-order correlation functions. Additionally, the system's behavior is characterized by complex relationships between its various correlation functions, which are not simply determined by a single order parameter. This unique property makes the two-Yang-Baxter model a valuable model for studying the interconnections between different correlation functions in many-body quantum systems. Lastly, the system's phase structure is found to depend on how its various correlation functions are connected, which can be interpreted as a form of "quantum family symmetry." This concept is explored further in the accompanying commentary.

Nevertheless, it still relies on the underlying assumption that relevant information is contained within neighboring items, which may not always be the case. Therefore, we introduced a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement module in this study to dynamically control the degree of preference enhancement based on the identified aspects. By incorporating GAPE into LightRCNN, the model was renamed GAPE-RCNN. Experimental results on two real-world datasets showed that GAPE-RCNN consistently surpassed LightRCNN and an additional baseline method in predictive accuracy. Moreover, ablation studies confirmed the effectiveness of each component of GAPE-RCNN. Notably, this method also outperformed other state-of-the-art user preference learning methods in various settings. Furthermore, empirical analysis revealed important insights into aspect-based preference construction, which can guide the development of future recommendation systems. The proposed method was implemented using PyTorch and is available on GitHub for public use. All experimental data have been uploaded to GitHub as well. A weighted least squares (WLS) learnability framework has been developed for achieving efficient function approximation. Within this framework, we introduce an WLS algorithm that is stable and provides optimal function approximation results, especially when dealing with exact sample data. This algorithm's performance results reveal that it requires no dimension increase, even when dealing with smooth and bounded functions. We also prove that it reaches the optimal rate of convergence for functions with bounded dual norms. Notably, this algorithm is also conditionally optimal for functions with bounded and non-bounded derivatives. Like traditional least squares, this WLS algorithm becomes optimal for functions with a specific rate of growth in their dual norms, even when dealing with an infinite dimension of features. We also extend this framework to regression tasks involving high-dimensional data and provide an WLS analysis for generalized linear models under the framework of least absolute deviation loss. Additionally, empirical results confirm that this WLS approach provides a more accurate method for function approximation compared to traditional least squares. The space $\widetilde{X}_H$ represents the set of oriented edges of $X$ oriented towards vertices belonging to $H$, while the lasso topology is the convergence topology on $\widetilde{X}_H(G)\times[0,1)$ derived from the left action of $G$ on oriented edges. Moreover, the whisker topology is the weakest topology on $\widetilde{X}_H(G)\times[0,1)$ for which the map $\pi:\widetile{X}_H(G)\times[0,1)\to\widetilde{X}_H}$ is continuous. Additionally, if $H$ has finite width in $X$, then the whisker and visual topologies also coincide on $\widetilde{X}_H$. Furthermore, conditions have been established under which the whisker and lasso topologies do not coincide on $\widetilde{X}_H$. These results extend the previous findings of Epstein and Munkres, as well as those of Claudio Lazzha and ourselves in the connected graph case. Our work also presents new examples that demonstrate the disparity between the whisker and lasso topologies, as well as the visual and lasso topologies on $\widtilde{X}_H$. Lastly, the article describes the connectedness of $\widetilde{X}_H(G)\times[0,1)$ under the action of $G$ when $H$ is subtrinsic in $G$. This paper explores a novel, end-to-end control approach for serial robotic arms, integrating motion planning and control in a single learning process. Unlike existing methods in the realm of deep reinforcement learning, our motion planning stage is adapted to handle multiple goals and incorporates self-supervised exploration, facilitating the acquisition of universal motion planning skills. A key innovation is the use of a parameterized robotic arm model, enabling control without direct access to dynamics. Through a series of discrete actions, the system learns a probabilistic trajectory language, which is subsequently executed by a controller drawing from this language to achieve desired outcomes. Evaluations on simulated and real robotic systems highlight the effectiveness of our method in achieving efficient control. Notably, our approach enables the rapid deployment of new, unseen arm configurations and effectively leverages demonstration-based learning for more efficient skill acquisition. In cases with limited demonstrations, our method surpasses existing methods by employing goal-conditioned learning and incorporating strategic behavior, thereby improving generalizability to new goals. Moreover, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance when comparing control costs, with online learning costs only a fraction of traditional maximum likelihood estimation. Finally, the system's modular structure, comprising a high-level planner and a low-level controller, facilitates the seamless extension to more complex robotic systems, such as multi-arm systems, by simply adding additional parameters, as evidenced by successful evaluation on a two-arm setup. Our approach and associated datasets are publicly available. Jointly trained motion and force controllers are provided in the companion Supplemen-tary Material. The flow of gas onto a central black hole is typically regulated by a disk accretion process that draws material from a larger circumbholar gas disk. While this process is generally considered the primary means of black hole growth, a recent model suggests that an initial influx of gas from the disk may contribute significantly to the mass of the black hole over typical star-forming periods. In contrast to previous estimates that posited only a minor contribution of gas accretion to the mass of the central black hole, this model finds that an Eddington-type gas disk accretion flow can account for as much as 1-2 times the mass of the initial central black hole. As a result, the total mass of the central black hole, including both the initial influx of gas and the radiative effluence from the disk, is found to be greater than the mass of the initial central black hole by as much as 1-2 times, with the degree of this increase depending on factors including the efficiency of gas transport between the disk and the central black hole, the efficacy of gas transport between the disk and the central black hole, the properties of the central black hole, and the properties of the surrounding gas disk. In particular, variations in the efficiency with which gas travels from the disk to the central black hole lead to a wide range of possible increases in the mass of the central black hole, from less than half to as much as double the initial central black hole mass. In contrast, variations in the rate of accretion onto the central black hole by the disk has a relatively minor impact on the overall mass of the central black hole. In addition to the increased flow of gas onto the central black hole, the model also finds that these gas disk accretion processes result in a significant decrease in the mass of gas within the surrounding circumbholar gas disk, with as much as half the initial mass of the gas disappearing over typical star-forming durations in the universe. In particular, the decreased flow of gas onto the central black hole by diffusion results in a significant increase in the rate at which energy is lost from the surrounding gas, with as much as half the initial mass of the gas losing energy and becoming undetectable through various means. Deep neural networks are highly effective classifiers, but their complex decision-making processes lack transparency, making it difficult to trust their output predictions. While numerous studies have examined the role of confidence metrics in validating high-stakes model predictions, few have explored how uncertainty quantification can enhance classification results. By leveraging the properties of Bayesian deep learning, we propose a novel framework that combines the benefits of deep neural networks and Bayesian inference. This approach yields a model that produces predictive distributions and uncertainty estimates, ultimately enabling the calculation of a confidence-weighted softmax score. We conduct extensive experiments on 29 datasets from benchmark and real-world datasets and find that the confidence-weighted softmax score outperforms the standard softmax function and other state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we validate the robustness of our results through 12 different forms of data perturbations, demonstrating that the CWSS is an accurate measure of true classification error. Notably, the CWSS performs optimally when sampling sets are small to medium in size, making it suitable for a variety of real-world applications. To facilitate replication, we provide all code and data used in this study on our project website. Based on these findings, we recommend the CWSS as a reliable alternative to the standard softmax function for making classification decisions. Finally, we propose a new metric, called the confidence-weighted area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (CWAU-ROC), as a reliable method for evaluating binary classification models that produces reliable results even with limited data. This new metric surpasses the traditional AU-ROC in terms of reliability and performance, making it a more trustworthy option. Additionally, the benefits of this new metric extend to the binary positive predictive value, suggesting that it produces accurate results even with limited data, outperforming the standard PPV. These new proposals demonstrate the value of integrating uncertainty quantification into the traditional softmax function and the standard area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Overall, these contributions have the potential to improve the reliability and accuracy of machine learning models used for classification in real-world applications. All code and data used in this study are available on our project website for replication purposes. This study offers the first empirical evidence that demonstrates the advantages of preprints in accelerating research dissemination and increasing citation potential. Our analysis reveals that preprint articles receive initial attention from the research community at an average of 10 to 30 times faster than traditional published papers, and often generate significantly more citations upon publication. We also identify distinct advantages of preprints in different research fields, and find that field-specific evaluation criteria can effectively predict and explain these differences. Furthermore, our results suggest that authors' willingness to pay a prereview fee is associated with the potential rewards of faster dissemination and increased citation potential in their respective fields. To help authors make informed decisions about preprints in the future, we provide a new set of criteria for field-specific preprint evaluation policies that takes into account both general research standards and field-specific requirements. Based on these criteria, we propose a new system where preprints with strong potential for impact are given priority in the prereview process, and authors of highly influential research are exempted from paying the prereview fee. Ultimately, our study offers a framework for designing and improving peer review processes that are more flexible, tailored to specific fields, and capable of incorporating diverse article types, including preprints. We demonstrate the applicability of this framework by applying it to the ongoing transformation of theoretical computer science, where we provide field-specific recommendations for preprint evaluation and propose the establishment of a separate section dedicated to outstanding OCIs in top-tier TCSE journal. Additionally, we provide field-specific recommendations for the content and presentation of preprints, and suggest the development of a preprint specific section within top-tier computer science journals, such as CACM. Lastly, our study offers field-specific recommendations for how to increase public understanding and credit for preprints, and proposes the creation of a permanent preprint collection composed of exceptional articles that set a high standard in their respective fields. By providing these recommendations, we aim to contribute to the continued growth and development of the preprint ecosystem in the future. To facilitate the adoption of these recommendations, we have established a dedicated website where users can find more information, access the study's data, and participate in the discussion on preprint policy. The website is located at: https://osf.io/mu4tp/website. To ensure that the recommendations are regularly updated and reflect the evolving preferences of researchers, we plan to regularly collect feedback from the research community through an online survey, where the first results can be found at: https://osf.io/4by5f. The transition to automated data management in laboratory operations is crucial today. This shift not only streamlines processes but also minimizes documentation errors that can lead to misleading conclusions. Achieving automation involves several challenging tasks, such as integrating diverse data formats and structures, identifying patterns, and translating manual processes into automated tasks. This study investigates these obstacles and explores the solution strategies for overcoming them. Specifically, we examine how to integrate various data sources, extract meaningful information, and combine sample data, knowledge bases, and automated procedures. We present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed solutions. Furthermore, we highlight the important considerations for successful implementation and provide guidance on how to integrate automated data management into laboratory workflows, drawing insights from existing best practices and industry standards. This research is informed by our collaboration with laboratory professionals and technicians. The large materials space poses a significant challenge, prompting researchers to develop machine learning algorithms that can efficiently navigate and predict the phase formations and mechanical properties of materials with minimal experimental data. A mycelium-inspired computational framework is introduced in this paper, mimicking the underground vein-like networks of fungal hyphae to simulate and analyze material behavior. By applying this approach to predict the compressive strength of polymeric materials, researchers successfully simulated 576 samples and identified the most influential material constituents and their interactions. The simulation results matched experimental findings, demonstrating the potential of this algorithm in simulating material deformation and predicting mechanical properties. Due to its similarity to natural material growth, this algorithm may offer innovative insights into designing new materials with specific properties. A potential extension of this algorithm is its application in predicting the thermal conductivity of composite materials. The framework is anticipated to have a significant impact in the field of materials science, emerging as a unique and promising algorithm to predict material behavior. The proposed algorithm was used to predict the compressive strength of a polymer-based material consisting of cellulose, it was observed that increasing the cellulose content beyond a 70\% threshold doesn't significantly improve the material's mechanical properties. The study revealed that the material's microstructure plays a crucial role in determining its performance, offering a valuable understanding of the materials' behavior. The study of the $T_{CC}^{+\eta}$ decay into $D^2D\eta$ and $D^2\eta'$ channels is conducted to understand the influence of final state interactions. The analysis relies on the effective range formula and the scattering length parameters for $D^2D$ and $D^2\eta'$ to estimate the non-resonant contributions. The results indicate that the $D^2D$ final state contribution is more significant than $D^2\eta'$ in both channels. Furthermore, the $T_{CC}^{+\eta}$ production width in the $D^2\eta$ channel is dominated by the $D^2D$ contribution, followed by the $D^2\eta'$ contribution, which is then supplemented by the $D^2D$ contribution again. The calculated width for the $D^2D\eta$ channel yields $0.133\pm 0.005_{\text{exp}}\pm 0.006_{\text{th}}$ MeV, while the width for the $D^2\eta'$ channel is found to be $0.121\pm 0.005_{\text{exp}}\pm 0.006_{\text{th}}$ MeV. The study also reveals that the $D^2\eta$ contribution accounts for approximately 53% of the total width of the $T_{CC}^{+}}$ resonance. The obtained results are in line with the findings from a previous study, which examined the $T_{CC}^{+}}$ resonance in several decay processes and identified a significant $D^2\eta'$ contribution, which was previously underestimated. The calculated width for the $D^2\eta'$ channel in the present study is, however, lower than the estimated width in the previous study, which was found to be 0.164 MeV. The observed discrepancy may be attributed to differences in the $T_{CC}$ production mechanisms examined in the two studies. The results from the present study are further compared with data on the $T_{CC}^{+}}$ resonance and $T_{CC}^{+}}$ production, which was measured in beauty-baryon decays. The comparison reveals that the decay width for the $D^2\eta$ channel is lower than the measured width for the $D^2\eta$ contribution, which was found to be 0.162 MeV

The Sidon set problem concerns identifying the smallest number of subspaces in a finite affine plane that together encompass every vector in the plane. Researchers, including Sidon and Weisner, earlier proposed upper and lower limits for this number, which were expressed in terms of hyperbolas and ellipses. The current work revisits this problem, providing new bounds that are simplified and expressed in terms of the complete graph's characteristics. Additionally, the work considers variations of the Sidon problem involving specific subsets, including those comprising distinct vectors, as well as a related problem concerning pairwise intersections of subspaces. The findings are also extended to the projective plane, with a notable result being the identification of both upper and lower limits for the smallest number of subspaces that together encompass every vector in the projective plane. The validity of these limits is confirmed for certain cases but remains an open question for others. Finally, the work broadens its scope to include intersections of subspaces within the projective plane. The results obtained for the Sidon problem in this context are compared to those derived from a different approach, known as the 'covering' problem. The findings from both problems are presented, with the observed differences noted. The study also explores a variation of the covering problem concerning subsets of minimal size that can cover the projective plane, with the remarkable discovery being that the identified subsets are nearly optimal, with the presented bound being just a fraction larger than the suspected minimum. The complexity of this problem is further investigated, with the result of the bound being largely independent of the characteristics of the finite field being used. The presented bounds are largely expressed in terms of the characteristics of the complete graph, with the exception of a specific case involving a projective plane of order 16, for which a customized bound is proposed. Current methods for finding small binary matrices that are inconsistent with a given set of data rely on a statistical model that involves sampling these matrices according to a uniform probability distribution, applying certain constraints. However, we propose a new sampling strategy based on a non-uniform probability distribution, prove its efficacy in certain situations, and provide numerical evidence supporting its superiority for small binary matrices of sizes up to 128x128. This approach uses an evolutionary algorithm to generate the most consistent binary matrices according to the given data, outperforming existing methods in terms of log-likelihood and confirming our theoretical findings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the matrices obtained through this method exhibit a higher level of structural consistency compared to those obtained through the standard uniform sampling method. Based on these results, we suggest employing non-uniform sampling as an alternative to uniform sampling for binary matrix completion. Additionally, we provide theoretical justification for why the evolution of these matrices tends towards more consistent binary structures, specifically in the form of random walk on the binary Hamming graph, which exhibits distinct features such as absence of Hammings worst cases and presence of certain local minima. Moreover, we show that the RWBH exhibits certain properties such as minimality in the group of hamming type and presence of certain local minima as proven by brouwer's lower bound conjecture. This research aims to contribute to the field of binary matrix completion through the adoption of the non-uniform sampling strategy, and to shed light on the structural properties of the binary Hamming graph through the presentation of the RWBH. Also presented are the extensive numerical analysis and the code used for the study, which is available online. Finally, we discuss an interesting connection between our non-uniform sampling strategy and the celebrated Erdos-Renyi correlation conjecture. This finding, however, does not offer a solution to the Erdos-Renyi correlation conjecture, but rather indicates that the Erdos-Renyi matrix, which exhibits a specific structure, is likely to appear in the set of most consistent binary matrices obtained through the non-uniform sampling strategy. In the context of determining parton distribution functions (PDFs) through a fit procedure at varying scales using the DGLAP evolution equation, the nonlinear DGLAP evolution equation is employed. This approach leads to an evolution kernel that depends on the virtualities of the partons, unlike the usual linear DGLAP equation. Consequently, the whole process becomes an optimization problem that can be solved using a contrastive learning technique. This method can be used to fit PDFs at any scale without needing to assume their behavior at a reference scale. Additionally, the nonlinear DGLAP evolution equation is used to derive an unsupervised loss function that encourages the partons to conserve energy and momentum in a small region around the photon direction. This loss function is incorporated into a fitting procedure for PDFs at several scales using the DGLAP evolution equation. The results show that the fitted PDFs at different scales are well connected and have a smooth evolution, and the conservation of momentum is also observed. This is confirmed by calculating the momentum sum rule for the partons and finding that the fitted PDFs nearly satisfy this sum rule. Furthermore, the fitted PDFs at different scales are compared with those obtained using the usual linear DGLAP evolution equation and the MRST2006 NNLO PDF set. This comparison reveals small differences in the gluon distribution but significant discrepancies in the nonsinglet and sea quark distributions at large $x$. Finally, the fitted PDFs are used to make predictions for several phenomenological quantities, including the structure-integral $R$ and the charm quark distribution at large $x$. These predictions are found to agree well with experimental data. This paper introduces the Knowledge Discovery Mining framework (KDM), an open-source data mining toolset built upon the Java platform. KDM utilizes the ELKI framework, renowned for its data mining capabilities and highly optimized performance and scalability. To ensure seamless integration with SciView, KDM incorporates a range of enhancements, including enhanced user interaction, user interface improvements, and expanded user functionality. Additionally, KDM provides a flexible framework for developing and deploying custom data mining algorithms and user interfaces. Furthermore, KDM's documentation and source code are freely accessible through public repositories on GitHub, facilitating collaboration and feedback from the scientific community. KDM is now utilized in various data analysis applications across multiple sectors, including public health, geography, and astrophysics. 

Here are the contributions of the paper:
- Introduce the Knowledge Discovery Mining framework (KDM) and its key components
- Discuss the enhancements and modifications made to the SciView platform
- Discuss the benefits of utilizing open-source technology in data mining
- Describe the modifications and improvements undertaken in enhancing SciView's functionality
- Describe the open-source framework that underlies KDM and its data mining capabilities
- Discuss the growing importance of data governance in data mining applications
- Describe the collaborative development approach used in evolving KDM
- Introduce the KDM User Interface and its key features
- Discuss the potential for further development in the area of data mining, particularly in relation to data governance and FAIR principles
- Describe the utility of KDM in facilitating data mining applications across various domains, including public health, geography, and astrophysics. 
  One of the key benefits of KDM is its ability to streamline the data mining process and save resources. As such, we invite the broader data mining community to contribute to the further development of KDM. 
  Finally, we outline future plans for the continued evolution and growth of KDM. These plans include aligning KDM with data governance best practices, reviewing and revising the implementation of existing algorithms, and exploring the potential for integrating KDM with other data mining platforms and user interfaces. In the short term, we intend to prioritize these efforts, beginning with the review and revision of data privacy policies in the medium term, and then addressing the data governance challenges in the long term. In conclusion, the presentation outlines the current status and potential of KDM, while also highlighting the essential role of data governance in data mining applications. As such, we urge the data mining community to engage with KDM and contribute to its continued development and growth

We investigate the formation of microcomb lines in a microresonator driven by a multi-frequency pump, delivering a comprehensive model that explains how hole burning between pump-sidebands affects the microcomb spectrum and creates distinctive features. Depending on the sideband spacing, different hole burning patterns develop, while varying the pump power allows the microcomb lines to emerge and disappear in stages. Ultimately, our model generates accurate simulation results that match experimental observations, providing a fundamental understanding of microcomb formation. Moreover, our research identifies adjustable parameters that can be utilized to tailor the microcomb spectrum to meet specific requirements. As such, we propose a method to control the spacing between microcomb lines by adjusting the pump power and find that this technique is effective even in cases with complex pump configurations. Consequently, we demonstrate the ability to create custom optical frequency comb translators with precise control of the spacing between the comb lines. Specifically, we show that a set of microcombs with evenly spaced lines can be produced by taking advantage of a localized hole burning pattern that occurs at integer spacings, while also achieving a higher transmission efficiency compared to the typical hole burning pattern. Finally, we examine the potential of utilizing multi-frequency pumping in integrated photonic microresonators to create a multi-stable optical frequency comb translator that can be integrated onto a chip. Our research paves the way for the development of novel optical frequency comb translators and microresonators with customizable properties. Additionally, our study highlights the possibility of generating stable, wide-tuning-range optical frequency comb translators based on microcomb technology. Ultimately, we show that microcomb-based optical frequency comb translators can be used in spectroscopic applications that require high precision and fast scanning capabilities. As such, we successfully demonstrate the creation of a wide-tuning-range optical frequency comb translator with over 300 THz coverage, while also achieving fast scanning rates of up to 100 GHz/s and high precision of ~10 MHz. Moreover, we explore the potential of microcomb-based optical frequency comb translators in various spectroscopic applications, while also identifying the limitations associated with current technology. As such, we see a promising future for the development of optical frequency comb translators in spectroscopy, while also acknowledging the technical challenges that need to be overcome. Consequently, we see microcomb-based optical frequency comb translators as a key component in various spectroscopic applications, while also expecting significant improvements in their performance in the near future. As such, we see a wide range of potential applications for optical frequency comb translators, while also anticipating their increased usefulness in various spectroscopic applications.

This achievement addresses an unresolved question from the research of Richard Kenyon and Jeonghwan Horan. The subgroup in question is generated by a finite set of random elements, which perform a comprehensive permutation across all natural numbers, interacting in a positive manner. Furthermore, a more general family of subgroups within $S_\infty$ can be defined, whose parameters vary continuously, allowing us to explore an open region in the plane and pinpoint the upper limit for the subgroup's rank. Research suggests that the bulk entropies of boundary entropies must adhere to the principle of monogamy of mutual information. This means that in a system consisting of three parts, the total entropy of two components cannot exceed the entropy of the third. This guideline can be expressed mathematically as an inequality. Studies have demonstrated that for boundary entropies associated with holographic duals, this inequality is converted into an equalities, indicating that boundary entropies are strictly defined. This reveals that boundary entropies are actually a measure of the unique information held within a system, rather than its total informational content. This understanding led researchers to reframe the system to account for a 'core' of information that is indistinguishable from its bulk counterpart, thereby reducing the system and allowing the total entropy to be calculated more accurately. Using this revised system, researchers were able to show that the original inequality is transformed into a valid equality. Furthermore, researchers found that similar patterns exist in systems of higher dimensions and found a new general inequality that holds for all systems, independent of dimension. Additionally, researchers were able to derive a new inequality that relates boundary entropies to each other in systems of higher dimensions. These new inequalities provide a valuable new tool for understanding the behavior of bulk boundary systems. However, researchers noted that the same expressions that are equal for boundary entropies are now strictly unequal, but found that the values they yield are on average accurate. This led researchers to propose a new notion of monogamy of mutual information, one that is weaker yet more accurate, and tested it to be true for the system of a three-sphere. This study compares the outcomes of combining stabilization methods and optimization algorithms. Specifically, we examined the effects of merging Total Variation-Stable Marching Squares and its variants with gradient descent and its variants on signal recovery tasks. Our findings suggest that merging these stabilization methods and optimization algorithms can yield highly effective signal recovery algorithms, which we have empirically validated through various experiments. To obtain these results, we first derived analytical guarantees for the variants of TV-SMS, and then observed that optimizing a TV-SMS cost function using generalized gradient descent leads to a highly regularized solution. Notably, our findings indicate that optimizing TV-SMS using first-order methods results in solutions with comparable smoothness to those obtained through exponential smoothing. Moreover, we propose a family of TV-SMS minimization algorithms that combine regularization and optimization in a single step, and provide guaranteed exponential decay of error terms. Our experimental results confirm that these algorithms offer superior performance over standard TV minimization and other alternative methods. To facilitate the comparison of these algorithms, we introduce a suite of experiments that evaluate performance using an objective function that balances data fidelity, smoothness, and computational complexity. Our empirical results indicate that merging stabilization methods and optimization algorithms can lead to highly effective algorithms, which often perform better than algorithms that utilize stabilization or optimization alone. One such algorithm, TV-SMS with incremental averaging, stands out for its exceptional balance of regularization, accuracy, and efficiency, and demonstrates superior performance over existing methods in various experiments. Furthermore, we anticipate that this new approach will inspire further research in the development of computational algorithms for partial differential equations. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/visualpcr/TV-SMS/tree/open-access/pcr/alphapyle. Recently, Quantum Deep Learning has gained significant attention, yet its safety depends on its source. To ensure the trustworthiness of quantum models, the origin of its quantum circuits needs to be verified. Research has made progress in verifying quantum circuits, but complex quantum circuits require substantial time to verify. To address this, a novel approach called Randomized Circuit Verification through Quantum Augmentation (RCVA) has been developed, which employs quantum augmentations to facilitate rapid verification of complex circuits. Although effective, RCVA is susceptible to errors when dealing with noisy quantum hardware. To overcome this limitation, a improved variant called Randomized Circuit Verification through Quantum Augmentation with Noise Mitigation (CVQA) has been created. CVQA incorporates error-reducing measures utilizing classical and quantum techniques, thereby significantly mitigating errors. As a result, a new verification protocol called Constant-Volume Quantum Circuit Verification through Quantum Augmentation with Noise Mitigation (CVQC) has been developed, providing rapid and reliable verification of intricate quantum circuits. CVQC leverages the principles of augmented reality and constant volume computing, enabling the verification of intricate circuits with minimal overhead. Specifically, CVQC can verify significant sections of quantum circuits within constant volumes, at an speedup of O(n^3) and reduced overhead. To further minimize errors in complex circuits, a novel variant called Constant-Volume Quantum Circuit Verification through Quantum Augmentation with Noise Mitigation for Large Scale Quantum Systems (CVQC-LS) has been created. CVQC-LS incorporates an advanced large-scale noise mitigation technique, thereby providing a robust solution for verifying large-scale quantum systems. Consequently, CVQC and CVQC-LS significantly surpass existing verification protocols in terms of speed, while also offering enhanced resilience to noise in quantum hardware. In particular, CVQC can provide rapid verification for intricate quantum circuits with reduced overhead, whereas CVQC-LS can verify large-scale quantum systems with minimal overhead and significant improvements in verification efficiency. In the biomedical field, image analysis is a crucial component that has been heavily researched over the years. Unlike traditional applications, where image synthesis was initially used for visual purposes, in the biomedical domain, synthetic images can assist and augment existing techniques. Specifically, we are focused on improving cell shape synthesis to enhance radiotherapy treatment planning. By generating a diverse range of cell shapes, we can simulate various tumor cell shapes that could develop from a single cell over different time periods. This capability can be employed in several analysis tasks, such as cell tracking and segmentation. To achieve this goal, we propose a deep generative model called the $2$DFRGNN, which is based on a combination of generative adversarial networks and graph neural networks, tailored to handle radiotherapy-related cell synthesis. Our proposed model is unique in its ability to generate cells with varying shapes and sizes while maintaining their correct morphology. We evaluated several generative adversarial network backbones and discovered that the incorporation of graph neural networks significantly improves the generation of cell shapes with correct boundaries. To further enhance our model, we created a dataset of artificially generated cytochrome blastoma cells, which serves as a reference point for the synthesis of tumor cells for radiotherapy. We utilized the created dataset to compare different deep generative models, including our proposed $2$DFRGNN model, which outperforms existing models in the generation of tumor cells with accurate nuclei placement. The effectiveness of our proposed model has been validated through visual evaluations and statistical analysis that demonstrate its superiority over alternative methods. Ultimately, we aim to utilize this synthesized data to improve radiotherapy treatment planning by generating a range of tumor cells that could develop from a single cell over different time periods. This research has the potential to accelerate the development of cell shape models that can inform radiotherapy decisions, thus reducing the need for manual model creation and data collection. To facilitate the replication of our research, the proposed $2$DFRGNN model has been made available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/krishan-govind/2DFRGNN. Additionally, the synthesized data and the proposed model have been uploaded to the Codespace at https://codespace.io/project/2DFRGNN. Reinforcement learning algorithms are often evaluated by their capacity to recognize patterns in reinforcement signals and sequence data. The persistence of features in these sequences significantly impacts their geometric properties, which has been recently discovered. This work explores the relationship between feature persistence and performance in geometric tasks, finding that persistent features enable more efficient reinforcement learning, particularly when features are directly used to navigate a geometric environment. The persistence of features also significantly affects the performance of look-ahead algorithms, which integrate information from multiple time steps. A notable finding is that look-ahead performance is highly sensitive to feature persistence, while plain reinforcement learning is not. To formalize these observations, a new measure of sequence persistence is introduced, which is connected to the geometric properties of these sequences. This measure is shown to be relevant across various types of sequence data, including a geometric environment, Cart-Pole swing-up, and a sequence prediction task. The relationship between feature persistence and performance is consistent across different levels of reinforcement learning performance. The research also identifies a threshold below which feature persistence negatively affects performance, as features become too similar and redundant. The findings suggest that feature integration is sensitive to feature diversity, which is critical for its performance. Ultimately, feature persistence is shown to be a significant factor in sequence data, which is worth considering when designing reinforcement learning algorithms. The research presents an initial evaluation of the sequence's geometric properties, which may provide insights for future reinforcement learning algorithms. Data augmentation has been widely adopted to enhance vision-based models, however its effectiveness for sound event detection remains unclear. A thorough investigation into the impact of data augmentation on sound event detection is presented, focusing on the augmentation of input sound waves rather than frequency spectra as is more commonly applied. Our study introduces a suite of sophisticated spatial data augmentation methods, including mix-up, cut-mix, and wrap-mix, distinct from the typically applied shift-mix. A state-of-the-art DTCM model is utilized as the base model to evaluate the efficacy of these methods. Experiments reveal that while shift-mix yields reasonable results, the novel spatial data augmentation methods yield superior performance, especially on larger datasets. Moreover, the analysis reveals that the combination of cut-mix and wrap-mix yields the best outcomes. To promote reproducibility, the study's findings, models, and code are openly available for scrutiny and utilization. Our study aims to stimulate the development of more advanced data augmentation techniques for sound event detection. Additionally, the study's results highlight potential pitfalls of utilizing frequency-based data augmentation methods, potentially harmful in sound event detection tasks. Finally, the study's outcomes suggest that the benefits of data augmentation are more pronounced on larger datasets; a finding potentially informative for future research endeavors. This solution is accompanied by an algorithm that can accurately identify the permanent current for small networks, whereas larger networks can be solved using an iterative computational approach. Moreover, we propose a new measure, known as the synchronized cluster entropy, which quantifies the level of synchronization within each cluster and uses the permanent current to determine the number of clusters. This new measure enables us to assess the organization of clusters and the degree of synchronization within each cluster. We support our findings with numerical examples that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. We have created a versatile, easy-to-use module for generating realistic trajectories in small-scale cosmological simulations that models the growth of structures through gravitational collapse. This module, designed for the GIZMO code, simulates the movement and clustering of particles by incorporating an analytical model that accurately produces smooth, connected web-like patterns, mimicking the distribution of galaxies in cosmological simulations. This module can be used in a variety of simulations, such as studying galaxy formation, black hole formation, and the distribution of dark matter. Furthermore, this module allows for the efficient generation of multiple particle trajectories, reducing computation time by up to two orders of magnitude compared to traditional phase-space methods. Several demonstration projects are included in the module to help users learn its capabilities. Additionally, this module comes with an option to produce synthetic observations, enabling researchers to study various astrophysical phenomena without running expensive, large-scale simulations. Further details about this module can be found in the accompanying paper and on the GIZMO website. This work was supported by the NSF and the NSF's CAREER program.

The second law of thermodynamics is often challenged by systems that can efficiently convert energy, a concept historically rooted in classical physics.
