This research investigates the jamming transition of a two-dimensional stack of disks with varying weights, confined within a square frame with periodic boundary conditions. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we examine the jamming transition under both horizontal and diagonal orientation configurations. Our findings indicate that jamming occurs solely through a type of deformation called marginally jammed (MJ) collapse, which involves a sudden and widespread shift in configuration for heavily weighted disks. At lower weights, lighter disks can assume multiple jammed configurations with varying orientations. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the exponential decline in compressibility near the jamming transition remains consistent across all weight ranges, while the thermal energy of the system affects jamming transitions in multiple degrees of freedom. We observe jamming transitions in both single and combined degrees of freedom, which show different characteristics. Based on our findings, the effects of disk weight on jamming behavior can be understood through a scaling analysis, which considers two factors - the weight of individual disks and the area of the confining frame. These factors influence distinct jamming behaviors for lighter and heavier disks. When the area is large compared to the weight, lighter disks jam first, while heavier disks require more compression. Conversely, when the area is small compared to the weight, the behavior is the opposite. Due to the unique characteristics of jamming through a single degree of freedom, these systems can act as unique thermal insulators or regulators, depending on the confining boundary conditions. By modifying the weight of individual disks, the jamming transition can be precisely controlled, making these systems useful for a range of applications. This research lays the foundation for further investigations into jamming transitions through deformation in various three-dimensional configurations. It is expected that the effects of weight and geometry will have similar implications for jamming behaviors in three-dimensional systems. Based on these findings, the jamming transition can be understood as a general physical phenomenon that can be controlled through a combination of material characteristics and geometric constraints. By varying these factors, jamming behaviors can be observed in all dimensions, which can be predicted through further theoretical analysis. This understanding of jamming can be applied to a wide range of natural systems where their behavior can be observed to some degree of precision. Our framework addresses the privacy concerns associated with location-based services that utilize spatial copulas by incorporating differential privacy. A key challenge in maintaining user privacy is dealing with conditionally dependent data, necessitating the application of hierarchical models. Within this context, our main contribution lies in developing a straightforward and efficient approach for maintaining the privacy of individual users' location data while preserving the dependence structure maintained through aggregate statistics. This achievement is crucial for real-world practicality, as existing solutions either sacrifice dependence or require significant computational resources. Additionally, our methodology is versatile and can be applied to various types of data, encompassing both spatial and multivariate data scenarios. A comprehensive numerical study is presented to illustrate the efficacy and practicality of our approach, focusing on real-world datasets and benchmarks. Notably, our implementation is available online as an open-source R package called priviGMM. 

In an effort to further address privacy concerns, our framework also incorporates an innovative metric to quantify the privacy loss incurred when privacy-preserving techniques are applied to spatial data. This development represents a significant advancement, as existing literature has largely focused solely on introducing privacy measures, thereby overlooking the privacy loss they entail. This gap in understanding can significant, as it impairs researchers' ability to compare the privacy loss associated with various methods, a crucial aspect during method selection. Our proposed metric enables a more comprehensive evaluation, allowing for a nuanced comparison of different techniques and their associated privacy losses. This insight is particularly useful, as it has practical implications in fields such as public health, where understanding the privacy loss of data protection methods has tangible consequences. This study is unique in that it introduces a measurable aspect of privacy, thereby bridging the divide between theoretical concepts and practical applications. As such, our work represents a significant advancement in the literature. 

Ultimately, our goal is to facilitate the adoption of our framework and the proposed privacy loss metric in statistical practice, aiming to inspire further research in this domain and encourage scientists to address the intricate privacy issues associated with complex data structures. The study of brain connectivity across different states has gained significant attention, and advancements in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have enabled researchers to explore this phenomenon. However, the prevalent single-subject analysis approach may result in compromised generalizability due to inter-site variability, and the increasing availability of multimodal data has not been fully leveraged to enhance analysis reliability. In this research, we address these two issues by developing a multivariate pattern classification framework that differentiates individual and group differences in brain networks across various states while considering inter-site effects. The proposed method is validated through experiments on two publicly available datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance in predicting individual differences and distinguishing group differences in brain networks. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential of utilizing multimodal signal combinations to improve reliability in brain connectivity analysis. The proposed method can be applied to a diverse range of problems, including classification tasks involving functional brain connectivity, state-dependent brain network identification, and understanding inter-site effects in brain connectivity datasets. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ratheejay/SSVI/tree/mlmc_paper/CMT. Additionally, the Neurosynth analysis tool can be accessed at https://neurosynth.org/, and related results are available in the paper's Supplement section. This article investigates the underlying mathematical connections between the heat flow and concentration of measure inequalities. Specifically, it explores how the heat flow can be derived from a more general principle in a unified manner. This general principle, known as the gradient estimate, can be derived using various other methods. Once established, the gradient estimate can be used to prove various concentration of measure inequalities, including a fundamental log-Sobolev inequality. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the heat flow can be derived as a consequence of the gradient estimate, incorporating both bounded and unbounded domains. Our derived heat flow formulas are in accordance with existing literature. Additionally, we provide a brief overview of the methods employed to prove the concentration of measure inequalities. Our results are particularly relevant to settings involving rough Riemannian manifolds and geometric flows.

We've proven that for a compact Riemann surface, the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class can be precisely represented as the intersection of the Brauer classes of its 1- and 2-cycles. This leads to a direct connection between the MM^2 and MM^1 groups for such surfaces, and we've shown that MM^2 is topologically invariant and cohomologically trivial. This result follows from a broader statement that relates MM^2 to the Chow group of 1-cycles with boundary, which holds true for a broader class of varieties, including those with the BBP property. This general result draws upon the surface's specific characteristics, and we've identified key conditions that would need to be met for this statement to be valid for all types of varieties. Furthermore, our work includes cohomologically trivial characteristics for the MM^2 group across a range of varieties, and this includes certain Hironaka varieties, certain projective varieties, and varieties with the BBP property. We've also provided an example of a smooth projective surface that has non-trivial MM^2 but trivial Chow group of 1-cycles. Additionally, our work includes an interpretation of the MM^2 group as the first Chow group with 1-cycles for certain types of surfaces with abelian differentials. This interpretation holds true for canonical models of such surfaces, and this result draws upon previous work by Raoul Kubicki. Finally, our work includes an analysis of the MM^2 group across a range of hyperbolic surfaces, and this includes those with a finite area, those with arbitrary area, and those with specific geometric properties. This analysis arises from connecting MM^2 to the Chow group of 1-cycles with boundary, which is itself derived from connecting MM^2 to the second symmetric product of the surface's 1-cycles. This connection arises from the work of Raoul Kubicki and myself in an earlier paper. This means that for a surface with a finite area, MM^2 can be precisely represented as the Chow group of 1-cycles with boundary. This result draws upon previous work and incorporates theoretical developments across multiple disciplines, including the theory of Teichmüller, the Schmidt subspace problem, and the Mumford-Morita-Miller theory. This study shows that any irreducible, ergodic Markov process has a unique quasi-stationary distribution that converges exponentially in $L^2$ to a steady state distribution. While this result was previously demonstrated for discrete-state Markov chains, this work generalizes it to a broader range of Markov processes, including those with continuous or semi-continuous state spaces. Additionally, the study provides a more precise estimate of the convergence rate, which can be applied to identify the mixing time of certain Markov processes, such as the $p$-chain used in random walk polling order for simulating network reliability. An important aspect of this work is that it also addresses the uniqueness of quasi-stationary distributions for continuous-state Markov processes, which was a notable omission in previous research. By building on existing results for continuous-state processes, this study provides necessary and sufficient conditions for the uniqueness of quasi-stationary distributions in continuous-state processes, which are equivalent to conditions for the uniqueness of invariant distributions in ergodic Markov processes. Finally, the study provides examples of continuous-state Markov processes with unique steady states and non-unique quasi-stationary distributions, as well as a counterexample demonstrating that the converse is not true. Furthermore, the study shows that uniqueness of quasi-stationary distributions is preserved under certain transformations of the state space and Markov process, such as continuous or semi-continuous changes in the state space and the addition of 'frozen' states. Conversely, the study provides a counterexample demonstrating that uniqueness of invariant distributions is not necessarily preserved under these transformations. The study also addresses open problems by providing a partial solution to the long-standing conjecture that unique steady states imply exponential convergence in $L^2$ for discrete-state Markov chains. While the study does not resolve this conjecture for all discrete-state chains, it provides counterexamples and alternative conditions, previously overlooked, that are both necessary and sufficient for exponential convergence in $L^2$. Notably, the study provides a new and significant condition that is more robust and easily applicable in practice. Finally, the study provides a substantial extension of the conjecture to a more robust form, involving the $p$-chain, which holds true for a significant class of random walk polling orders. The study presents a new and efficient algorithm for simulating network reliability using the $p$-chain, offering a significant improvement over previous results. Specifically, the study provides the first known estimate of the mixing time of the $p$-chain under a random walk polling order

In our analysis, we examined the responses of different search engines to queries related to "YouTube alternative." The study revealed a notable pattern: most search engines in the Western world fail to acknowledge YouTube as a possible answer. To better understand this phenomenon, we conducted an in-depth investigation into the underlying causes. Our research highlights the inherent biases present in search engine outcomes, emphasizing the significance of the initial set of returned links, known as the "long tail." Additionally, our analysis reveals how the ownership structure of search engines and platforms can influence the representation of alternatives. Furthermore, our case study identifies potential limitations of reliance on crowd-sourced evaluation, highlighting the importance of considering the intentions and perspectives of users from diverse cultural backgrounds. Ultimately, our work suggests that the "long tail" of search engine results may reflect a nostalgic reminder of the homogenous information environment of the past, where globalization was perceived as a force for cultural uniformity. Conversely, the diverse set of YouTube alternatives often goes unrecognized, demonstrating the complex interplay of globalization and cultural fragmentation in the information age. To address this, we propose the development of platforms that proactively promote cultural diversity in the information environment, actively curating and connecting users from different cultural backgrounds based on their shared interests. Such initiatives could foster greater understanding among cultural groups, while also providing easily discoverable access to the diverse range of services and applications rooted in these cultures. To this end, we present the design of a novel information system, known as Culturo, which aims to promote cultural resilience by identifying and preserving cultural heritage services and promoting cross-cultural connectivity among users. This design can serve as a model for the broader search engine community, offering a potential solution to the inherent biases present in search engine outcomes. By acknowledging the intentional design of search engine results, we can work towards creating a more inclusive information environment that bridges cultural differences and promotes cultural diversity for years to come. The $\beta$-function in theories incorporating general monodromy defects is explored, with specific cases studied including defects from non-Abelian T-duality and sine-Lee-Yang-type defects. Formulations of the $\beta$-function are developed for systems with defects and without them, allowing for comparison. The behavior of the $\beta$-function with and without defects shows notable similarities and differences. While both cases exhibit similar infrared and ultraviolet traits, the presence of a non-zero $\beta$-function without defects contrasts with the zero value with defects, generally speaking. However, specific exceptions arise, such as in the example of a free fermion model, where a non-zero $\beta$-function is found with defects, indicating that the role of the twisted sector can't be overlooked. Additionally, the findings with defects corroborate the previously established connection between the $A$-type anomaly and the $\beta$-function. A proposed extension of the Wess-Zumino-Witten term to include defects is also discussed, with support provided by non-Abelian T-duality tests. Semi-supervised inductive node classification in graph neural networks involves training models on limited labeled nodes to make predictions on unlabeled nodes. Pseudo-labeling is a technique that can enhance model training by supplementing labeled nodes with predictions from unlabeled ones. However, relying solely on model predictions can result in biased labels due to initial training errors. Despite their potential, applying pseudo-labeling to graph neural networks has limitations due to their high training costs. This has prevented widespread adoption, limiting improvements to date. We introduce a novel method called Pseudo-Label Propagation, combining expert knowledge and high-quality model predictions to create an improved dataset, reducing label dependence and training costs. This method initially removes nodes with inconsistent labels, assigns expert labels to the remaining nodes, and supplements them with refined model predictions. We evaluate Pseudo-Label Propagation on six benchmark datasets and 12 configuration variants, outperforming existing graph neural network pseudo-labeling methods and matching state-of-the-art graph neural network performance on four of the tested datasets. Notably, on the most challenging dataset, Pseudo-Label Propagation achieved 11.32% and 3.47% improvement over model-dependent pseudo-labeling and model-only baselines, respectively. In the standard treatment of optomechanics, quantum effects are typically expressed using coherent states, with the occupation number of the mechanical state being the key factor that determines the degree of quantumness. However, when this occupation number is substantial, the classical electric circuit model is more applicable, and the quasi-particle description is more effective in capturing the linearized mechanical behavior. This paper bridges the gap between the standard quantum and coherent regimes by incorporating the classical electric circuit model into the standard framework. The new description maintains the standard's advantages, including its ability to accurately model both input and output fields, input impedance, and the ability to manipulate occupation numbers. Additionally, the model provides new insights, such as the ability to use classical techniques to determine quantum properties. We demonstrate this improved description through analyses of both non-dissipative and dissipative systems, considering scenarios where occupation numbers may be substantially large. We also discuss the potential benefits and limitations of using this improved description. Ultimately, the classical electric circuit model offers more intuitive and efficient solutions, which could be particularly beneficial in designing large occupation number experiments. Furthermore, the improved description may be useful in analyzing systems where the standard quantum description is no longer effective. Such systems include those with significantly larger occupation numbers, as well as those influenced by strong non-linearity or dissipation. We anticipate that the improved description will contribute to a deeper understanding of optomechanical systems across a broader range of occupation numbers. Additionally, the improved description may also be applicable to other types of quantum systems. The asymptotic behavior of this weight function near zero is examined, showing that it exhibits a similar, yet distinct, pattern compared to the generalized Airy weight. The corresponding orthogonal polynomials associated with this weight function are studied, specifically regarding their leading coefficients, which are found to be non-zero, in contrast to the case of the generalized Airy weight. The spectral problem is further developed to establish a connection with a second linear problem, whose solution involves a super-symmetric relationship between the two relevant Jacobi matrices. The resulting zeros of the associated orthogonal polynomials are found to be confined within the same real interval for both weights, despite the notable difference in the leading coefficients. The generalized sextic Freud weight is found to be compatible with any monic Jacobi matrix with a finite number of points, thereby extending the previously established results for the generalized Airy weight, which was confined to bipolynomial type systems. The study concludes by presenting numerical examples that validate the findings on zero distribution, corroborated by the computational analysis of the corresponding orthogonal polynomials. Multivariate Gaussian processes can be utilized to model multiple processes that adhere to specific structural relationships, which are reflected in a directed acyclic graph, by confining the dependencies between distinct processes. In this context, we develop predictive models for individual processes, which incorporate the predictions from all ancestor nodes, calculated using Monte Carlo methods, to show the effectiveness of this approach. In addition, we derive an approximate message-passing algorithm to facilitate efficient computation, enabling the estimation of model parameters. This methodology is applied to the analysis of longitudinal data that contain at least one censored variable. One of these applications involves the joint modeling of event times and continuous measurements, with the event times conditioned on the measurements, and the other involves the dependence structure of multiple event times, with some conditioned on others. Our methodology is primarily demonstrated using simulations and an real-world study on kidney transplantation. Notably, our findings align with those obtained using existing methods.

Our proposed framework, called "RQCtool", utilizes recurrent quantum circuit patterns to efficiently compute the ground state properties of molecules by adapting the quantum circuit series convergence principle. It generates RQC patterns based on the molecule's graph structure, and our results show that these patterns can predict molecular properties with accuracy in small molecules, and we have also demonstrated the application of tool in studying the chemically reactive bond dissociation, a process that typically requires complex quantum circuits to compute. Additionally, we have found that the ground state properties of molecules can be computed with a relatively simple RQC pattern, and by combining this with the reactive bonds computed by more complex quantum circuits, we are able to achieve a more complete understanding of the bond dissociation process. Our study reveals that the complexity of RQC patterns scales polynomially with the number of atoms in the molecule, and we hope that "RQCtool" will serve as a valuable resource for researchers to apply quantum algorithms to large-scale molecular problems. Furthermore, we suggest that "RQCtool" can facilitate the development of more efficient quantum algorithms by identifying simpler RQC patterns that still accurately predict molecular properties. This study proposes an adaptive probabilistic data association algorithm that uses a computational efficient method to estimate a mobile agent's position in real-time, focusing on situations where direct global localization is impractical or impossible. Our approach develops a LIDAR-based mapping technique grounded in a adaptive multi-hypothetic fast slam framework, incorporating a versatile algorithm capable of generating multiple hypothetical paths to mitigate the effects of dynamic obstacles. To improve robustness, we leverage a probabilistic data association algorithm to weigh the credibility of each hypothetical path, effectively reducing noise and emphasizing the likelihood of each trajectory group. To further optimize performance, we utilize a particle filter, implementing a adaptive resampling technique to reduce computational costs. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of our proposed method in accurately localizing the mobile agent despite varying levels of noise and obstacles. Our approach achieves this with lower processing costs, specifically 8.5 milliseconds, making it suitable for real-world applications. Our solution excels in mobile robot localization, particularly in scenarios with intense dynamic obstacles and complex environments, where existing solutions fall short. Comprehensive comparisons with other prominent approaches, both classic and modern, highlight the superior performance of our proposed method in terms of localization accuracy and computational efficiency. Our approach demonstrates these benefits with minimal loss of efficiency, as evidenced by our results. Our solution is now available for others to use. In the low-energy sector, we investigate the geometric properties of the effective action, demonstrating that the Cotton tensor vanishes in the vacuum state, which indicates the presence of a conformally flat space. This discovery reveals that the Wess-Zumino term generates the Cotton tensor. Furthermore, we analyze the high-energy behavior, showing that the effective action's geometric properties are dictated by a non-zero Ricci tensor in the external space. This leads to the development of a novel geometric representation. As a result, we derive a more general expression for the effective action's geometric properties, encompassing both low- and high-energy behaviors. This study provides a geometric understanding of the nonlinear sigma model, which may also be applicable to other models such as the Skyrme model. The increasing adoption of AI-powered code review tools is revolutionizing the way programming code is reviewed, with human reviewers now able to rely on AI-assisted recommendations for identifying potential errors. However, these tools have limitations, and the quality of code reviews significantly suffers when AI and human perspectives conflict. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of multi-statement proofs, allowing us to evaluate the consistency of code changes at multiple levels, and leverage these proofs in code reviews to enhance decision-making processes. To automate the generation of these proofs, we've developed MPROVE, a novel system that combines the insights of state-of-the-art program transformers with specialized reasoning capabilities, providing accurate representations of logical proofs for use in code reviews. We've also created a new dataset, called the Multi-Statement Prover Dataset, comprising 3,500 code changes from popular open-source projects, annotated with 9,000 program-dependent logical proofs. Experimental evaluations confirm that MPROVE surpasses recent advances in program transformation by 8.3% and 8.6% in terms of precision and accuracy, respectively. Additionally, our findings on proof generation through human AI collaboration illustrate the potential for generated proof representations to serve as discussion starting points, facilitating more efficient code reviews. Specifically, AI-powered code reviewers incorporating MPROVE outperformed the state-of-the-art code review tool, DeepHound, in 7.4% and 5.9% of cases, according to our code review dataset, while also showing promise in augmenting human code reviewers. A newly developed method, PRETerminated Primal-Dual AWL (PREPD AWL), is an enhancement of the Primal-Dual AWL (AWL) interior point method created to increase solution efficiency. This enhancement employs an early termination technique that allows for inner calculations to be halted when the AWL termination criteria are nearly met, enabling significant acceleration. Mathematical proofs have been established to guarantee the method's convergence and preservation of key AWL properties, specifically feasibility, bounded iterates, and monotonicity. Furthermore, numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate that PREPD AWL consistently outperforms the original AWL method. Additionally, comparisons with other state-of-the-art methods, such as Primal-Dual YoshidaAWL and the Cfr2 method, reveal that PREPD AWL excels in terms of computational speed and overall efficiency. These results showcase the effectiveness of the early termination strategy in enhancing the performance of interior point methods. The PREPD AWL implementation is now available through the MATLAB implementation on GitHub of Primal-Dual AWL, allowing for direct evaluation of the results in the study.

When complex systems comprise several components, such as hardware and software, defining and maintaining detailed execution checks can be extremely challenging. Existing monitoring systems typically rely on specific, individual specifications, often ignoring discrepancies between different process definitions or specifications. These systems usually focus on verifying a single, designated property or query, rather than resolving conflicts among multiple specifications. In contrast, this paper introduces a more comprehensive monitoring approach, capable of resolving conflicts and reconciling differing specifications, by incorporating a centralized control mechanism that can merge and synchronize individual specification checks. By utilizing a data structure that combines execution records from multiple specifications, this monitoring system can address conflicts, reconcile specifications, and provide consistent monitoring results, even in the presence of conflicting specifications. Additionally, we demonstrate the monitoring capabilities of this system by providing examples in the context of distributed hardware systems. Furthermore, we outline open directions for specifying and monitoring complex, interactive systems. Finally, we confirm the correctness of our monitoring approach through formal verification. Experimental evaluations have been conducted to validate the monitoring system's performance and efficiency. Specifically, the evaluation involved testing it on the specifications of a TIVITRAS distributed system, while introducing various levels of concurrency. The results indicated that the monitoring system's performance remains comparable to that of individual specification checkers, even under high levels of concurrency. Furthermore, the evaluation involved analyzing its capacity to reconcile specifications with up to 50 active, concurrent processes. The source code for the monitoring system, as well as the experimental evaluation, is freely available at https://github.com/amirlevy/Reconciling-Specifications. Additionally, the TIVITRAS distributed system and its specifications are accessible at https://github.com/amirlevy/TivitrAS. In terms of future work, the integration of human interaction could potentially involve utilizing techniques similar to those applied to the interaction between specifications. Conversely, the exploration of verifying system properties could be accomplished by developing individual, dedicated specifications. Ultimately, the monitoring system and its capabilities offer versatile tools for addressing a range of complex, real-world problems in distributed hardware systems. For instance, the reconciliation of specifications could potentially be applied to other domains, such as software or biomedical systems, by adapting the used communication mechanisms. Similarly, the monitoring of execution checks could be integrated with property verification techniques, used for diagnosing issues in distributed systems. Lastly, the definition of execution mechanisms provides a foundational groundwork for exploring more advanced techniques in distributed system monitoring. This paper presents Proto-Quipper-M, a high-level, functional programming language dedicated to designing quantum circuits. Designed in collaboration with the Quipper team, Proto-Quipper-M incorporates innovative functional programming techniques to ensure the quantum system's integrity. Unlike previous quantum programming languages, Proto-Quipper-M employs a novel, functional approach to state cloning, wrapped in a pure functional framework. This novel method employs a hybrid function-circuit structure, allowing for a more concise and efficient way to specify quantum circuit arithmetic operations. Furthermore, Proto-Quipper-M's functional wrapper for state cloning automatically enforces the non-cloning rule of quantum states. Cloning can be achieved by combining hybrid functions that represent reversible measurements, accompanied by a classical register update. Researchers have developed multiple, efficient ways to create these hybrid functions, including an approach using classical simulation and another leveraging known cloning methods for specific purposes. These developments enable the efficient compilation of Proto-Quipper-M programs into standard quantum circuit descriptions. To verify the correctness of Proto-Quipper-M programs, a formal proof system has been established and formalized using the Agda proof assistant. Additionally, a set of executable Coq proofs provides additional verification support. Currently, a working implementation of the Proto-Quipper-M compiler is available, allowing quantum circuit design specifications to be translated into the OpenQASM standard. Details about Proto-Quipper-M and its compiler can be found at https://proto-quipper-m.github.io. A technical overview is presented in an arXiv paper (arXiv:2105.08303). A series of instructional videos is available on YouTube (https://www.youtube.com/ProtoQuipper-M). Additionally, the Proto-Quipper-M system is hosted on https://github.com/Proto-Quipper-M/Proto-Quipper-M. These difficulties arise from zero entries and a non-commutative mathematical structure. The ILR transformation successfully tackles these issues across both types of data. Despite this progress, the application of ILR is hindered by a non-differentiable formulation that hinders various statistical analyses. The development of an analytic framework for ILR is crucial for obtaining derivatives and conducting statistical inference. We introduce a novel approach based on the Adam optimization method, incorporating the ILR's Jacobian and a regularization technique to address the overfitting issues. The Adam-IJR method is then extended to support multiple dimensions and efficient gradient calculations. Furthermore, this approach is successfully demonstrated on data from the BRCA dataset and point process data from the Simpson dataset. The results show that using Adam-IJR leads to better Clustering and classification results compared to not using it. The code for this new method is available on our GitHub repository. This research studies the behavior of angular two-point clustering patterns in 0.15 deg x 0.15 deg fields of LoTSS galaxies at redshifts 0.01-3.02, examining whether this pattern adheres to the predictions of the ΛCDM cosmology. Specifically, the study uses 131 narrow-band LoTSS fields containing 104,174 galaxies across an area of 1913 deg^2, accounting for any biases associated with galaxy selection and photometric redshifts. The results show that galaxy clustering data over different redshift ranges is consistent with the ΛCDM model, but this finding varies depending on the specific characteristics of the galaxies, particularly their mass, which cannot be directly determined in this study. Additionally, the study considers the effects of limitations in photometric redshifts on its findings, finding some residual discrepancies that may become apparent when more precise redshifts are available. Further analysis is conducted to rule out potential systematics that could be influencing the results, confirming that the observed clustering data is largely unaffected by foreground contamination and other observational biases. The study concludes that, on a broader scale, the galaxy distribution is found to be consistent with the predictions of the ΛCDM model, exhibiting no significant differences in terms of galaxy bias and the rate of galaxy distribution at different redshifts. However, some residual discrepancies remain, and more precise data, both in terms of galaxy clustering and individual galaxy redshifts, is required to fully understand the structure of the universe. Finally, potential sources of bias are investigated, including galaxy selection and photometric redshifts, both of which are found to have an insignificant impact on the results. The study is found to be insensitive to any residual biases that may still be present, meaning that further work is required to fully understand these sources of bias. We demonstrate that there's always a singular universal protocol achieving the lowest possible rate of entropy production. This contrasts with previous findings, which showed the optimal entropy production rate isn't necessarily unique or constant. Furthermore, we prove that the optimal entropy production profile is non-monothonous, which is to say it can't be smoothly described using a single, continuous function. This threshold behavior is consistent with the notion that organisms operating near the maximum possible rate of entropy production are more resilient to changes in their environment. As an example, we show that the optimal protocol for a model system involves suddenly shifting between two different states to minimize entropy production. This abrupt transition occurs when the system is subjected to a new parameter value that allows it to switch between two different equilibrium states with distinct temperatures. This unexpected mechanism for reducing entropy production could have implications for understanding how living systems regulate their levels of entropy. This new theory for controlling entropy could be useful for optimizing processes that involve heat transfer and chemical reactions in both natural and man-made systems. As a test of this new theory, we show that it accurately predicts the optimal entropy production profile for a system involving heat transfer between a system and its surroundings. This new theory for controlling entropy production could have implications for optimizing processes that involve heat transfer and chemical reactions in both natural and man-made systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that the optimal entropy production profile can be accurately predicted using a reduced model that describes the system's behavior using a series of time-varying temperature profiles applied uniformly across the system. As the consumption of cloud-based AI services grows, so does their environmental impact, which needs to be considered during their development and deployment. Currently, measuring and comparing the environmental effects of AI models is limited by a lack of standardized evaluation methods. To enable effective assessment, we apply life cycle assessment to evaluate the environmental impacts of AI models trained using different infrastructure options, specifically our case studies on object detection and language modeling. We develop tailored assessment scenarios that consider not only the production phase of AI models but also the deployment and usage phases, while incorporating methodology transparency and uncertainty analysis. Our analysis compares the results for various models and infrastructure combinations, which can serve as a foundation for future research and development in this field. This work is hosted on GitHub at: https://github.com/cdesa/ai-lca. Additionally, we initiate the creation of an open specification for describing AI systems, which will promote standardized communication and facilitate comparative assessments of AI models. To promote collaboration, we invite interested researchers to join the effort in two main areas: developing new life cycle assessment scenarios and evaluating the environmental effects of AI services in specific application fields. The primary goal of process monitoring is to identify anomalies in business processes. Currently, most research focuses on detecting irregular cases, while prescribing corrective actions to ensure processes run smoothly. However, the practical effectiveness and validity of these prescribed actions are rarely considered. Furthermore, existing methods typically rely on artificial data and case studies to assert their validity, whereas the efficacy of these methods in real-world settings is yet to be established. To address this gap, this study introduces an evaluation framework that assesses the accuracy of prescribed decisions using real process data from event logs. Using two publicly available datasets, the study reveals that the performance of prescriptive methods is contingent upon the quality of event logs and the definitions of process models, while a well-designed interactive system can facilitate the identification and correction of anomalies. Notably, the study finds that while these methods can pinpoint cases with deviations, they may incorrectly flag cases without issues. These findings suggest that process owners should interpret these alerts critically and verify them through domain expertise, underscoring the need for further research to improve the precision of prescriptive process monitoring methods. Moreover, the study emphasizes the importance of manually reviewing and validating detected anomalies by process owners to mitigate false positives, thus enhancing the overall effectiveness of the method. Based on these findings, the study proposes a novel approach, called Collaborative Prescriptive Process Monitoring, which involves process owners in the evaluation process to assess the precision of prescribed decisions, ultimately providing insights for method improvement. This research is the first to quantify the relationship between event log quality, process model accuracy, and prescriptive method performance, setting the stage for further research. Additionally, the study introduces a new performance measure, called Prescribed Decision Accuracy, providing valuable insights for process monitoring. In our investigation, we explore the temporal evolution of opinion dynamics within a system where individuals possess one-dimensional opinions ranging from -1 to 1. Opinions are updated in accordance with a simple rule, yet give rise to intricate, recognizable patterns in the collective order. These patterns emerge from a complex interplay between opinion interactions and symmetries inherent to the system. We show that opinion clusters form due to the breaking of continuous and discrete symmetries in opinions, whereas in the case of bipolar opinions, the breakdown of discrete symmetry gives rise to these clusters. Conversely, the maintenance of continuous symmetry in opinions results in uniformly distributed opinions across the real line. Similarly, in systems where individual positions are defined on a grid, specifically in two-dimensional cases, the breakdown of discrete symmetry leads to interesting patterns, including the emergence of a chiral distribution of agents' positions. This finding sheds light on the potential social implications of such opinion dynamics, potentially influencing the formation of social groups and their geographical distribution. Lastly, we examine how these patterns in opinion dynamics and agent movement relate to each other. The process of transcription is delayed between the time gene expression starts and when mature mRNA is produced due to various factors such as mRNA processing, transcription elongation, and nucleotide synthesis. The length of the delay caused by these factors varies among different genes, suggesting the need for individual analysis rather than relying on average values. In this study, we developed models to describe the production of mRNA in length and time and used them to identify processing rates, free nucleotide pools, and transcription efficiency, which are otherwise inaccessible through experimental measurement of mRNA and protein levels. By applying maximum likelihood estimation to analyze time course data of ERN4 mRNA in Arabidopsis, we found that it takes around 2 hours for ERN4 mRNA to mature, which occurs after transcription completion, which is around 120-140 nucleotides away. The delay in ERN4 production is primarily attributed to nucleotide synthesis in the nucleoplasm and polyadenylation processing in the cytoplasm. The cytoplasmic processing appears to be the rate-limiting step in ERN4 mRNA maturation, which takes around 1.5 hours, or around 90% of the transcription time. Model prediction shows that increasing polyadenylation efficiency by a factor of 1.5 or keeping the same efficiency but shortening the free nucleotide pool by a factor of 2 would significantly decrease the delay in ERN4 mRNA maturation. In contrast, speeding up transcription by a factor of 2 would have a negligible effect on reducing the length of delay. Our model indicates that the length of delay is mainly influenced by polyadenylation efficiency, which shows an exponential decrease with a decay constant of 0.01, while transcription efficiency shows a linear decrease with a decay constant of 0.0005 for ERN4. Our analysis also shows that increasing processing rates in the cytoplasm no longer affect the delay in mRNA production when they reach a certain level, which is around 20 RNP complexes per hour for ERN4. In contrast, a rise in free nucleotide synthesis rates has a significant direct effect, as it now takes around 80 minutes less to produce ERN4 mRNA when these rates increased by a factor of 2. Our study demonstrates that individual analysis of gene length and transcription characteristics such as processing rates, free nucleotide pools, and transcription efficiency is required to accurately predict the production of mRNA in length and time. Our model indicates that speeding up transcription by a factor of 2 would have a negligible effect on reducing the length of delay

To test these predictions, the researchers used transmission spectroscopy methods in space-based data from the Kepler, K2, TESS, and HST telescopes for planets orbiting late-type stars. The study discovered that its observations aligns well with the theoretical results, specifically that planets close to their stars are underrepresented in the super-Jupiter mass range. Our previous research revealed that scalar, pseudoscalar, and axial-vector mediators leave distinct signatures in dark matter direct detection experiments. In this follow-up study, we delve into the properties of a singular, non-Standard Model particle - a dark matter candidate - in a specific set of valid parameter space. The study focuses on a type-I Higgs portal dark matter model, in which the Higgs boson acts as a portal that facilitates communication between the Standard Model and the dark sector. The study centers on the mass relationships between the mediator, dark matter, and Higgs boson. In the model, a heavy mediator with a mass comparable to or greater than the dark matter mass has a coupling constant ($\lambda$) that is typically larger than the elementary Higgs coupling ($1/g_H$), resulting in an exceptionally large spin-independent dark matter cross-section. In contrast, a light mediator with a mass smaller than the dark matter mass exhibits a reverse property, with a lower $\lambda$ requiring a darker state with a smaller coupling to the Higgs boson. The study finds that the induced, long-range mediator-mediated interaction in dark matter direct detection experiments is notably similar in the high-$m_\phi$ regime to the corresponding interaction in the "velocity-dependent" Higgs portal dark matter model. In addition, the study finds that LHC searches for the rare $h\bar{b}b$ decay can serve as a highly effective means of validating the type-I Higgs portal dark matter model. The study further finds that future dark matter direct detection experiments with optimal sensitivity may be able to exclude a substantial portion of the valid parameter space, with the type-I Higgs portal dark matter model still standing even in such a scenario. The framework's effectiveness has been validated on multiple datasets and tasks, including image classification, semantic segmentation, and medical image diagnosis, with the results consistently surpassing state-of-the-art performance across these studies. Estimating scene geometry is a fundamental visual task that requires
understanding the 3D layout of objects. While geometric estimation is more
complex and therefore perhaps less accessible as a pre-training task
compared to image classification, it may be the key to unlocking more
advanced visual capabilities. Unfortunately, conventional supervised
methods can be overly restrictive, limiting generalizability to new,
unseen settings. In an effort to overcome these constraints, researchers
have begun exploring self-supervised geometric estimation techniques.
These self-supervised methods are often founded on the core principle of
self-consistency, utilizing 2D or 3D self-similarity to establish basic
object representations. However, existing self-consistency-based
approaches to geometric estimation are primarily two and a half-dimensional,
relying on projected 2.5D poses rather than full 3D poses. In an effort to
advance this area of research, a new method, named SGE, has been developed.
SGE introduces an innovative framework for self-supervised 3D geometric
estimation, one that incorporates a comprehensive system for 3D pose
prediction. SGE achieves this through the use of an indirect, novel loss
function that leverages the relationship between a point's 3D displacement
as it moves between two poses and the corresponding change in its 2D
coordinates. This specialized loss, when combined with an efficient
network design, allows SGE to accurately predict full 3D poses at a
fraction of the cost of existing self-consistency-based approaches to
geometric estimation. Extensive experiments are presented, demonstrating
the efficacy of SGE in both 2.5D and full 3D geometric estimation tasks. Additionally, SGE's developed features prove valuable in grounding
visual common sense, as exemplified in a new task introduced. SGE's
performance is found to surpass state-of-the-art methods in both
self-supervised geometric estimation and visual common sense, as
validated in experiments. Code and pre-trained models are available for
replication. https://github.com/alex1998yu/SGE.git. SGE.git.

Through a new set of equations representing a rotating, disk-like object at the center of a rotating, dark matter halo, researchers have found an exact analytical solution that mimics the behavior of a rotating, self-gravitating disk. These new equations accurately replicate the Tully-Fisher relation, observed in many galaxies. Additionally, the models allow for analysis of density and surface density profiles, revealing how these change as a disk forms within a dark matter halo. By comparing the smooth core of a dark matter halo to the broken symmetry of a surrounding disk, researchers are exploring the potential diversity in galaxy rotation curves. Multiple core scenarios are possible, each with its own characteristic rotation curve, even without invoking non-Newtonian physics or dark energy. Conversely, the broken symmetry of a disk leads to similar rotation curves for different mass ratios, although the presence of a dark matter halo does affect the symmetry of a disk's mass distribution. These new models provide a theoretical foundation for further study into the mass distribution within galaxies, offering a unique perspective on their behavior. Individual actions, such as reducing energy consumption or adopting sustainable transportation, can help slow global climate change, but many people struggle to take these steps, primarily due to a lack of connection between their personal values and climate action.  This gap can be bridged by employing a cognitive mismatch measure, which identifies potential value discrepancies and suggests compatible alternatives, enabling people to align their values with pro-environmental behavior.  A network representation, where various actions are linked to corresponding personal values, can facilitate efficient identification of relevant variables in need of adjustment.  Two algorithms are offered to achieve this efficiently: a greedy approach and a more comprehensive, second-order algorithm.  Both techniques have been proven to reach an optimal equilibrium where suggested value modifications maximize an individual's overall value satisfaction.  Furthermore, the proposed system was tested on real data collected from the World Wildlife Fund's Climate Savings Platform, demonstrating its effectiveness in successfully aligning personal values with climate action.  Users who engaged with the system exhibited considerable improvements in value satisfaction, as well as increased their intent to take climate-action compatible actions.  A comparative analysis reveals that employees in environmental sectors tend to have dissimilar values related to climate action compared to the general population, highlighting potential value discrepancies that could be addressed through targeted value modification suggestions.  This research offers a unique perspective on personal values, showcasing their varied configurations across different industries and their influence on climate action intentions.  Ultimately, the values and actions network provides a useful framework for understanding the complex relationships between human values, climate change, and human behavior, paving the way for further research in these domains.  The presented approach has significant practical implications, enabling the development of personalized recommendation systems capable of facilitating climate action by aligning personal values with pro-environmental behavior, which could be applied to employees in environmental sectors to enhance their motivation.  Such innovative features can be incorporated into existing applications, like the Climate Savings Platform, to make them more effective at promoting environmental awareness and behavior change.  The proposed framework and methods can be adapted to identify compatible personal values for other types of actions, in addition to climate action.  The studied approach and techniques can be applied to address other types of mismatches or discrepancies, not just those related to personal values. Recent research in sentiment analysis in healthcare aims to reduce the cost and resources required for diagnosing and providing healthcare services. By reducing the need for manual data annotation through semi-supervised techniques, such as multi-task learning and domain generalization, these models can efficiently extract symptoms and provide basic diagnostic information. However, current approaches are limited by their reliance on extensive training data, which is not readily available in many developing countries. To address this issue, we introduce a new framework that leverages self-supervised domain generalization and multi-task learning for effective symptom extraction. By incorporating self-supervision to utilize unlabelled data more effectively and employing a shared knowledge representation for better shared knowledge extraction, the framework significantly improves performance compared to conventional multi-task learning methods. Extensive empirical evaluation on four datasets from diverse domains, such as consumer reviews and medical chat, showcases the framework's ability to achieve superior results with reduced reliance on annotated data. Moreover, the framework's domain generalization capabilities enable the models to successfully adapt to new domains with only a small number of target dataset examples. Notably, the framework's performance in symptom extraction exceeds current state-of-the-art approaches, both in domain-specific and domain-generalization scenarios. A key strength of this framework lies in its ability to produce natural language representations that capture key features, such as part-of-speech-based symptoms, which are highly desirable in real-world applications. The source code for this framework is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/amanbasu/Self-Supervised-DG-MTL. Empirical evaluation supports the effectiveness of this approach in reducing resource requirements for diagnostically relevant feature extraction. As such, this framework offers a viable solution for reducing the resource-intensive nature of sentiment-based healthcare applications while promoting generalizability across domains. The framework's potential to reduce the resource requirements by 75% (from 120 GB to 30 GB) also further minimizes these requirements. Autonomous driving systems powered by Recurrent Neural Networks have gained significant recognition in partially observable environments, thanks to their ability to approximate invariant policies. Although practical implementations often involve approximations such as sum-product argumentation and policy smoothing, their impact on performance is not well understood. In our study, we focus on policy smoothing and its two primary variants: epsilon-greedy and uniform sampling. By developing an analytical framework that combines theoretical analysis with empirical evaluations, we have found that policy smoothing is indeed a viable approach for achieving causal reinforcement learning. However, it may result in substantial causal losses, which are worst-case quadratic in the planning horizon. Empirical results confirm our theoretical findings, showcasing the trade-offs between causal performance and uniformity. Building on these insights, we have derived conditions under which causal reinforcement learning is possible with arbitrary causal structures, provided they satisfy a specific graphical condition. Our study offers valuable insights for designing more efficient causal reinforcement learning methods in real-world autonomous driving applications. Moreover, it highlights the need for further research in the area of causal structures in recurrent policies. As an example use case, we have applied our theory to the autonomous driving problem of staying in the lane. By analyzing the causal structure of this problem, we have found that it supports at least causal reinforcement learning with uniform sampling up to a 100-step planning horizon. Our study is the first to establish the connection between the causal structure of recurrent policies and their causal causal reinforcement learning capabilities. Our method is also compared with state-of-the-art approaches such as causal structure learning, transparent reinforcement learning, and deep causal reinforcement learning, demonstrating that it outperforms these methods in at least one use case. Our study contributes to the causal reinforcement learning literature by presenting a novel approach to solving this problem, as well as providing valuable insights into the relationship between the causal structure of recurrent policies and their causal reinforcement learning capabilities. Our method, on the other hand, is inferior to state-of-the-art approaches such as deep reinforcement learning, transparent reinforcement learning, and deep causal reinforcement learning in at least one use case. Our study extends the work on causal reinforcement learning with recurrent neural networks, which previously considered only a specific class of causal structures, by exploring its applicability to more general structures, such as the one found in the autonomous driving problem of staying in the lane. The advancement of deep neural networks has enabled exceptional results in various applications, yet their intricate architecture and high energy consumption have significant implications for deployment on portable, resource-constrained devices and medical devices where electrical interference can have adverse effects on patients.

This study proposes a novel, general-purpose classifier based on a symmetric, hierarchical structure of synaptic weights in a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network, referred to here as S-H LSTM.

In this work, we demonstrate that S-H LSTM, an essentially symmetric LSTM, can serve as a feasible approximation of traditional ANNs, thereby validating the efficacy of this neural network for classification tasks.

Subsequently, we investigate the underlying principles behind the symmetry of S-H LSTM, revealing that its properties are akin to those of a Gabor filter.

Lastly, we explore the potential of S-H LSTM in tackling binary image recognition, an area where traditional ANNs often suffer from difficulties in accessing their underlying decision-making processes due to their complex, dense connectivity structure. By leveraging the symmetry of S-H LSTM, we can easily derive the weights of its convolutional form from the weights of the original, hierarchical LSTM, thus facilitating the extraction of feature maps, local circuits, and their interactions that contribute to final classification outcomes. This unique feature of S-H LSTM enables it to offer superior performance compared to existing hardware-implementable binary neural networks, as well as improved explainability through the identification of more plausible visual features and their greater presence numbers. Moreover, the hierarchical structure of S-H LSTM allows it to operate efficiently while consuming lower power, making it a more suitable binary neural network for deployment on portable, resource-constrained devices. The efficacy of the proposed S-H LSTM has been validated through comprehensive experiments on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and deep learning benchmark QuickDraw, yielding remarkable accuracy results. Furthermore, we successfully applied the symmetry of S-H LSTM to derive a corresponding, efficient binary form of the ResNet, an otherwise complex and difficult-to-implement deep neural network, thereby significantly enhancing its performance and reducing its size. This novel binary ResNet, developed using the proposed S-H LSTM approach, can serve as a highly efficient, compact, and trainable binary neural network for a wide range of applications. Lastly, we investigated the potential of S-H LSTM as a viable solution for tackling real-world, time-dependent classification tasks, such as predicting the future, as exemplified by the task of estimating the future position based on the current and past driving records. This research investigates the behavior of a strong magnetic field on spin-polarized strange quark matter under various conditions, utilizing both the MIT bag model and a microscopically derived model based on the Nambu-Mossbaer effect. We examined how the equation of state and energy density change in response to magnetic field variations, considering different values of the bag constant, quark mass, and deformation parameter. Our findings also include calculations of the star's mass and radius, providing insights into the possible effects of a strong magnetic field on quark stars. We discovered that a powerful magnetic field can significantly alter the microstructure of spin-polarized quark matter at low temperatures, leading to changes in both its energy density and alignment. However, the changes in the energy density are largely mitigated when calculated on a per-proton basis. Nonetheless, a strong magnetic field can induce distinct quark star properties, such as greater mass and smaller radius, depending on its intensity. By contrasting our results with current observational data from pulsar masses and radii, we found that a strong magnetic field has a substantial impact on the structure of a more massive quark star, but its influence is much weaker on a less massive quark star. Ultimately, our research suggests that a strong magnetic field leaves an observable imprint on the structure of a more massive quark star, but its effect is much weaker on a less massive quark star. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that a strong magnetic field can cause a more massive quark star to have a smaller, denser core. Additionally, we noticed that as the magnetic field increases, the curvature of the quark star's interior becomes less pronounced, and in certain situations, a strong magnetic field can even cause the star's density to drop at higher depths. We also calculated the gravitational redshift and surface gravity of a quark star immersed in a strong magnetic field, and found that these effects are more pronounced in a more massive quark star. In particular, as the magnetic field grows in intensity, the surface gravity of a quark star can undergo a significant enhancement, and our findings suggest that a strong magnetic field can induce a substantial increase in the surface gravity of a more massive quark star. We hope that our results will contribute to a better understanding of the behavior of quark matter under the influence of a strong magnetic field, and look forward to comparing our findings with future observations, such as those that may be obtained from X-ray spectroscopy or the study of pulsar glitches. By harnessing the power of collaborative, distributed computation on personal devices and networks, Pando accelerates scientific breakthroughs while adhering to stringent data privacy requirements. This innovative solution enables the efficient computation of genetic analyses on personal devices and networks by dividing tasks into smaller, manageable components, which are then distributed among available resources. This approach, combined with the ability to dynamically add or remove computation resources as needed, sets Pando apart from traditional distributed computing systems. With the help of Pando, researchers can perform extensive genomic analyses using small-scale, personal device infrastructure, thereby reducing computational costs and overcoming obstacles posed by limited resources. This flexibility enables seamless integration of computation and data, as demonstrated by a 15-minute whole-genome alignment of a single human genome, which would take much longer using individual devices or traditional systems. By allowing researchers to focus on the essentials of their work, Pando frees scientists from computational constraints and data transport hurdles, thus expanding access to distributed computation and data. This work presents detailed evaluations of Pando's architecture, its benefits, and performance results. Additionally, the source code is available for review at https://github.com/Ceri-Science/Pando. This research introduces an adaptive sampling technique that accelerates the computation of eigenvalues using a direct method, achieving results comparable to the quasi-minimal polynomial approach with many fewer samples. By incorporating a detailed analysis of the eigenvalue estimation process, the method dynamically adjusts the sampling frequency based on the estimated uncertainty of each eigenvalue, thus optimizing sampling efficiency. Furthermore, the algorithm is modified to calculate eigenvalue pairs, achieving optimal sampling efficiency for approximating pairs of eigenvalues. This adaptive method is implemented in a publicly available MATLAB code and compared to other eigenvalue approximation techniques, demonstrating its adaptive and efficient nature. Two challenging problems are used to test and validate the method, and it is found to be robust in a variety of non-normal matrix types. This approach is particularly suitable for small to medium-sized matrices. All associated code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexjw98/AdaptiveEigenvalueApproximation. The code can be compiled into a static library by executing the command'mcc -T def input.m' where 'input.m' is a user-defined script that generates a test matrix, as detailed in the associated GitHub repository. We investigate properties of survivor sets resulting from finite compositions of standard beta-transformations with non-integer bases and show that they exhibit fractal structure. It's also demonstrated that sets derived from these survivors in dimensions two and above possess unique properties, particularly concerning badly approximable numbers in respective bases. These findings are further validated through various graphical illustrations. These results are trigged by the discovery of a new property for survivor sets of beta-transformations with irrational bases and a companion paper by Bruin, Clark and Nekrasov that explores survivor sets of beta-transformations with rational bases containing prime numbers. This work extends their findings for irrational bases by removing the requirement for the base to be a prime number. Additionally, our research partially matches their results for survivor sets of beta-transformations with rational bases consisting of only two different prime numbers, except for the specific case of base 5, by showing that sets derived from survivors in dimensions two and above have full Lebesgue measure. Interpreting the predictions of black-box models is a critical task in understanding machine learning outcomes.  We have introduced a novel explanation tool, Attribution Curves, which generates intuitive plots that reveal how input features influence the prediction of a black-box model.  Each curve represents the feature's impact on the prediction outcome at different feature value settings.  This approach is unique in that it offers a feature disentangled perspective, which is not limited to exploring features one by one but can be used to analyze how the model's predictions change in response to variations in multiple features simultaneously.  In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of this tool, we applied it to a bike-sharing dataset and discovered some unexpected results, which we shared in the form of an anecdotal arXiv post.  The application of Attribution Curves to the bike-sharing dataset revealed some interesting findings, such as the model's sensitivity to the day of the week and holidays, which provides valuable insights into how the model makes predictions.  The full source code of this tool is available on GitHub, and we encourage researchers to use it and modify it according to their needs.  We also used this technique to investigate the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the bike-sharing market, and our findings are presented in a separate arXiv post.  The presentation slides are also available online.  The research was supported by a grant from the National Science Foundation. To maintain user data confidentiality, current approaches rely on existing privacy-preserving strategies. Nonetheless, these strategies have considerable computational costs and limited efficiency when dealing with large datasets and complex models. Developing driver code for microcontroller units can be both lengthy and challenging. Verifying the accuracy of driver code on these small devices is even more difficult due to limited resources. To address this issue, we have created a testing framework that runs on Ubuntu-based systems, using a virtual environment with QEMU, to simulate and test driver code on microcontrollers such as the STM32. This framework incorporates a driver model, a testing model, and an interface that extract specific characteristics from the driver and testing code, allowing for evaluation through formal verification. By applying the domain-specific concepts of contract-based verification, we have confirmed the correctness of the testing framework and verified that it correctly tests the driver code. We have also used this framework to evaluate and validate real-world driver code for the STM32. To facilitate reproducibility and provide support for developers, we have made the testing framework available on GitHub at https://github.com/verifstellar/test-mcu-driver. A brief video demonstrating its functionality can be found at https://youtu.be/7pM7MfMfK7U. All software used in this research is freely accessible under the Apache-2 license at https://github.com/verifstellar/test-mcu-driver. A formal document outlining the process for testing driver code on microcontrollers can be found at https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-02476377. Additionally, the verified testing framework is documented in a formal study at https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-02476379. This paper presents an evaluation of the Timeloops application blocker, a pioneering tool addressing unmanaged system calls in languages like PHP and Python. Timeloops employs a novel checking technique, allowing for system call filtering with tracking capabilities. Our study compares Timeloops' performance to that of Scheck, a well-established application blockader, by running both tools on real-world targets and artificially created apps. Timeloops outperformed Scheck in terms of execution speed, achieving an average speedup of 30 times, and demonstrated better scalability in blocking unmanaged system calls. Furthermore, Timeloops successfully blocked all managed system calls identified in the Scheck evaluation, in addition to detecting previously unreported calls in widely used applications. Overall, our findings validate Timeloops as a more efficient and comprehensive tool for addressing unmanaged system calls, paving the way for a more secure development process. As a contribution to the security community, the evaluation methodology, tools, and data are made publicly available on our website. Additionally, the Timeloops source code is accessible on GitHub under the BSD 2-license. This research was previously presented as two papers at CPSVW'19 and CPSVW'20, with significant expansions and new findings presented here. Recent advancements in single-cell RNA sequencing technologies have generated large amounts of data, enabling the discovery of novel cellular states and their associated regulatory mechanisms through reverse engineering of biological systems. However, the data's high dimensionality poses significant classification challenges, making it difficult to accurately identify cellular states from sample expressions. Current approaches for classification tasks in single-cell RNA sequencing data have demonstrated success but are limited by the assumption that the data follows specific statistical distributions (e.g. Gaussian) or uses complex schemes that are hard to extend to new data points and categories. In contrast, our study presents a groundbreaking method that offers improved classification performance with reduced computational complexity by exploiting the data's inherent geometric structure in the sample expression space. Through thorough evaluation on various datasets and approaches, we have found that our method achieves superior performance (5-15% increased accuracy) over existing techniques in both low-dimensional and high-dimensional spaces. In our investigation of the asymmetric noisy voter model, where individuals take action based on their personal preference for similar or unique aspects, we find that the competition between two species can lead to diverse outcomes. These can include the extinction of one species, coexistence of both species, or a state where one species dominates while the other becomes extinct. Mathematically representing this scenario as a birth-death process, where species sizes fluctuate, we derive the stationary probability distribution of the population dynamics. This allows us to identify the conditions under two species coexist, and to calculate the average species sizes, as well as the disparity in their distributions, under both small and large asymmetry. Furthermore, tracing the model's dynamics, we find that the transition towards the stationary state often involves sudden size fluctuations, where one species temporarily goes extinct, allowing the other to surge forward. This rapid change can be unsettling when observing the model's progression. Additionally, when there are multiple species, where each individual bases their action on similar or unique aspects, the model's behavior becomes even more intricate. These more complex scenarios are explored both analytically and numerically, where we find that the distribution of species sizes follows a specific pattern, and, in one instance, the distribution even resembles a normal distribution, where we use the method of series expansion to derive the multi-species probability distribution. Ultimately, our findings show that the species sizes converge, on average, to a specific value, where the disparity in their distribution diminishes with increasing asymmetry. This research was inspired by and conducted in collaboration with [1].

We take advantage of the comb model to count the number of ways a simple walk can pass through a set of points in d+1 dimensions, and express this count as a well-defined formula in terms of smaller-dimensional walks. This allows us to identify a specific formula expressing the difference in walk counts between d dimensions and d+1 dimensions, and this difference turns out to relate to the number of indecomposable posets of rank k and size n in the comb model. This discovery leads to a number of new results, including specific formulas for walks in d+1 dimensions and a general formula for the difference in walk counts between two related lattices in the comb model. This general formula has the property that it is zero when the two comb models are isomorphic, and it defines a non-trivial equivalence relation on the set of all comb models. This equivalence relation turns out to have interesting properties, such as it implies that there are only two comb models whose poset of covering elements is comparable. The quality of text-to-speech systems is evaluated not only by how well they recognize speech, but also by how natural and expressive the synthesized speech sounds. Current systems use statistical models trained on large datasets, but these models are limited in their ability to capture the complex patterns of speech. A new system called MaskedSpeech has been developed that uses a more effective approach to speech recognition and synthesis. In a study, MaskedSpeech was compared to a leading state-of-the-art TTS system, and the results showed that MaskedSpeech outperformed the TTS system on all metrics, while also providing a significant time efficiency boost. The study also found that MaskedSpeech was able to synthesize speech that was more natural and expressive than the TTS system, particularly in its ability to extend it to unseen inputs such as new words, new speaking styles, and new speakers. The improvement in naturalness was measured and confirmed through various automatic and human evaluations. Furthermore, the study discovered that MaskedSpeech was able to create novel speech patterns that were not present in the training data, and that these patterns were often preferred over existing speech patterns by human listeners. The ability to create new speech patterns from scratch is a major breakthrough, and opens up new possibilities for creating customized speech for applications.
