Recent research has focused on developing methods to classify DNNs vulnerable to adversarial example attacks, specifically manipulating input data to inflict errors in classification. This work diverges from that approach by investigating whether DNNs can detect Man-in-the-Middle attacks, which involve intercepting traffic and modifying images or sounds to compromise security. Unlike traditional adversarial attacks, M-i-M attacks modify the communication channel, raising questions about whether DNNs can effectively detect these changes. To date, no study has explored this topic; in our research, we examine whether DNNs can detect M-i-M attacks on image transmission or sound playback, and whether specific defenses can prevent these attacks. Our results indicate that DNNs cannot reliably identify M-i-M attacks, nor can associated methods prevent these attacks from occurring. This study offers initial insights into this area of research, with potential applications including protecting DNN-based systems from M-i-M attacks and improving overall security. Additionally, additional analysis reveals that the primary challenge in detecting these attacks lies in accurately classifying corrupted media. This raises broader questions about DNN robustness and the potential for improved research in this field. Climate change is increasingly viewed as a global crisis, but the reliance on it as a topic for misinformation is limited. Our research reveals that climate change is frequently discussed in conspiracy theories but less often as a topic itself. These theories are disseminated mainly by individual social media users, overcoming restrictions imposed by platforms. In this study, we examined all notable English-language conspiracy theory-related posts about climate change on Twitter from 2019 to 2020. These posts were shared by users who followed fringe extremist groups, and users who were newly recruited, and often received feedback from other users. Our analysis shows that users who are active on extreme right groups consistently promote climate change conspiracy theories, and these groups use the platform to promote their own agendas. These groups utilize existing climate change conspiracy theories, and modify them to align with their own ideologies. These modified theories are then shared by newly recruited users, and often receive feedback from other users. In contrast, users who are not affiliated with these groups primarily share existing conspiracy theory content related to climate change. These findings highlight the importance of addressing the grassroots source of conspiracy theory dissemination, and indicate the need for platforms to reassess their measures aimed at combating the spread of conspiracy theories. These measures should address the network structure of conspiracy theory propagation, and take into consideration the role of user recruitment in the dissemination of this type of content. Our research also reveals the necessity of accurately categorizing conspiracy theories, and encourages the development of more effective counter-narratives that can be utilized in future interventions. Additionally, our study provides users, platforms, and policy makers with actionable insights that can be employed in the fight against the spread of conspiracy theories in the fight against climate change. These insights can be found in our recommendations for platform moderation, user interaction, and public discussion surrounding conspiracy theories. Recent dark matter experiments have employed novel targets and dual-phase dark matter detection technology to screen an expansive portion of dark matter models. Despite these efforts, no discrepancies with standard model predictions have been observed. As a result, there is an acute need to adjust the experimental strategy to boost sensitivity to a considerable array of post-standard model theories. This research proposes incorporating Grid Compensator detectors into dual-phase dark matter experiments to increase their sensitivity to an extensive set of beyond-standard model theories. By analyzing data from the Majorana Demonstration Plant, it was found that incorporating Grid Compensator detectors could enhance the experiment's capability to detect dark matter by a substantial factor. Furthermore, it was discovered that combining the analysis of both the ionization signal from electron recoil events and the gamma-ray background from natural nuclei can substantially improve the experiment's ability to detect post-standard model theories. Overall, incorporating Grid Compensator detectors into dual-phase dark matter experiments can substantially boost their sensitivity to an extensive set of beyond-standard model theories. Our research highlights the importance of taking into account the distinct contexts and priorities of different countries when advising high school students on career choices. In neuromorphic computing, the goal of on-chip learning is to adapt circuit properties in response to incoming data, eliminating the need for explicit classification. Unlike conventional learning, which relies on backpropagation, on-chip learning often requires a template or a reference model for adaptation. However, finding this template can be challenging, leading to inefficient hardware implementations. This study develops a template discovery algorithm, enabling the extraction of a suitable template on custom hardware. The proposed method integrates template discovery with on-chip learning, allowing subsequent adaptations to refine circuit properties. The technique was demonstrated using a 65-nm spiking neural network chip, where a template was discovered and used for on-chip learning from raw video data. The results show that repeated template discoveries are not necessary, and the discovered template can be used for further refinements. A potential factor contributing to the reduced luminosity observed in supermassive black holes, such as those in Sgr A* and M87*, could be the accretion of dust and solutes from surrounding stars, as proposed in a recent theoretical framework. Utilizing handwritten text recognizers in conjunction with Generative Adversical Networks allows for the improvement of degraded document images. However, handwritten text recognizers are typically designed to operate on high-quality images, making them ill-suited for use on low-quality images. To overcome this limitation, we develop a method that simultaneously improves both handwritten text recognition and image quality. This is achieved by leveraging handwritten text written by a human, allowing the system to learn what accurate handwritten text looks like. Experiments conducted on the UNIPEN handwritten text dataset reveal that our approach results in improved image quality and handwritten text recognition accuracy, with the former measured at 0.55 and the latter at 0.94, on a scale from 0 to 1. Notably, these gains are entirely attributable to the improved image quality. We refer to this method as co-training for handwritten text and images, emphasizing its reliance on two distinct inputs. Further research is necessary to fully realize the potential of this technique. The source code is freely accessible at https://github/CoTraining-Handwritten-Text-and-Images. This research focuses on utilizing Natural Language Processing (NLP) to improve text extraction from ID cards with variable formatting, which can hinder traditional OCR technology's effectiveness. An ID card's layout is comprised of fixed and dynamic components, making extraction challenging due to varying font sizes, styles, and positions. To address this issue, a multi-directional Page Oriented NLP model is proposed, designed to handle ID cards with multiple lines of text, incorporating a novel algorithm for analysis. An experimental prototype was developed to validate the model's performance, utilizing ID card images from two countries, namely India and Japan. As a key step, the model must accurately detect the ID card boundary, followed by analysis of fixed layout regions, such as the card's logo, background, and whitespace. For dynamic regions, like the card holder's name and photo, specialized detectors using convolutional neural networks were developed, along with an innovative layout character recognition model. An evaluation of this prototype demonstrated superior extraction accuracy compared to conventional OCR technology. Notably, all major fields were accurately extracted from Indian ID cards, whereas Japanese ID cards presented some extraction errors due to their complex layout. These results provide a foundation for further advancements in this area. An open-source implementation of this prototype is available at https://github.com/Research-PCG-IDCard. As a contribution to the community, the source code is accessible at https://github.com/Research-PCG-IDCard. Additionally, the 2021 ID Carde Challenge dataset was utilized for the analysis of Indian ID cards. For the analysis of Japanese ID cards, the Research Institute of Electronics, Communication and Connected Systems (RIEC) dataset was used, comprising both normal and altered format types. However, it is worth noting that the normal format type IDs do not accurately represent real-world scenarios, as most ID cards exhibit variable formatting due to the inherent nature of the dynamic region. Therefore, the proposed page-oriented NLP model was found to be more effective in comparison to the normal format type IDs. As a potential future direction, the page-oriented NLP model could be modified to differentiate between ID cards of distinct formats presented in the same batch. This is achievable by incorporating a new module that can recognize layout characters in set I, as initially proposed by Layout Character Recognition Model-1. Furthermore, the page-oriented NLP model presents another potential avenue known as Multi-Page NLP, which is capable of recognizing multiple ID cards presented in the same batch. This is feasible by modifying the multi-directional attention mechanism to target multiple card boundaries

This study examines the performance of channel estimation in massive MIMO systems using underlay cognitive radio and deep learning-based prediction. We compare the outcomes of two scenarios: one where channel estimation is carried out simultaneously by the primary and secondary user, and another where the primary user conducts channel estimation while the secondary user does so independently. We find that a deep learning-based solution, specifically an LSTM model, enhances channel estimation by approximately 104% in comparison to a conventional method in high-mobility scenarios. Furthermore, integrating LSTM with underlay cognitive radio results in a 35% improvement in comparison to a self-contained secondary user system. We demonstrate that combining the two approaches results in a more robust system, able to decrease the training symbols ratio to 20% and still surpass the performance of a self-contained secondary user system with no self-learning. In addition, we identify that incorporating self-learning and underlay cognitive features simultaneously leads to considerable gains in both scenarios. We analyze several key performance indicators, including channel estimation, covariance matrix prediction, MIMO performance, and cognitive user MIMO performance. We also investigate the effectiveness of LSTM in predicting the varying channel correlation in high-mobility scenarios, finding that a limited number of recent pilot symbols is sufficient to accurately anticipate future channel correlation. We explore several strategies for implementing underlay cognitive radio, incorporating the recent advancements in Massive MIMO, and discuss the potential of combining the technology with the LSTM-based solution. We conclude that the incorporation of cognitive radio and a deep learning-based solution, specifically an LSTM model, significantly improves the performance of a Massive MIMO system, paving the way for the widespread adoption of the technology in future wireless networks. We show that these innovations result in a more robust and efficient system, capable of delivering a 109% improvement in covariance matrix prediction, 104% in channel estimation, and 56% in MIMO performance compared to conventional methods. Overfitting is a significant challenge in training deep neural networks, particularly when the number of network parameters exceeds data points. A novel algorithm called Adaptive Regularized Neural Networks, or ARNN for short, has been developed through a novel mathematical approach to mitigate overfitting. By modifying the traditional backpropagation algorithm used for regular neural networks, ARNN's approach results in a general solution for estimating the optimal L1 and L2 regularization terms. By incorporating these estimates into the cost function, ARNN's algorithm prevents overfitting without requiring specification of regularization parameters. Furthermore, ARNN's adaptive regularization terms can also be applied to existing neural networks, providing a versatile solution. Experimental results on standard datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ARNN in preventing overfitting and achieving improved generalization performance compared to traditional regularized neural networks, with additional benefits including accelerated convergence and enhanced robustness against data noise. A theoretical analysis suggests that ARNN's adaptive regularization terms model the uncertainty inherent in the data and inhibits overfitting, with the L1 term reducing overfitting by eliminating redundant features and the L2 term limiting the magnitude of parameters. The source code for ARNN is available at https://github.com/tkfatemi/ARNN. The proposed algorithm offers a general solution for adaptive regularization that can be applied to various neural networks, with the source code provided at https://github.com/tkfatemi/ARNN. The development of graphene-based photonic structures has garnered significant interest for their potential to generate and control photonic modes in the optical domain. Recently, researchers successfully created line waves in a graphene waveguide by capitalizing on the structure's unique electromagnetic properties. However, the efficacy of this approach is hindered by graphene's inherent nonreciprocity. In this study, a novel design is presented for a graphene patch that not only enables the propagation of line waves but also ensures reciprocal and robust mode selection. By placing two identical graphene patches back-to-back on an optical waveguide, researchers can break reciprocity and confine photonic modes within the graphene patches. By adjusting the graphene coverage, the gap between the patches can be tuned to match the wavelength of the line waves, effectively trapping these modes and ensuring reciprocal propagation. Furthermore, numerical simulations demonstrate that the line wave modes remain robust against graphene imperfections. In addition, the design's versatility is showcased through two practical designs, highlighting its potential for optical signal processing applications. In one instance, the reciprocal propagation of line waves through an optical ring resonator is achieved, while in the other, the design is modified to enable the control of optical coupling between two waveguides, successfully demonstrating nonlocal optical interference. In conclusion, the proposed graphene patch design presents an innovative approach for controlling photonic modes in the optical domain, offering a promising platform for photonic device applications. In particular, the concept holds potential for extending existing photonic device designs into the optical regime, potentially enabling the development of novel photonic devices. Furthermore, the design presents a unique example of an emergent photonic property arising from graphene's unique electronic properties, providing a valuable case study for the design of photonic structures. In addition, the study's findings are anticipated to inspire new ideas at the intersection of graphene and photonic design. In this regard, the proposed design serves as a landmark, marking the transition from traditional photonic design to the optical domain, and its innovative approach may find new applications in the near future. In conclusion, the proposed design presents an exciting new development in the field of photonic design, and its practical implementations hold promising possibilities. In particular, the design holds potential for the creation of novel photonic devices, and its successful realization may pave the way for future innovations in the optical domain. We introduce a new family of estimators that achieve optimal bias reduction while also accounting for the smoothness of the underlying function. Our approach incorporates the logarithmic bias reduction of Sebastien and van Havere into a composite object, leveraging the smooth nature of spectral functions. We develop a variational smoothness estimator, analogous to the one proposed by Hall and Turlach, using least-squares minimization. This new estimator inherits smoothness properties and is consistently estimated, with its optimality extended to spectral estimators. Our approach surpasses previous results on bias reduction, particularly in terms of optimality for certain estimators. Effective processing of signal inputs is crucial in numerous machine learning tasks, but the precise mathematical representation of these signals is often unclear. As a result, machine learning models often employ general functional representations that can be inefficient for signals with low dimensionalities. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel method by representing inputs as functions defined on specific, high-dimensional, finite graphs. By generalizing the graph structure and assigning coordinates to graph nodes, we can project these graphs into Euclidean spaces while maintaining the original function's properties. This scheme enables the learning of meaningful coordinate systems that efficiently represent signals in these spaces, thus facilitating generalization. To optimize this learning process, we propose a new graph neural network model that can be trained end-to-end. We evaluate our method on multiple synthetic and real-world data sets and demonstrate its ability to outperform conventional representations. Additionally, we showcase the effectiveness of our method on two challenging image inversion tasks. To further illustrate the potential of our representation, we use it to improve semantic segmentation in image processing. Experimental results reveal that the graph representation and associated learning process result in superior performance compared to conventional approaches. Conversely, machine learning models excel at identifying patterns in data but lack a deeper understanding of the problems they solve. If we could combine the strengths of these approaches, we might be able to use data to discover new causal relationships and improve expert models. Although this is the general idea behind causal discovery, there are two significant challenges: the need for the model to account for the changing causes and effects of a target variable over time, and the requirement that it incorporate domain expert knowledge to ensure accuracy. In response to these challenges, we propose the semi-generative model, a hybrid of probabilistic graphical models and recurrent neural networks that can learn causal relationships from data while incorporating domain expert insights. Finally, we employ multi-objective optimization to balance competing goals, such as incorporating more expert knowledge and using data to inform the model. Our key finding is that certain critical points of the loss function are situated on a parallel to the model's latent space manifold, an observation that motivates the development of accelerated training methods. Furthermore, we identify a connection between latent spaces and distance metrics, enabling us to introduce new distance metrics that improve the separation of classes. Our proposals are substantiated through empirical analysis in the context of a CIFAR10 image classification problem. Deep neural networks are inherently opaque, which poses a major challenge when attempting to gain insight into their decision-making processes. A crucial aspect in addressing this issue involves assigning meaningful interpretations to each network layer based on its input. We propose a novel approach called layerwise relevance propagation (LRP), which formally formalizes the concept of layer interpretation and establishes a framework for its calculation. This framework enables the calculation of relevance values for any network layer, and by doing so, we prove its applicability to a broad range of network architectures, including those with shared parameters, like convolutional neural networks, as well as conventional fully connected networks. Through comprehensive testing using various benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in producing consistent results that align with established feature extraction principles. This finding leads to two distinct cases: when the tunneling time allows for a full non-intersecting path, or when an initial deviation from the standard path results in a new, non-intersecting trajectory with a longer distance. Specifically, the ring's properties can be fully captured using the parameters of its ideals $I \subset M_n(K)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the parameter space of $M_n(K)$'s ideals is a free topological space, thereby providing a novel characterization of this space. Additionally, we show that the characteristic property of $M_n(K)$'s ideals holds for any ring that satisfies the Bergman theorem. Lastly, we explore the analogous problem for the ring of upper triangular matrices over a countable field. If the field is finite, it meets the given characterization, but if it's countably infinite, it fails. For the field of real numbers, the characterization also fails. Finally, we prove that the ring of $2 \times 2$ matrices over the real numbers has a rich topological structure that cannot be captured using its ideals' parameter space. The proliferation of social media has led to a surge in online posts, each with their own stories comprising multiple events in chronological order. While machine learning has made progress in classifying posts based on their content, the narrative structure that underpins them is largely unexplored. Yet, grasping the sequence of events in posts could facilitate more effective argumentation by allowing users to pinpoint specific occurrences and link them to supporting evidence. In this study, we introduce the first approach to modeling the narrative structure of social media posts. We develop a new task, FPN, which entails identifying the chronological order of events from distinct posts. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that there are limited labeled datasets available, which hinders the performance of narrative structure models. To address this issue, we create a small dataset of annotated posts based on human annotations. In experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses alternative strategies and achieves better results when combined with content-based models. Additionally, we showcase the potential applications of our model, which results in more effective argumentation, as demonstrated in an evaluation involving both human assessors and to whom it may concern. This research introduces a sophisticated event detection system that incorporates flexible spatio-temporal analysis to identify incidents from diverse data sources like social media and sensors with varying spatial precision. It utilizes a hierarchical approach, comprising a temporal fragmentation module that fragments time intervals and a spatial partitioning module that adapts to different spatial resolutions. A novel fusion algorithm then combines fragmented time and spatial elements with incident characteristics to generate distinctive event prototypes. Finally, a discriminative event classification module leverages these prototypes and geographical locations to classify areas using a probabilistic model. We evaluate the effectiveness of our system through comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets, demonstrating its capability to handle varying spatial resolutions and data source biases. Moreover, our method achieves high accuracy and outperforms competing methods, showcasing its superiority in incident classification. The proposed system can potentially streamline incident response and resolution processes. This work has been made available on GitHub at: https://github.com/sivanav/Adaptive-Spatio-Temporal-Event-Detection.

This framework's effectiveness is proven through several tests on standard datasets, which show its ability to withstand sophisticated attacks while maintaining high accuracy. Furthermore, this framework provides secure predictions in scenarios with uncertain or manipulated input data. This robustness is achieved through the regularization term of the model, which also enables the detection of hostile samples with notable accuracy. Ultimately, this framework offers a solid foundation for developing secure deep neural networks that are resilient to various attacks and data manipulations. Experimental results validate the framework's robustness and the associated code is available on GitHub at the given link. We develop a new amplitude model, derived from a Hamiltonian representation, in the context of the exact S-matrix formulation of quantum field theory. This model, at the level of individual interactions, adheres to conserved quantities and crossing symmetry, but its overall structure differs from the standard parquet amplitude in a manner that has non-trivial consequences. Building on the exact coefficients of the spin-chain conformal field theory, we compute the coefficients of the new amplitude model and demonstrate that it contributes additional, small-scale effects not present in the standard parquet amplitude. These effects are proportional to the ratio of the ultraviolet cutoff to the infrared mass, present in the holomorphic dispersion relations, which allows them to be negligible in the standard decoupling limit of the S-matrix. However, the difference between the two amplitudes becomes relevant at finite infrared scales, influencing the structure of the parquet amplitude and, by extension, the Hamiltonian representation. Ultimately, the structure of the new amplitude model sheds light on the underlying Hamiltonian representation of quantum field theories based on integrable spin-chain conformal field theories. Additionally, the model we have proposed may serve as a more suitable candidate for theories such as ${\cal N}=4$ SYM, given its adherence to gauge symmetry. We further apply our formalism to the discrete holomorphic sector of $A_{N-1}$ coset minimally supersymmetric conformal field theory, deriving the parquet amplitude for this specific model in the decoupling limit, as well as its modification arising from the exact coefficients of the spin-chain S-matrix. This is contrasted with the standard approach of replacing the S-matrix with the 1d CFT Lagrangian. Lasting consequences of this discrepancy are also discussed. We investigated the many-body corrections within the time-dependent density-matrix perturbation theory, incorporating higher-order corrections beyond the adiabatic approximation in monolayer TiSe2. This involved analyzing the photoemission spectroscopy and dynamic structure factor. Our findings suggest that exciton condensation occurs in monolayer TiSe2 at finite momentum within the charge-density-wave state, contrary to earlier expectations. This research was conducted using in-house software, with all calculations performed at the University of Alberta's Theoretical Physics and Computational Physics groups. Our analysis confirms that exciton condensation does not stabilize a static insulating state but rather gives rise to a non-equilibrium state characterized by slow dynamics, where exciton phonon coupling plays a crucial role. Furthermore, we observed that phonon energy resides within the same scale as the exciton energy as predicted by the Euler-Heisenberg approximation. This led us to the realization that excitons, phonons, and electrons form a interconnected system with slow and fast components. The understanding of this interplay could be generalized to other materials like WTe2, which we have found exhibits similar behavior. Emergency call centers around the world rely on text-based incident reporting systems that process a substantial number of requests from the public. These systems, which dispatchers use to collect information from callers, involve a series of structured questions tailored to different types of incidents. A key challenge in enhancing the efficiency of these systems lies in identifying questions that vary depending on the incident and the information required to effectively respond. Previous studies on incident classification have focused on categorizing calls based on caller intent, but neglected to consider the impact of classification on customizing query sets. In our research, we analyzed over 88,000 real-world incidents from three countries and discovered that incident type was closely linked to both the purpose of the report and the information needed by dispatchers. We also found that while some incidents involve a standard set of questions, others are customized due to factors like location or caller provided information. In contrast to traditional approaches that rely on fixed incident categories, we propose a more dynamic model called Adaptive Incident Categorization. In this model, incident categories are constantly updated based on data from a knowledge base, user reports, and expert insights. Additionally, we investigated the characteristics of questions related to incident type and identified topics that are unique to specific incidents and others that are shared across multiple incidents. In an effort to reduce the manual work involved in creating custom incident categories, we developed AdIC and conducted an experiment that involved human evaluation. The results showed that AdIC's accuracy was comparable to that of human assessors, even when they were familiar with the data, and significantly better than traditional approaches, which were only accurate in 33% of cases. In another evaluation, we found that AdIC produced responses in under 200 milliseconds, while human assessors took around 1-2 seconds. In conclusion, AdIC offers a novel and effective approach to incident categorization that takes into account the dynamic nature of incident questions, relies on high-level concepts, and draws upon existing knowledge sources. Further research is needed to investigate the impact of human preferences on incident categorization and to develop more precise algorithms for matching incident requirements. In terms of practical applications, AdIC could be used to automatically classify incidents, customize query sets, identify missing information, and identify areas where questions can be consolidated or removed. Research into superconductivity's broader implications on materials' electronic properties has been minimal. A initial study found that the superconducting electronic band structure's modifications are reflected in the changes of the electronic density of states. This conclusion was verified using a 2D superconducting material, Na$_{0.75}$Co$_{0.75}$Mo$_{0.75}$(OH)$_{2}$. This material has a large magnetic sensitivity that can be observed by analyzing the changes in its Fermi surface after it becomes superconducting. Using Na$_{0.75}$Co$_{0.75}$Mo$_{0.75}$(OH)$_{2}$'s known band structure, the density functional perturbation theory was used to calculate both the total density of states and the magnetic susceptibility in both normal- and superconducting states. These calculations confirmed that the changes in the density of states are directly related to the modifications in the electronic band structure. Additionally, this study found that the magnetic susceptibility in the superconducting state is determined by the Fermi surface's connectivity, while the total density of states is determined by the area of the Fermi surface. Both conditions were satisfied in Na$_{0.75}$Co$_{0.75}$Mo$_{0.75}$(OH)$_{2}$. Experimental measurements of the material's magnetic susceptibility as a function of temperature supported these predictions, verifying that the superconducting electronic band structure's modifications are reflected in the changes of the electronic density of states. Furthermore, this study found that the superconducting electronic band structure's modifications are unique to the materials being studied and are not influenced by the London penetration depth. Ultimately, this research demonstrated the value of combining theoretical and experimental methods to understand the electronic properties of materials. Traditional minimax active learning algorithms focus on generating challenging, semi-labeled data by selecting samples that create maximum confusion between classes. However, these methods rely on well-designed query functions and assume that labeled samples are of high quality, which is not always the case. In response, we develop an active learning algorithm with semi-supervised and uncertainty- and diversity-aware guidance. The algorithm optimizes entropy-based query functions simultaneously according to label quality and utility, ensuring that they are robust to label noise and utility maximization. By achieving a balance between label quality and utility in semi-labeled data, our method effectively addresses label noise issues and biases, leading to more reliable label feedback. Furthermore, we investigate modifications to traditional minimax active learning algorithms that mitigate label noise and utility biases. Our methods are evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets and demonstrate improved performance compared to state-of-the-art algorithms. Notably, we find that our entropy-based query functions are more diverse and utility-rich, and our semi-supervised approach is more resilient to label noise than supervised training. This letter outlines a novel approach using real-time data from the B-factory at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center to establish the tau mass by incorporating analytical QCD results. This method utilizes radiative corrections in e+e- collisions to provide the desired tau mass output. A growing concern in machine learning research is out-of-distribution detection, with the goal of identifying instances that do not fit in the training data. While significant progress has been made in developing model-based and pseudo-labeling approaches for out-of-distribution detection, these methods are largely unsupervised and rely on posterior densities or nearest neighbor classifications, which have shown limited success in challenging scenarios. In this study, we introduce a new, unsupervised method for out-of-distribution detection based on Bayesian neural networks and pseudo-labeling. By incorporating a set of anchor data points and generating synthetic labels for them, our method aims to establish a robust in-distribution dataset. Given that generating posterior densities is computationally expensive, we instead utilize a approximation based on noise functions, which provides precise estimates without the need for additional computations. When evaluated on the challenging miniImageNet dataset, our method outperformed existing approaches, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness in out-of-distribution detection. Furthermore, our method exhibited favorable performance when applied to IncFwD, a synthetic in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution dataset generated using image transformations. We believe our method's success can be attributed to its ability to effectively utilize posterior densities and pseudo-labels, which provides a more robust representation of in-distribution data, resulting in improved accuracy and robustness in out-of-distribution detection. This approach, trained solely on pose-estimated images, is able to generate precise 3D maps without labels. In this study, a novel extension to MemoNav is presented, which integrates top-down aerial views to create a unified understanding of a building's layout. This new model, called AeroMemo, combines both structural and geographical connectivity, and is capable of generating detailed 3D maps from a variety of perspectives. Experiments have shown that AeroMemo outperforms both MemoNav and state-of-the-art self-supervised methods in navigating around corners and localizing places within a building. Using this graph, a new method, called LAGNav, is presented, which can provide navigation efficiency up to 44% more than state-of-the-art self-supervised methods. In this study, we explore different modes of 5G NR/6 GHz coexistence and propose novel sharing patterns, such as "uplink only" and "downlink only" access, to increase overall system throughput. We also create a tool to help system planners determine the optimal sharing configuration by automatically selecting the best coexistence options. Our results show that the "uplink only" sharing mode consistently provides the highest system throughput in various scenarios and outperforms other possible configurations. Additionally, we use this tool to investigate 6 GHz spectrum sharing in different scenarios, such as urban and indoor settings, and find that the "uplink only" sharing mode can increase the overall system throughput by up to 300% in such environments. We also found that dynamic spectrum sharing among different 6 GHz frequency bands can increase the overall system throughput by up to 50% when combined with "uplink only" sharing mode. This review examines how spin-orbit coupling impacts the superconducting properties of phosphorus-based materials, including their pairing mechanism, superconducting energy gaps, and stabilization of topological defects through a combination of analytical and numerical methods. This understanding of spin-orbit coupling's influence on superconductivity in phosphorus materials provides a basis for investigating the materials' topological properties through experimental measurements of local density of states and scanning tunneling spectroscopy. The SEM-TAB-FACTS shared task was an ongoing effort to develop systems for extracting data from scientific articles. Combining four successful tasks from previous years, it was presented at two conferences with modified evaluation criteria and attracted a significant level of participation. There were over 50 registered teams, with 46 submitting results for the abstract role, 45 for the full paper role, 44 for the relation extraction task, and 40 for the classification task. In this study, we evaluate the effectiveness of each team, summarize their techniques where possible, and provide further analysis of the results. Additionally, we feature three selected winning teams and provide context for the emerging trends in the field. The shared task's data, software, and evaluation resources are available at semtabfacts.org.

Alongside this, we'll demonstrate how the principles of Quantum Mechanics can be applied to both real and complex function spaces. Furthermore, we'll compare our approach with the existing axiomatic formulation of Quantum Mechanics, initially established by John von Neumann. Additionally, we'll explore the implications of our findings, especially the possibility of real solutions, on the fundamental aspects of Quantum Mechanics. Our investigation is motivated, in part, by the notion that the inherent complexity of Quantum Mechanics may be an inherent property of the underlying theory. We'll examine this idea by analyzing the formal structure of Quantum Mechanics, effectively deriving the conditions set forth by von Neumann, and revealing any inherent limitations of the real number framework in the process. Our analysis suggests that the real number framework is insufficient to fully capture the behavior of Quantum Mechanics. We propose that the inherent complexity of Quantum Mechanics is an inherent characteristic, much like how complex numbers are inherently required in the theory. We'll also explore the potential connections between this characteristic and the concept of categorification commonly used in high energy physics. For the case where the aquifer's boundary towards lower levels is sealed and the boundary towards higher levels has a constant head, the solution to the flow equation can be found by converting the equation into a linear differential equation through a transformation that incorporates the conductivity's vertical variation. Once the flow equation is solved, the cumulative flow rate and average fluid velocity in the aquifer can be determined, leading to the derivation of these parameters, which are then expressed in terms of the conductivity's vertical variation and dimensionless parameters. Ultimately, the solution indicates that these properties are independent of time, but rather depend on the conductivity's distribution and geometric characteristics of the aquifer. In the event that the conductivity is constant, the solutions reduce to well-established formulas. We introduce a concept for a new type of tree-based model called Indecision Trees that can handle partial observations and provide a way to represent inference as a series of questions about the inference process's current state. By doing so, we are able to derive a specific algorithm for a structured form of Indecision Trees that can learn to efficiently calculate marginal distributions of key variables. This approach is similar to existing methods such as structured SVMs, but uses tree structures instead, which allows it to reach the same level of accuracy while being at least on par in terms of efficiency. Furthermore, we show that Indecision Trees can also be used for solving partial optimization problems in a suprising number of cases, and provide specific examples for the validation of our model. Overall, the goal of this work is to introduce a new method for solving complex problems in a more efficient and effective way. The proliferation of IoT data and digital assets has led to an exponential growth in stored time series data, prompting the development of more efficient time series similarity search techniques. Recently, the introduction of pruning techniques has enabled sub-linear time search performance, but these techniques are largely limited to single predicate searches. Our study introduces a concept called early abandoning to optimize prune-and-rearrange-based techniques, allowing search termination with multiple predicates. By analyzing the statistical behavior of time series data, we derived two probabilistic thresholds for predicting search results and introduced a statistical prune depth predictor to facilitate premature termination. Experimental results on three real-world datasets showcase a significant reduction in computation time, averaging 2.3 to 9.9 times faster than the original prune-and-rearrange approach, with minimal 0.04 to 0.16 percentage points more false drops. Our proposed approach also offers efficient memory usage, requiring only 2 to 4 bytes per time series, a minimal overhead. Our findings suggest that early abandoning is a viable strategy for time series similarity search in various applications, including predictive analytics, data mining, and analytics services. This study examines the effectiveness of giving feedback to programming students, particularly when the feedback is vague or precise. We looked at three distinct feedback scenarios: providing no feedback at all, providing negative feedback, and providing positive feedback. To compare the outcomes under these feedback scenarios, we conducted an experiment involving 100 students who worked on a program written in Java as part of a classroom setting. We tracked various metrics, including the code students wrote and reviewed, and a final programming evaluation by an instructor, and found that the precise feedback group outperformed the other groups in code metrics and actual coding quality, but not in the instructor's evaluation, likely due to the precision feedback sometimes contain errors. We found that the vague feedback group tended to produce similar results to the no feedback group in code metrics, but the instructor's evaluation revealed the students in this group performed poorly. Interestingly, the negative feedback group performed similarly to the precise feedback group in code metrics and the instructor's evaluation. We further investigated how these findings relate to the concept of the Pygmalion effect, which suggests that high expectations of students can lead to better outcomes. Our results suggest that the impact of feedback is more nuanced than previously thought, and that the type of feedback provided affects student performance more so than the expectations of the instructor providing the feedback. We verified this lack of correlation between instructor expectations and student outcomes through statistical analysis. To facilitate the replication of our study, we provide the code and data used in this research on our website. Additionally, as the field of programming feedback is relatively new, we created a set of guidelines and best practices for conducting similar studies in this field, and encourage researchers to use the code and data from our study as a benchmark for future evaluation. This approach is similar to how other fields, such as data visualization, have established established best practices, and can help the programming feedback community share knowledge and advance the field. Interpretable machine learning techniques are crucial for understanding complex computer vision models. While symbolic models are valuable for gaining insight into decision-making processes, they are often difficult to apply to image classification tasks that require extensive computational resources due to the complexity of visual data representations. In response, researchers have developed new methods, such as deep learning-based symbolic regression, that can create more efficient symbolic models by leveraging pre-trained neural network features. However, these innovations are hindered by significant performance limitations, forcing them to compromise on accuracy, intersection, and interpretation. In contrast, we present a novel framework that tackles these challenges by generating simple, accurate symbolic models from visual abstraction features. The method employs a hierarchical graph representation that reduces complexity, then utilizes machine learning and constraint satisfaction to derive logical expressions from this structure. The results show that this approach surpasses state-of-the-art models, delivering improved performance, precision, and interpretability on baseline datasets, along with enhanced user experiences. Over-smoothing in Graph Convolutional Networks is a significant concern that restricts the network's ability to capture complex connections. Current approaches aim to prevent this over-smoothing by limiting the number of relational layers, while neglecting the underlying factors contributing to over-smoothing. Without addressing these factors, it's challenging to develop effective algorithms to mitigate over-smoothing. This paper contributes two key findings. Firstly, a mathematical proof is provided that explains how local smoothening contributes to over-smoothing. Secondly, a model called Node Feature Displacement (NFD) is proposed to quantify the effects of underlying factors contributing to over-smoothing. Through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, the study finds that features, noise, and network structures substantially influence over-smoothing, and reveals novel insights into over-smoothing not previously addressed in current literature. The NFD model can serve as a future research direction to develop algorithms to mitigate over-smoothing. Additionally, the source code is available at https://github.com/indigojoe/NFD. Research into crystalline materials grown on graphene substrates has been enhanced by the discovery of multiple growth modes influenced by the unique properties of graphene. It's discovered that the epitaxial relationship between ZnO and a specific configuration of carbon atoms on the graphene surface influences the material's physical properties. Various epitaxial domains of ZnO are found to form at different growth temperatures, and their formation is facilitated by defects in the carbon substrate. An X-ray diffraction technique reveals that the material's domain structure can be determined by analyzing patterns of diffraction. By studying the material's physical properties, it's possible to control the configuration of carbon atoms on the graphene surface, making it possible to create materials with desired properties. The unique properties of graphene provide opportunities for creating new materials and controlling their configuration. In this research, a precise control over the material's physical properties is achieved by varying the growth temperature, resulting in a unique structure of crystalline rods. This research offers a revised estimate for determining the number of shared random trends among multiple time series. Initially, this estimate was created by Johansen and Nielsen (2019) as a test statistic in a context where the series follow vector autoregressions with stable coefficients, but our work refines it to be an efficient estimator that remains accurate even under significant deviations from typical assumptions. Specifically, in cases where data follows t-distributions with 4.5 or lower degrees of freedom, the new estimator remains consistent with the true number of common random trends, provided the sample size is large enough (n ≥ 140). Furthermore, both the original test statistic and our new estimator demonstrate similar behavior in terms of variance, but our work also shows that these estimates are justifiable even in scenarios where data follows truly non-stationary processes. In practical applications, these estimates are simple to calculate and perform well in conjunction with various other statistical measures. To support our findings, extensive numerical analyses and visualizations have been included in this study. Furthermore, we establish that weakly natural transformations provide an equivalent condition for adjoint functors with certain limitations, and these results are applicable in non-elementary contexts as well. Notably, our work does not rely on the law of excluded middle. We also discuss the implications of our findings for the concepts of representable objects and sections in a functorial context. In the course of our investigation, we prove that a functor is representable if and only if it has a section as a right adjoint, and identify an example of a functor that is not representable but has a right adjoint for any given object. Additionally, we find that the category of presheaves on a presite does not have a representable object, and explain why a proposed alternative by John Baez does not provide the desired result. We also discuss the similarities between our work and the concepts of'small' and 'large' in the context of functors. We conclude by exploring extensions of our findings to the context of 2-categories and weakly natural transformations, and briefly discuss in what manner these concepts may not fully generalize to the context of weakly natural transformations in 2-categories that are not homotopy equivalent to a 2-groupoid. We discuss this result in the context of weakly naturally trivializable 2-functors and the possibility of them serving as a candidate for a 'weak 2-Nat duality'. We demonstrate that certain higher-order cross-sectional moments of stock returns are directly linked to the corresponding moments of asset returns. Specifically, the first four cross-sectional moments are directly connected, whereas higher-order relationships become indirect. This study leverages a generalized version of the Black-Scholes model to provide explicit expressions linking cross-sectional moments to asset moments, thereby shedding light on the underlying mechanisms. Additionally, we show that common techniques used to measure cross-sectional moment dispersion, such as kernel smoothing and rank-based methods, necessarily produce indirect relationships to asset moments. Only methods employing symmetric functions can measure cross-sectional moments that directly reflect asset moments. Furthermore, applications of our framework to CRSP stocks from 1994 to 2015 reveal that the first four moments are directly connected, but higher-order moments of asset returns are absent in asset returns, whereas they are present in asset distributions. Finally, our results imply that widely observed non-Gaussian behavior in cross-sectional moments is largely a consequence of indirect relationships to asset moments, rather than a direct property of asset returns. However, asset returns may exhibit non-Gaussian characteristics in terms of higher-order moments. Conversely, the presence of non-Gaussian characteristics in asset returns does not necessarily translate to non-Gaussian characteristics in cross-sectional moments. The novel insights provided by our framework are relevant to theories seeking to explain non-Gaussian behavior in asset returns and are used to interpret the observed non-Gaussian characteristics in cross-sectional moment distributions. Detecting cardiac diseases such as myocardial ischemia relies heavily on accurate heart rate variability analysis. However, this can be challenging in noisy environments, preventing reliable detection results. Recent advances in Deep Learning have significantly improved the performance of various signal processing tasks. Nevertheless, their effectiveness is hindered due to the limitations of available datasets, preventing generalization to new, unseen data. In this research, a novel, Deep Learning-based method is introduced, utilizing data enhancement techniques to create multiple variations of limited-dataset signals, thereby expanding the available training dataset. In turn, this enables the model to achieve better performance and higher generalization capabilities. The proposed method was evaluated using three distinct datasets, demonstrating notable improvements over existing approaches, with an average accuracy gain of 11.4% for F1-score and 13.3% for geometric similarity, when compared to conventional techniques. Furthermore, this method achieved a high overall accuracy of 94.8% in detecting myocardi ischemia and 90.6% in identifying normal or abnormal heart rhythms. As a result, the proposed method offers superior performance and increased generalizability, making it an improved solution for cardiac disease detection and rhythm classification, especially in noisy environments. Additionally, its ability to efficiently use available data enables it to achieve better results with smaller datasets, thereby reducing the need for extensive data collection. The $n\rightarrow n\pm1$ electric dipole transitions in linear-regulated heavy-ion fusion states have been theoretically studied. Employing non-relativistic coupled-electron model for $^{16}$O$_{\pm1}$ $^{40}$Ca$_{\pm1}$ and $^{48}$Ca$_{\pm1}$ $^{60}$Ni$_{\pm1}$ excitations, the analysis separates the transition processes into three parts: a primary contribution involving $\alpha$-particle movements, a core-contribution involving M1 transitions, and less significant tail-effects originating from the nuclear PPE. Calculations show that while the core-contribution dominates, the PPE-affected part significantly lowers the primary amplitude by approximately 0.3-0.4, with the ratio of total amplitudes for $n\rightarrow n+1$ and $n\rightarrow n-1$ transitions being around 1.2-1.3. Furthermore, the studies on $^{16}$O$_{\pm1}$ $^{40}$Ca$_{\pm1}$ and $^{48}$Ca$_{\pm1}$ $^{60}$Ni$_{\pm1}$ linearly coupled heavy-ion states support the assumption that the total electric dipole transition amplitude can be approximated as the sum of amplitudes for $n\rightarrow n\pm1$ transitions, with the least significant part (tail-contribution) influencing the total amplitude being proportional to $(n^2-m^2)$, where $n$ and $m$ are the initial and final $n$-shell numbers, respectively. This research paper investigates twists in actions of a finite group on a torus. To accomplish this, it develops the equivariant cohomology ring for the torus using the Hochschild-Maschke theory, drawing from 'equivariant algebra' principles. By establishing this framework, the paper gains access to molecular formulas for twists, as well as other results, ultimately connecting them to the study of group actions on surfaces, as seen in the study of wall crossing phenomena in Fano polynomial equations. To facilitate this connection, the paper presents several results regarding the action of the group on the 1-forms of the torus, including an explicit description of the equivariant cohomology ring up to a certain degree, as well as a determination of the group's action on the higher-degree components. Additionally, the paper introduces 'equivariant twists' and demonstrates that equivariant twists correspond to 'equivariant shifts' in Fano polynomial equations. Finally, the paper provides formulas for the number of equivariant twists of a specified order and outlines a strategy for determining the orbits of the group action on the torus, as well as provides specific examples to illustrate these concepts and results. Specifically, it examines the actions of the cyclic group of order two and the additive group of order three on the torus, presenting corresponding molecular formulas for twists in these scenarios. Overall, the research offers a valuable general framework for the study of twists in group actions on the torus, as well as a wealth of useful results and examples in this area. Despite the significance of this area of research, only a single reference is cited in this paper - further investigation could yield many valuable findings and contributions. Based on this premise, several potential research directions and areas for further investigation are outlined at the conclusion of the paper. Specifically, it suggests the need for additional study in the following areas: confirming that the equivariant cohomology ring constructed in the paper is isomorphic to the homotopy equivariant cohomology ring, examining the properties of 'equivariant atomic twists', investigating the relationship between 'equivariant twists' and 'equivariant shifts', generalizing the results of the paper to actions of groups on surfaces, and applying the principles of the paper to the study of group actions on surfaces, as well as perhaps other mathematical objects. Overall, the research presented in the paper offers a valuable contribution to the field of research in this area, as well as a wealth of useful results and useful insights that could be applied to a variety of research directions in algebraic topology

Creating an inclusive academic environment is crucial, encompassing a comprehensive approach that spans recruiting practices, curriculum design, and overall cultural transformation. Developing a sensitive and inclusive culture is an ongoing process that requires sustained effort, beginning with a thorough assessment of the existing climate. This study introduces the Inclusion, Diversity, and Access (IDA) climate survey, a 36-item questionnaire designed to evaluate the academic climate in physics departments. The IDA survey was administered to members of the APS Committee on Minorities in Physics and resulted in 1,214 responses from physics department members, including chairs, faculty, and staff from 91 different departments. Data analysis yielded reliable and valid results, enabling meaningful comparisons among groups within the physics community. The study provides initial results from the IDA survey, offering baseline measurements of the current climate in physics departments. The data highlight areas where departments can improve and highlight the importance of addressing recruitment and retention challenges. The full IDA dataset is available on the APS website, enabling departments to assess their progress over time and compare their climate to national standards. This study serves as a foundation for ongoing work to monitor and improve the academic climate in physics departments, facilitating a sustained effort to create a more inclusive and welcoming environment for everyone in the physics community. The research received support through grants from the American Physical Society (APS), the National Science Foundation (NSF), and the Joint Institute for Laboratory Astrophysics (JILA). Additionally, the researchers acknowledge the input and guidance provided by the APS Committee on Minorities in Physics. The full IDA survey can be accessed at https://www.aps.org/units/smp/climate/index.html. All survey responses are accessible under a confidentiality agreement, except for a small subset of 66 responses from individuals who requested anonymity. The primary findings have been shared with the departments and committees representing the individuals involved. The full analysis and data are available upon request to the relevant departments and committees. The survey's development and implementation were facilitated by the APS Office of Diversity and Inclusion, which actively seeks to promote and support inclusive practices within the physics community. As an initial step towards creating a more comprehensive approach to climate assessment, the IDA survey will contribute to this ongoing effort, which will continue to evolve and expand in the future. One potential direction for growth is by incorporating climate assessments from physics students, which could provide valuable insights into their experiences and help identify areas for improvement in the educational environment. This study investigates the theoretical foundation of online auctions administered by software, revealing vulnerabilities in both the sellers and bidders. Our primary conclusion regarding the seller arises from observing human behavior. Even though software-enforced rules can deter auction rule violations, the threat of detection does not motivate sellers to seek maximum revenue when participating in non-credible second-price auctions. This occurs because violating auctions often yield better financial gains for the seller. Additionally, our research highlights a common misunderstanding among bidders, stemming from overconfidence, which increases the likelihood they will recognize an unfair auction as such. Our analysis also considers the potential impact of cultural influences, as exemplified by the case of an auction for a $0.16 item, showing that bidders from certain cultures are more likely to suspect an unfair auction, compared to bidders from other cultures. Our study identifies a potential remedy for these auction vulnerabilities, proposing the implementation of auctions that are both fair and lucrative for the seller. These auctions utilize the second-price Vickrey auction model and demonstrate a significant increase in seller revenue, obtained by incorporating an auditing system that minimizes the likelihood of the seller violating the auction rules. Our study relies on a combination of methods, including experimental design, cultural influence analysis, and agent-based modeling, conducting twenty-four sessions with 390 bidders and selling 7,826 items. Our results are further substantiated by an economic agent-based model simulating auctions involving 75,000 bidders, governed by 15 cultural parameters, and evaluated through statistical analysis and non-parametric tests. Our study contributes to auction theory, while also exploring the interplay between culture, trust, and deception in online transactions. Our investigation has practical implications, stemming from our observation of a real-world auction, promoting the development of software that can both detect and promote fair auctions while generating substantial revenue for the seller. Our study sheds light on the auction industry, prompting important questions, and offering a comprehensive view of the complex interactions between culture, trust, and deception in online transactions. We demonstrate that in the early universe, isotropy gradually replaces anisotropy
as the fluctuations diminish, using a measure of anisotropy in the universe's scalar
stability, derived from a system that mathematically describes the interplay between
isotropy and anisotropy. This measure, which is based on the average difference
between anisotropy and isotropy, allows us to analyze the effects of fluctuations
in the universe's geometry in terms of their impact on isotropy. One of the key
findings of this research is that the fluctuations, which are initially extreme,
eventually decrease to zero in a way that is symmetrical and uniform in all
directions. This is in line with the idea that the universe is either completely
isotropic or completely anisotropic, but in a state of transition in either case.
Furthermore, we use this measure of anisotropy to explore the behavior of FLRW models
that are either flat (with an infinite geometry), or not (with a Minkowski or de Sitter
geometry), and find that the anisotropy in these models does not necessarily indicate
the presence of isotropy. However, by using the average anisotropy as a gauge of the
isotropy-anisotropy transition, we find that the anisotropy in these models does gradually
decrease as the fluctuations diminish, leading to an isotropic universe. Ultimately,
this research validates the idea that isotropy is the natural state of the universe,
either as a steady state or as the result of fluctuations in an anisotropic universe. 
Anisotropic universes, on the other hand, are transient and will inevitably give way to
an isotropic state. Conversely, we also find that there is no guarantee that an isotropic
universe will remain isotropic, as fluctuations can still arise and lead to local regions
of anisotropy within an otherwise isotropic universe. Nonetheless, as these
fluctuations diminish, the anisotropy in these regions will decrease, leading to
an isotropic universe, albeit one with a more complex geometry. Finally,
this research confirms the anisotropy of de Sitter universes, whether as a steady state

We present QASPER, an extensive dataset designed to enhance question answering capabilities by linking questions from diverse sources, including natural language inference, question answering, and complex text, through specialized attributes and multi-attribute questions. Each data point represents a group of statements and questions from the same source, annotated with both individual and combined attribute sets. Our work addresses three major challenges: multi-attribute question annotation, source detection, and question coverage assessment. The proposed QASPER dataset comprises 32,000 data points from 11 distinct sources, covering 14 different attributes and 20,000 statements. It serves as a resource for studying multi-attribute question answering and source detection in natural language processing, also facilitating the exploration of diverse question types. Our initial evaluation reveals that models relying solely on the question text often fail to identify the required attributes, whereas using both the question and associated context significantly improves accuracy. Ultimately, the QASPER dataset is expected to stimulate research in multi-attribute question answering and source detection, potentially leading to breakthroughs in natural language inference and question answering advancements. The dataset is accessible at https://qaser.org.

This approach combines high-resolution simulations of core collapse supernovae with an analytical method for identifying and following instabilities. In explosions, the instabilities occur behind the shock wave and are amplified by the varying density, while in failed explosions, they are reduced due to the uniform density. We find that in successful explosions, the instabilities occur throughout the ejecta and are distributed evenly. However, in failed explosions, the instabilities are confined to a smaller area and their distribution is uneven. When a failed explosion collapses into a black hole, the instabilities behind the shock wave can survive and mix material up to a certain radius. In some cases, the instabilities can survive behind the accretion disk and mix material up to a certain radius, while in failed supernovae, the instabilities do not survive the high acoustic barriers in the progenitor star. However, in some cases, the instabilities can survive inside the star and mix material in a large area. In general, the instabilities have similar characteristics in various contexts and can mix material up to a certain radius. Accurate diagnosis of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is crucial for proper treatment and education. Traditionally, ADHD diagnosis relied heavily on clinical interviews, making it essential to have effective tools for early identification. Although deep learning techniques have improved ADHD recognition, they often struggle due to the difficulty in gathering labeled data or performing costly, time-consuming annotations. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel approach utilizing Region of Interest (ROI) information to train a robust ADHD classifier with minimal reliance on accurate annotations. By incorporating an attention mechanism and modifying existing deep learning models, the proposed method achieves high accuracy on the ADHD-200 dataset II while training with only the most important ROIs. Notably, the modified models accurately classified ADHD across different subtypes with an accuracy of 70.46%, highlighting their efficiency for diagnostic purposes. Furthermore, the proposed approach demonstrates its ability to outperform state-of-the-art techniques on fMRI data without the need for extensive training data, making it an exciting development for future research. The source code for the proposed method can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/amanrmiaad/ADHD-Decomposition. The proposed method has potential applications in other medical diagnostics, as well as other computer vision and image processing tasks that involve UCI datasets. The recent advancement of medical diagnosis models based on augmented data has been noteworthy. Despite the increased usage of this technique in various medical tasks, its reliability in scenarios with limited clinical information is uncertain. To address this gap, we conducted an investigation on how available clinical features influence the efficacy of data augmentation in medical image classification for malaria diagnosis. We used the Malaria Mosaic Dataset, a recently introduced dataset, to compare the performance of models trained with and without augmented data. The analysis also underscores the importance of incorporating expert input for both model fine-tuning and diagnostic decisions. Additionally, the proposed method offers potential benefits for regulating the use of augmented data in machine learning, potentially reducing diagnostic mistakes and protecting patients' privacy. In probabilistic origin-destination demand modeling, a probabilistic framework often utilizes a probabilistic formulation of the transport problem to derive a solution based on the covariance matrix of origin-destination counts. However, this method is heavily impacted by the noise in origin-destination data. Recent studies have shown that using Lasso regularization on the covariance matrix results in a more accurate and sparse estimation of the matrix. Building upon these findings, this paper introduces a new form of Lasso regularization, known as the Symmetric Lasso, and uses it to derive a new formulation of the transport problem. A transport problem with Symmetric Lasso regularization has a more accurate and sparse structure compared to the traditional Lasso formulation. A numerical study is conducted using synthetic data to compare the traditional Lasso and Symmetric Lasso formulations, and the results show that the Symmetric Lasso formulation leads to better demand estimation and model accuracy. Furthermore, this method is robust to different levels of noise in origin-destination data. These findings are substantiated with an actual-world application involving traffic network demand estimation. When used on real data, the method provides a more accurate and sparse structure, aiding in demand estimation and network representation. Additionally, the demands obtained from this method are closer to actual values, highlighting its effectiveness in probabilistic origin-destination demand modeling. A computational study is performed to evaluate the computational efficiency of the method, and the results indicate that it is feasible to use Symmetric Lasso in practice. Specifically, for a network with approximately 44,000 nodes and 19,000 directed links, solving the transport problem with Symmetric Lasso takes around 3 minutes and 30 seconds. Therefore, this method is suitable for various large-scale scenarios. A new music dataset called MusicTM-Dataset has been created from a combination of two existing datasets, MusicNN and MusicLM. This dataset is designed to improve cross-modal retrieval in music representation learning by providing a large collection of music samples with accompanying acoustic features and lyrics. Unlike other music datasets, MusicTM-Dataset is uniquely structured to facilitate retrieval tasks that involve matching music audio with its accompanying lyrics. Since existing pre-trained models are tailored to specific tasks, they are not readily applicable to cross-modal retrieval. As a result, there is a lack of pre-trained models that can effectively perform this task. To address this, a new pre-trained model, called MusicTM, has been developed specifically for cross-modal retrieval on the MusicTM-Dataset. By comparing MusicTM with other leading pre-trained models, it is shown that MusicTM outperforms the alternative models in both cross-modal retrieval and music classification tasks. Furthermore, experiments have demonstrated that fine-tuning MusicTM on a small dataset can achieve superior results on the more challenging MusicLM dataset. As an added benefit, the music transformation tasks used to pre-train the MusicTM model can also be utilized as effective data augmentations to improve the performance of existing models. Consequently, the music dataset and the pre-trained model it is based on can be considered valuable resources for the entire music community. These can be found at https://github.com/openiipc/MusicTM-Dataset and https://huggingface.co/OpenIIPC/MusicTM.

Our research identifies a new learning paradigm, dubbed 'curriculum fusion,' which involves merging multiple optimal curriculum configurations to expedite the learning process. The manipulation of polarization is becoming increasingly crucial in various areas, including spintronics, nonlinear optics, and quantum physics. While traditional methods rely on labor-intensive techniques using beam splitters and delay lines, a new approach presented here leverages the unique properties of a beam shaper and a table-top material effect, enabling the rapid manipulation of polarization in a compact format. This novel method achieves this goal through interaction with a thin layer of Te film, where it nonlocally changes the polarization of an incident laser beam by adjusting the wavelength-dependent transmission. By combining numerical simulations with experimental results, a detailed analysis reveals that the first-order diffraction beam produces a highly efficient way to manipulate circular polarization, exhibiting nearly complete transmission with around 90% efficiency for one polarization component and nearly zero efficiency for the other. This unique property allows for an advanced degree of control, where the ratio of opposite polarization components can be adjusted to an almost perfect 100:1 ratio. Moreover, this technique can be easily integrated into a variety of applications due to its inherent compatibility with different formats, including Gaussian, Bessel, and dark solitonic beams. Ultimately, this new method provides a faster, more efficient way to control polarization, opening up new avenues for research in nonlinear optics. Additionally, this study's integrated framework can benefit research in various fields by quickly calculating beam stabilization and predicting polarization behavior, where many experimental data collections could be recreated virtually. Furthermore, this innovative polarization control method can also be applied at an atomic scale by manipulating atomic beams. As a table-top technology, it is accessible for general use, where its principles can be adapted into portable devices with comparable functionality. This novel approach promises to inspire new ideas in various fields, where the concept of nonlocal transmission may find extended applications beyond polarization control. Based on the analyzed results, it is anticipated that this method's efficiency could be further improved to achieve a nearly complete polarization conversion by adjusting the wavelength-dependent transmission parameters. This new method is versatile and can likely be applied at other technological levels, where a similar beam shaper technique could also enhance the efficiency of traditional microscopes by extracting hidden features from the signal beams. Lastly, it is also possible that this method's efficiency could be affected by incorporating dynamic nanostructures into the Te film, where the incorporation of nanostructures in the film in an alternating structure can introduce new features in the transmission parameters, where this new structure can enhance the polarization control by adding new circular polarization components. This framework leverages the uniqueness of each feature and the variety of sources to generate actionable information for resource allocation. By applying the Featurization framework to data from 292 COVID-19 patients, we identified key features that distinguish high from low ICU resource patients. This analysis reveals how specific features related to admission differ between these groups and highlights the importance of integrating multiple clinical sources. These findings will enable hospitals to develop more effective COVID-19 resource allocation strategies, both during the current pandemic and in future medical evaluations.
