Our proposed model, VASEGAMI, demonstrates superior performance in various dialogue understanding tasks and significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving a remarkable 11.47% relative improvement, as validated by the 2021 Dialogues Understanding Challenge results. VASEGAMI's unique feature is its ability to segment and represent dialogues through a multi-disciplinary approach, integrating techniques from vision and language models. This is made possible by its two-stage training process. Firstly, the model is trained using a vision and language pre-training method, leveraging a vast text-based external database, TAPE-D. This initial training enables the development of rich, universal sentence representations. Secondly, the model is refined using a multi-task finetuning approach on various dialogue understanding challenges. This stage is characterized by segmentation and representation learning of utterances, aided by a dynamic attention mechanism that identifies and extracts key segments from dialogues. Additionally, the model's ability to capture contextual and semantic relationships is enhanced through a graph attention mechanism. Our results show VASEGAMI's ability to effectively segment and represent dialogues, as well as its outstanding performance in multiple dialogue understanding tasks. This is particularly evident in the SEMEVAL 2019 Task 5: Detection of irony, in which VASEGAMI achieved a 7.01% relative improvement, surpassing existing state-of-the-art models. Our source code is available at https://github.com/sfhuang9/VASEGAMI. VASEGAMI has been accepted for oral presentation at the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing.

We investigate the effect of different loss sampling techniques on the performance of Object Relationship Detection models. By analyzing the impact of these techniques, we identify a strong correlation between optimization speed and data sample diversity and propose a new Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling method, incorporating a dual sampling framework that optimizes model performance. Through extensive experiments on the MultiObjectRelationships dataset, we demonstrate the superiority of BNPS over existing loss sampling methods and find it surpasses the state-of-the-art approach by a significant margin, with 4.6% higher accuracy and up to 40% faster optimization times. The proposed technique is further validated by achieving superior results on real-world applications, including image classification and object detection. The corresponding implementation is available on GitHub at https://github.com/indigoindigo/BNPS. Additionally, the optimized model weights can be downloaded from https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/research/mor/. VNPS has the potential to contribute to the development of efficient Visual Relationship Detection models, and we anticipate it will be a valuable resource for researchers in this field. VNPS is a general loss sampling strategy that can be applied to various detection tasks with minimal adaptation required. Furthermore, the technique is highly versatile and can be applied to both single-stage and two-stage Object Relationship Detection models, as evidenced by our experiments. To facilitate further research, we provide a more detailed explanation of the effect of BNPS on model performance in Section 5 and encourage the use of an adaptive learning rate decay, as employed in Deep Relative Attributes, as an effective approach to accelerating model convergence. Lastly, the implementation of the proposed method is fully compatible with modern Object Relationship Detection models, including Relative Attributes and Object Relationship Detection. To verify the generality of the technique, we also test it on the more complex RPN-based approach and find it yields comparable results, highlighting its potential to improve the efficiency of more complex detection models. The effectiveness of the proposed method is further validated by evaluating its impact on the performance of the RPN-based approach on three datasets. The results show BNPS leads to significant improvements, with average precision increasing by 2.6% and model convergence speeding up by 30%. Specifically, the RF Toolbox includes modules for designing radio frequency cavities, computing radio frequency phases, and performing radio frequency heating and cooling, particularly in the context of plasma physics. This paper provides an overview of the RF Toolbox and its integration with the Accelerator Suite, as well as its potential applications in radio frequency applications. A case study is presented to demonstrate the capabilities of the RF Toolbox in performing radio frequency heating and cooling simulations. Additionally, the paper highlights future development plans for the RF Toolbox. This approach enables the parsing of diverse images with minimal additional training through propagation of annotated tree structures. Semantic segmentation tasks involving hyperspectral images are typically restricted to recognizing basic color attributes. However, the inherent detail of these images allows for more precise labeling possibilities. By incorporating refined label information, we can enhance the segmentation capabilities of conventional semantic segmentation models. Nevertheless, supplying additional labels comes with a heightened risk of overfitting, which becomes particularly pronounced when working with complex hyperspectral images. To mitigate this limitation, we have developed a innovative approach that makes the most of extra label information while minimizing the likelihood of overfitting. This is achieved through the utilization of an unlabelled data generator, created using a self-supervised anisotropic diffusion process. The newly developed model is capable of utilizing extra label information in an unmodified PDE-based diffusion model, thereby improving the purity of segmented regions. Comprehensive experiments have demonstrated that our approach leads to significantly cleaner segmentation results, accompanied by enhanced semantic segmentation performance. Furthermore, we have found that our unmodified diffusion model is better suited for hyperspectral segmentation tasks, displaying improved results compared to other state-of-the-art diffusion models used in the industry. To support our findings, we have made our source code, dataset, and self-supervised anisotropic diffusion generator available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/asharakeh/ASHAR. This unusual spin pattern cannot be explained using conventional models of stellar rotation. Our analysis focused on identifying periodic changes in the star's light that could indicate the presence of a binary companion. Despite initial indications of these periodic changes, our further examination found no conclusive evidence to support the idea of a binary star system. These star spots form a spiral pattern due to a slight irregularity in the star's shape, called an ellipsoidal variation. Briefly, the task involves finding the solutions of a polynomial system over the integers, resulting from a combinatorial problem formulated in reference [3]. Due to its complexity, existing computational methods failed to obtain the solution within a reasonable time frame. Using the newly developed algorithm, a solution was finally obtained after 20.5 hours of computation on a shared resource, yielding the first known integer solution of this polynomial system in 37 variables. Furthermore, the Gröbner basis algorithm with a pre-determined signature proved effective in solving various problems in the field of geometric combinatorics, as demonstrated by the successful resolution of two challenging problems [4], [5]. The computation time for these problems was significantly reduced, taking around 0.5 and 1 minutes respectively. These results illustrate the practical applicability of the proposed algorithm. In addition, the collaboration measured a decrease in photons and charged particles in Cu+Cu collisions at 200 GeV but did not observe a decrease in Au+Au collisions at 62 GeV, suggesting a energy dependence difference between photons and charged particles. Drawing multiple connected lines is a fundamental task in graph drawing and visual analytics. A common issue arises when the algorithm fails to accurately render the starts and ends of these lines as intended, particularly if they intersect at specific points. A novel, efficient algorithm is proposed, capable of effectively rendering connected lines, including those that pass through critical points, where the algorithm can predict and adjust their intersection points to match desired critical configurations. This approach leverages a dynamic programming technique to find optimal intersection point positions, ensuring the generated paths have the lowest total cost based on the original drawing costs and penalties for deviating from the critical specifications. A proposed DP algorithm efficiently solves this problem in linear time, complemented by an additional method that can solve a constrained version of the problem in quadratic time. Through experimental results, it's evident that the standard line joining algorithm struggles to match desired critical configurations, whereas the proposed algorithm excels in this aspect, also outperforming other drawing methods in various quality metrics. Furthermore, a heuristic technique is introduced to accelerate the DP algorithm, utilizing path similarity to reduce computations and demonstrate the feasibility of solving this problem. A key observation shows that when the cost of drawing a line is independent of its endpoint coordinates, the algorithm can predict and adjust critical configurations without altering the drawing costs, facilitating the use of standard drawing methods. A new method is introduced to determine when this property holds for a set of lines. A novel interpolation formula derived from radial basis function interpolation will be presented. This new quasi-interpolation formula is based on a non-uniform scalar mesh and can be designed to maintain convexity and monotonicity properties. Unlike most explicit quadratic schemes, this one is stable and can solve elliptic problems without requiring an iterative process. Furthermore, it possesses an intrinsic error estimate of O(h^1.5), making it a highly efficient method. Its inherent smoothness also enables it to be the basis for developing smooth adaptive mesh refinement techniques. Several numerical experiments will be presented to demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of this new scheme. Pulsar halos are large, extended structures composed of energy generated by pulsar wind neutron stars. They are an essential area of study for understanding the cosmic positron excess and the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess. A pulsar halo's radiation pattern is affected by the electron-positron flux originating from the pulsar wind, as well as the inverse Compton interaction of this flux with cosmic microwave background photons and synchrotron radiation produced by the electron-positron flux. By using a numerical code capable of solving the relativistic Mott cross-section equation, this research computes the flux and spectrum of high-energy electrons and positrons produced by the pulsar wind, and applies this data to calculate the spectrum and spatial distribution of gamma-rays produced by inverse Compton interactions and synchrotron radiation within a pulsar halo. The study finds that synchrotron radiation dominates the gamma-ray spectrum at higher energy levels, while inverse Compton interactions produce a harder spectrum due to the interaction of electron-positron flux at higher energy levels. The diffusion of high-energy electrons and positrons within the pulsar halo, as well as energy loss through radiation, are also considered in the theoretical model. The research demonstrates that a pulsar halo's emission has a distinct spatial and spectral profile, which can be verified through observations of a gamma-ray telescope. Several pulsar halos with notable cosmic and gamma-ray features are identified, including PSR J1833-0653, PSR J0534+421, and PSR J1903+32. The research suggests that a comprehensive multi-frequency investigation of these pulsar halos can provide key information about the location, energy loss mechanisms, and radiation patterns of high-energy electrons and positrons. The research further proposes that a joint investigation of a diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess and a cosmic positron excess should focus on local star-forming regions, globular clusters, and pulsar halos, which exhibit distinct radiation patterns and spatial distributions. The research demonstrates that a detailed analysis of a diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess and a cosmic positron excess can provide key information about the formation and evolution of these regions, the rate of supernova, and the star formation rate. Data augmentation using mask-based techniques, such as super pixel delimiting masks, can enhance the performance of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). This method changes the image structure by grouping pixels into distinct regions during training. Unlike other techniques that alter the position of pixels, this method affects the organization of pixels, potentially introducing a correlation between depth and structure that could impact the classification outcome. This correlation might be observed in datasets of images, such as buildings, where architectural styles are influenced by the layout of walls and floors. To investigate this correlation, we applied different super pixel delimiting mask patterns to a dataset of building images and analyzed the resulting effects on the organization of pixels, as well as the performance of a pre-trained CNN. Our results show that an optimal mask pattern can improve the accuracy of the CNN by up to 4.8%. Additionally, we found that using this method allows the CNN to generalize better across different categories of building styles, reducing the error rate by at least 6.4%. This research highlights the potential of using structure-based data augmentation to improve the performance of CNNs, as well as the importance of considering the underlying structure of images in classification tasks. Furthermore, we identified two key features - average height and number of delimiting mask regions - that significantly impact the accuracy of the CNN. Our analysis suggests that these features offer a compact and interpretable way to improve the performance of CNNs, potentially making it a more viable method for structure-based data augmentation in various image classification tasks. Overall, our study indicates that using super pixel delimiting masks can be a valuable tool for augmenting datasets and mitigating the overfitting problem in CNNs. This method is intriguing because it affects the organizational structure of pixels, potentially opening up new avenues for data augmentation that are independent of the position of pixels. Based on our findings, we propose an efficient way to utilize super pixel delimiting masks as a data augmentation technique that can enhance the performance of CNNs. Our proposed framework involves using various mask patterns to generate building images and adjusting the depth of the delimiting masks based on the style of the building. This depth-adjusted structure is then used to group pixels in a way that simulates the style of the building, providing an efficient way to improve the performance of CNNs without the need for manual delimiting masks. Using the most comprehensive academic database, we track the publication of research on climate change from 1948 to 2017 in 24 leading scientific journals and find that, relative to other important scientific topics, climate change publications have increased rapidly. Nevertheless, the enthusiasm of policymakers for climate change research is significantly less evident than it is for general interest science, economics, or evenatory science. Notably, the interest of scientists in climate change varies widely depending on specific subfields, with researchers in meteorology exhibiting a greater interest than others. We also find that the interest in climate change research correlates with the severity of weather-related disasters, as well as the media's coverage of these events. Interestingly, the interest in climate change research shows seasonal variations, peaking during the UN Climate Conference. Ultimately, our study highlights the intricate and dynamic nature of climate change research, which is influenced by a complex interplay of scientific, social, and political factors. We demonstrate that scientists' changing interests can serve as an effective indicator for detecting these shifts. We use corresponding factors to explain the variation in scientists' interest in climate change from 1948 to 2017 through the application of topic modeling and analyze the probable consequences of their trends, which are then evaluated using self referential data, including the growing interest in climate change research, the increasing concern of scientists, the limited engagement of policymakers, the requirement for continued persistent research effort, the necessity of addressing the social and political complexities, the potential for transfer of knowledge from climate change research to other scientific fields, the limited interest in some climate change subfields, the potential for transfer of knowledge from other scientific fields to climate change, and the variation in interest in climate change research among diverse scientific fields. Additionally, we use an econometric model to analyze the effect of climate change research on the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States from 1990 to 2017. Our study demonstrates that the interest in climate change research is a multifaceted phenomenon that is difficult to comprehend with a single theory. Consequently, we propose a new theory, known as the interacting multiplet theory, to explain the behavior of scientists. This research paper reveals the effectiveness of the Koopman operator theory in controlling soft robotic systems by generating control moves that maintain the system in a desired, stable state within its deformation range. The technique exploits the spectral properties of a data-matrix constructed using system measurements at various deformation points. The study utilizes a programmable silicone hand as a test case, employing the Koopman operator theory to identify an control action that returns the system to a specific target state. The approach's ability to detect intrinsically stable states is confirmed through a control experiment, with results showing that it can successfully return the system to a desired configuration. The proposed method has the potential to increase control precision and reduce the risk of system damage by minimizing the complexity of control moves. Additionally, the study highlights the potential for integrating the Koopman operator theory with machine learning techniques, such as neural networks, to expand the range of valid system configurations. Our research examines the spectral patterns of features associated with dusty emission in five high-redshift AGNs selected from the Complete Redshift Survey. Using the power's spectral density function provided by the PLCKGEECS collaboration, we investigated the spectral features observed in the AGNs' spectral energy distributions between 0.3 and 4.2 micrometers. We discovered that the spectral features at lower wavelengths (0.3-1.2 micrometers) are consistent with absorption by silicates, while those at higher wavelengths (1.2-4.2 micrometers) are consistent with emission by various silicates and graphites. We noted a correlation between the wavelength at which features begin to develop and the amplitude of the emission, which suggests that more heavily obscured AGNs exhibit more pronounced features. We developed a model featuring a graphite torus to explain the observed spectral patterns in our study objects and others. This model successfully reproduces the observed spectral energy distributions and is consistent with theoretical predictions about spectral feature evolution with redshift. Our research also indicates that the featureless spectrum of QSO 140.49583+122.7622 could be attributed to a lack of foreground screening, rather than a lack of dusty torus material. Furthermore, our comparison of the spectral feature amplitudes with AGN luminosity reveals a negative correlation, which may indicate that more luminous AGNs exhibit featureless spectra. However, further research is necessary to confirm this relationship. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that the foreground screening hypothesis is unnecessary to explain featureless spectra in many high-redshift quasars. Instead, the spectral feature amplitude is primarily determined by the amount of dusty material in the foreground. Our research also suggests that the featureless spectrum of type-I AGNs is primarily due to the absorption by the host galaxy rather than a dusty torus. Our findings are consistent with the idea that a radially uniform dusty torus exists in all AGNs and that the front and back sides of the torus emit in the mid- and far-IR and absorb in the mid-IR, respectively. Using a specific radiative transfer code, we studied how varying the opacity and scale length affects the spectrum. This led us to propose modifications to existing spectral energy distribution models, which could improve the accuracy of future photometric surveys. Our research is relevant to studies using future missions such as James Webb Space Telescope, which will enable the analysis of featureless spectra in more than 300,000 high-redshift quasars. This work presents a lightweight, differentiable model, called Lite-ProSENet, for predicting survival times in patients based on semi-supervised lung cancer data. By incorporating a learning factor into the Kaplan-Meier estimator, Lite-ProSENet outperforms existing methods in both low-data and semi-supervised scenarios, and has achieved superior results on 12 datasets from the International Society for Research on Cancer, with results including an 8.9% improvement in concordance index and $p$-values less than 0.01 for 11 datasets. Additionally, Lite-ProSENet provides interpretable predictions and patient trajectories, as well as understandable features for medical professionals. Due to its lightweight structure, Lite-ProSENet is suitable for various applications, including clinical environments with limited computational resources. Further details and implementation details can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/jiakai1999/Lite-ProSENet. Researchers are encouraged to submit their own lung cancer data and related information to enable comparative studies. Technologies used for model development, data analysis, and visualization include PyTorch, Python 3.7, and Matplotlib 3.1.1. Reproducibility of results for specific datasets, such as those used in the study on survival times in lung cancer patients treated with surgery, is possible but would require access to additional clinical data. In terms of performance, Lite-ProSENet has achieved a concordance index of 0.8132 on that particular dataset. Overall, Lite-ProSENet offers a lightweight, differentiable model for survival time analysis with superior performance, making it a useful tool for clinical environments. As a differentiable model, Lite-ProSENet can be utilized in various tasks, such as semi-supervised learning, supervised learning, and gradient-based tasks. We employed the Multi-Component Modal Patchwork (MCMP) technique to evaluate the efficacy of patchwork power spectrum estimation. By analyzing simulated data sets derived from the QUESPA code, which mimics the Planck 2018 data scenario, we focused on three wavelength ranges: 1000, 500, and 200 kilometer. Our findings indicate that MCMP yields a highly accurate power spectrum reconstruction for the 1000 kilometer range but exhibits some discrepancies for the 500 kilometer range. Furthermore, significant deviations from the expected power spectrum were observed in the 200 kilometer range. These results are also compared to those obtained through the maximum likelihood estimator. While the ML estimator shows better agreement with the simulated power spectrum in the 1000 kilometer range, MCMP proves more effective for the 500 and 200 kilometer ranges. These findings suggest that MCMP may be more robust than previously assumed. Building on these outcomes, we outline potential improvements for future MCMP developments. As an additional byproduct, our analysis confirms that the likelihood-based power spectrum obtained through ML or CAMB remains accurate even at smaller scales. Additionally, we verify that MCMP's effectiveness can be enhanced through the incorporation of additional spectral modes. Nonetheless, we found that the 200 kilometer range remains challenging for MCMP to overcome. Therefore, we suggest that future efforts should prioritize improving the estimator in this scale range to enhance its overall performance. Based on these conclusions, we propose multiple research avenues for enhancing MCMP in the future. Additionally, we provide a detailed description of the MCMP code for the benefit of the scientific community. Although this code has not been formally released, it is now available for scrutiny through the GitHub repository marked as public. Furthermore, the repository contains all the code utilized in this research, including the analysis code, simulated data sets, and supplementary material. Conversely, the likelihood code utilized in this study remains subject to a formal release process by the COSMOMCC collaboration. We establish criteria to establish whether tensor product modules composed of highest weight modules and modules free over U(𝕙) are irreducible, with criteria diverging based on whether the highest weight module is non-trivial or zero. For non-trivial modules, we demonstrate that irreducibility can be resolved through the examination of isomorphic tensor products, while for trivial modules, the focus shifts to checking the irreducibility of image of restriction to a Borel subalgebra. As a consequence of these findings, we obtain a determination of when free U(𝕙)-modules are irreducible. Our results are illustrated through various examples. Ultimately, we conclude with an outline of future research goals. Throughout this work, we use 𝔨𝔯 symmetry to derive our findings, with the walled pattern in type A serving as a reference point for comparison with type B and C. Interestingly, similarities emerge between the types, with certain parallels proving useful in the determination of irreducibility in D4. This paper introduces a deep learning model that utilizes long short term memory (LSTM) to classify Twitter sentiment, specifically aiming to classify tweets as either positive or negative. The proposed model leverages Twitter's 2017 dataset, which comprises 18,095 tweets, and is optimized using a binary cross-entropy loss function and Adam optimizer. The role of roles in task-oriented dialogue models has often been overlooked. In this study, we highlight the significance of roles and develop a role-aware pre-training task, called Role-Aware Conversation Isolation, to enhance dialogue models. Our model is based on extracting semantic role information from unlabelled conversations, effectively capturing contextual dependencies between roles. By incorporating this role-aware pre-training, we observed improvements in conversation flow and overall performance, particularly when role-specific labels were missing. Our model achieved state-of-the-art results on the Dialogstate dataset and demonstrated adaptability across various role specification scenarios, ultimately yielding more natural and effective dialogues. In a practical application, we successfully adapted a model trained on a specific dataset to perform well on another dataset, showcasing the model's robustness and generalizability. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AlistairChen/RACI. In a broader context, our research aims to promote the utilization of roles in dialogue models through the development of role-aware pre-training methods, thereby enhancing dialogue system performance, adaptability, and ease of extension with roles. Our model's performance can be found on the DialoGLM dataset, which we created to evaluate the effectiveness of role-aware dialogue models in various applications, such as service maximization and role-specific conversation generation. Our method for role-aware dialogue generation involves framing both role specifications and conversation context as a graph, and employing a transformer model to predict role-specific responses while incorporating contextual information. Our model achieved state-of-the-art results on the DialoGLM dataset, which is available at https://dialoglmdataset.github.io/. We hope our model and dataset will facilitate the exploration of role-based approaches to dialogue generation and improve service-oriented dialogue systems. We envision a future direction of research, where role-aware pre-training methods and adaptors could be combined with role-specific downstream fine-tuning to produce more effective and adaptable dialogue models, ultimately enabling better data efficiency, model interoperability, and role extension capabilities. Our initial investigation of this direction yielded promising results, and we anticipate future advancements in this area. Our model's performance on the Dialogstate dataset can be found at https://github.com/AlistairChen/RACI. In a related study, we developed a role-aware dialogue generation method, which involves using role specifications and conversation context to produce graph-based representations of dialogue. This mechanism benefits from an inherent strong magnetic field, eliminating the necessity for fine-tuning, while its magnetic component, although not the primary mediator of supersymmetry breaking, can significantly contribute to it. Leptogenesis in this setup occurs through the one-loop decay of gravitinos, leading to a PeV-mass spectrum. This theory is compatible with dark matter, with its mass ranging from approximately 10 GeV to 1 TeV. Furthermore, the model predicts distinct signatures in neutrino oscillation experiments, primarily marked by notably high $\theta_{23}$ and $\delta$ phases in the lepton sector. This theory is an alternative to conventional models of supersymmetry breaking and provides a novel explanation for the observed high-scale neutrino data. Additionally, it offers a possible resolution to the $n-\bar{n}$ asymmetry problem within the standard model. Nevertheless, the predicted PeV-scale leptogenesis might be challenged by sub-TeV dark matter, forcing us to consider modifications to the neutrino sector for further verification. This theory's validity can be tested by various particle physics experiments, as well as astrophysics investigations involving neutrinos, dark matter, and cosmic magnetic fields. This theory, although highly testable, does not yield a fully deterministic outcome, given the existing uncertainties in particle physics and cosmology. As wireless communication systems continue to evolve, so too are their potential risks to people with medical implants, particularly in cases where cellular systems are involved.  Research has focused on minimizing interference to medical implants by developing escape channels with limited capacity, but at the expense of poor transmission quality.  This work introduces an enhanced escape mechanism with improved quality through energy harvesting.  By incorporating an energy harvesting gauge at the base station, the new system, called Enhanced Switching Channel (ESC), can efficiently detect both primary and secondary user transmissions.  Furthermore, ESC incorporates a precise timing recovery mechanism for medical implant transmissions, allowing for optimal ESC activation timing and minimized interference to medical implants.  Mathematical analysis and simulation results confirm that ESC offers superior transmission quality and reliability compared to current solutions, while also providing high interference mitigation to medical implants.  Furthermore, ESC is resilient to various distortions, including non-linear amplifiers, path loss, and fading.  Overall, ESC presents a promising approach for supporting medical implant communications with minimal interference. In the quest for enhanced word suggestions, researchers have delved into semantic-based models and explored ways to incorporate contextual words' meanings. While notable advancements have been made with models that prioritize either syntactic or semantic analysis, our innovative approach combines both methodologies within the framework of Semantic Matching, yielding exceptional results. Our novel model, Hybrid Word Suggester (HWS), leverages WordNet to create a Semantic Knowledge Graph, which provides rich semantic understanding. By integrating KNN and Graph Convolutional Networks, HWS captures both local and global semantic patterns. Consequently, HWS outperforms existing models, demonstrating the significant benefits of hybrid modeling over purely syntactic or semantic approaches, in addition to showcasing the value of Semantic Knowledge Graphs for word suggestion. Our source code is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/seopark/HybridWS. The propulsion of a dimer in a two-dimensional lattice fluid can be controlled by a mobile wheel that can adjust speed and direction, effectively allowing the dimer to navigate through the environment like a vehicle. By analyzing either the dimer or the wheel as the driving force, our research reveals a vast array of stationary states, including situations where the dimer moves at fixed speeds or pauses indefinitely. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that certain active dimer motions can be directly mapped to the effects of a rotating steering wheel in larger machines. Additionally, our study explores the dimer's ability to maintain traction with the wheel and identifies conditions under which the dimer can maintain this connection. Our results show that both the dimer and wheel can exhibit unstable, oscillating motion as well as stable, circular trajectories. However, the stability of the dimer depends on the presence of inertial effects, which can cause the dimer to deviate from the wheel's path. Our research also examines the dimer's response to speed adjustments and finds that either the dimer can adjust its speed to match the wheel, or the dimer can only increase its speed after a sudden change in propulsion. Lastly, our study derives a mathematical inequality that bounds the dimer's acceleration while being driven by the wheel. In all cases of stable motion, the acceleration remains negative, and the maximum acceleration is related to the difference between the dimer's speed and the wheel's speed. Our research provides insight into the intricate dynamics of active matter by combining analytical calculations with numerical simulations, ultimately contributing to the development of new inequalities that bound the dimer's acceleration. Additionally, our study finds that both the dimer and the wheel can exhibit a sudden, violent change in motion when propulsion is suddenly altered. Our research discovers that these abrupt changes can lead to repeated patterns of high and low acceleration in both the dimer and the wheel, thus demonstrating the non-Markovian nature of the system. Furthermore, our study finds that the dimer can maintain traction with the wheel under a wide range of sudden propulsion adjustments. Our research also reveals that the dimer can decelerate quickly when propulsion is high, but the dimer cannot accelerate quickly when propulsion is low. Our study finds that the dimer can maintain a steady speed when slowly propelled, but the dimer cannot maintain a steady speed when propelled quickly. This study links the eigenvalue problems for the Dirac operator and Heun's equation through nonlinear transformation, revealing a direct relationship. Additionally, it's demonstrated that solutions to the eigenvalue problems for the Dirac operator can be effectively generated from those of a related tridiagonal operator. This link enables precise numerical computation of Dirac operator eigenvalues by leveraging well-established methods for tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems. To illustrate the validity and utility of this connection, a range of numerical examples are provided. Furthermore, it's observed that certain Dirac operator eigenvalues occur repeatedly and multiplicatively in relation to the mass parameter, a phenomenon not previously reported in the literature. Such multiplicity is susceptible to mathematical interpretation, raising questions about the potential spectral degeneracy in Dirac systems under various physical transformations. Notably, while this degeneracy possibility is intriguing, it remains purely the subject of theoretical investigation at this point. Moreover, the study shows that the related eigenvalues of the tridiagonal operator derived from Heun's equation also exhibit multiplicity properties. Ultimately, this research provides a valuable connection between the eigenvalue problems for the Dirac and Heun equations, facilitating novel, numerically stable methods for computing Dirac operator eigenvalues. To achieve this, the study presents a practical algorithm that successively computes eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors for the Dirac operator through sequential computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors for a corresponding tridiagonal operator. By capitalizing on the operator's properties, the method has been shown to be more stable and efficient than alternative approaches. By way of example, the study notes that this algorithm has been successfully applied to the computation of Dirac operator eigenvalues in a range of diverse systems, including spinors in graphene and positronium. This paper investigates the properties of a large heterogeneous vehicular network, where multiple types of users compete for the same wireless resources, and relays are deployed across the system to manage traffic congestion. By leveraging large deviation principles and analyzing the effective rates of users, we demonstrate how the relay placement impacts the network, allowing us to generate adaptive strategies for user associations and relay transmissions that optimize the network's overall efficiency. Notably, these strategies lead to a significant improvement in the network's scalability and allow us to reduce the load on demanding users by prioritizing their transmission. Interestingly, our results show that increasing the deployment density of relays eventually becomes counterproductive, instead reducing the network's overall effectiveness in dense areas. Furthermore, we examine the cost-effectiveness of our proposed strategies through numerical evaluations, and find that deploying relays only in areas with high densities of demanding users is the most efficient use of relay resources. Additionally, our results confirm that optimizing user associations and relay transmissions independently is suboptimal, and jointly optimizing these factors is required to achieve the best possible outcomes in such complex networks. To summarize, our findings highlight the importance of accurately modeling complex networks and using optimization techniques to refine these models, ultimately leading to improved performance. Finally, we verify our analytical findings through extensive simulation experiments. Additionally, we observe that the standard uniform distribution assumption may not accurately represent the patterns of users in real-world scenarios, and an alternative mixture of uniform distribution may provide a better model for these situations. Therefore, our work suggests that the mixture of uniform distribution could be a more suitable model than the standard uniform distribution in such networks. To further validate this claim, we compare the results obtained under both the standard uniform distribution and the mixture of uniform distribution models, and find that the latter yields better outcomes, aligning more closely with the findings of recent numerical experiments. The task of assessing sentence quality is crucial in natural language processing, particularly due to its wide-ranging applications in text compression, summarization, and dialogue systems. Currently, relying solely on human-generated labels proves to be costly and time-consuming. Fortunately, leveraging Wikipedia's vast edits, comprising the actions of trained and inexperienced editors, can provide valuable insights into sentence quality assessment. Building on this idea, our study introduces the Wikipedia Sentence Quality Assessment dataset, consisting of 7,548 sentences revised by approximately 1,000 Wikipedia editors. By analyzing the editing behaviors of these editors, we establish a set of human-like labels, simulating the process of a trained editor learning from novice contributors. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that editors with more experience tend to employ more effective assessment labels, thereby enhancing the labeling process. To further mimic the Wikipedia's collaborative environment, editors with similar skills and abilities are grouped into 'communities.' When tasks are completed within these communities, editors benefit from the collective knowledge gained through previous assessments, leading to improved performance. Wikipedia's vibrant community of editors, comprising 90,000 contributors, represents an untapped resource, allowing us to investigate how harnessing the collective knowledge of a group can improve sentence quality assessment. By employing experienced editors as mentors, editing guidelines can be refined to better reflect the diverse perspectives of all contributors. Moreover, our model predicts that Wikipedia's current editors can solve 75% of the article's problems, as identified by editing behaviors, signifying a significant potential gain in efficiency. Building on these findings, our study outlines a collaborative strategy where novice contributors are assigned editing tasks within specific articles, supervised by experienced editors. By leveraging the Wikipedia community's collective knowledge, our proposed edit workflow can enhance article quality, alleviate the burden on experienced editors, and improve the overall efficiency of editors across the platform. DB3 uses an optimizer to create diverse student models by modifying training data or architecture, which are then learned from their parents through a guide network. Unlike traditional knowledge distillation, which pursues model diversity, DB3 focuses on optimizing the knowledge acquisition process itself. In contrast to other self-supervised distillation methods that aim for diverse students, DB3 changes how the students learn, creating a more efficient and accurate distillation process. DB3 can be applied to parallel training or pseudo-labeling and outperforms existing self-supervised distillation methods on various tasks. Additionally, DB3 can improve the results of other optimization methods for black-box distillation. }$ and $D^{*}{^+}K^{+}$ due to $b\to c\bar{c}$ transitions, utilizing data from LHCb Experiment 1.
The analysis considered decay processes involving the $D^*$
particle, obtained from $D^0\pi$ combinations, and used a model-independent approach to account for potential contributions from $B_s$ oscillations and $b\to u\bar{u}$ transitions.
The calculation took into account detector inefficiencies, event selection criteria, and systematic uncertainties associated with the $k$ and $r$ parameters, muon identification, and multiple interactions in collisions.
The study revealed the possibility of detecting $B^0_s$ decay patterns with a relative efficiency of 15.7% and 13.6%, respectively, while $B^0$ decay patterns had efficiency rates of 14.9% and 12.9% for the $D^* K$ and $D^*K$ combinations.
The calculated branching fraction ranges for $B^0_{(s)}\to D^*K$ are between $3.32\times 10^{-5}$ and $4.94\times 10^{-5}$, and between $3.15\times 10^{-5}$ and $4.56\times 10^{-5}$ for the $D^*K$ combination.
The findings provide a basis for future LHCb analyses of $B^0_{(s)}\to D^*K$ and potentially set upper limits on $B^0_s$ decay patterns in the LHCb's Run 2 and Run 3 data sets, as well as in the CMS's VIII data set. Additionally, the study provides a reference point for future ATLAS and CMS analyses of $B^0_{(s)}\to D^*K$.

In non-geometric string theory, a framework known as twisted membrane theory provides a fully specified two-dimensional quantum field theory that's independent of geometric considerations. A crucial property of twisted membrane theory is that it allows for classical descriptions in specific contexts. These classical descriptions are formulated as continuous-trace algebras, taking the form of Doplicher-Haag-Soriani algebras. Importantly, we find that twisted membrane theory doesn't accommodate classical T-duals in situations where the trace dimension changes. Instead, we demonstrate that the B-field invariant of the underlying double T-dual can serve as a definitive indicator of this lack. Furthermore, we derive a useful condition, analogous to the Fock property, that characterizes twisted membrane theories allowing classical descriptions. These results are validated by applying them to a class of non-geometric backgrounds supported by D-branes, illustrating the B-field's role in facilitating T-duals and the limitations imposed by the presence of branes. Ultimately, this investigation provides a more profound understanding of classical descriptions and the constructions of T-duals in non-geometric backgrounds. Additionally, we discuss the broader implications of our findings for the broader field of string theory. A key implication is that the B-field's effectiveness in enabling T-duals may be hindered by the presence of D-branes, rather than the twisted Chern-Simons field. Furthermore, we note that classical descriptions are feasible for twisted membrane theories not adhering to the Fock property, thus refraining from generating non-geometric backgrounds through T-dual transformations. Due to expert supervision being either impractical or too costly in certain real-world applications, our research focuses on overcoming the limitations of current imitation learning techniques. These methods either fail to achieve full mastery of expert-level skills or require extensive expertise to be learned through trial and error. Co-Imitation Learning addresses this challenge by allowing multiple agents to learn skills from each other, eliminating the need for expert guidance. Building on the foundations of Co-Imitation Learning, we have developed an innovative double Q-learning approach, known as Double Co-Imitation Learning, which successfully applies co-imitation principles to action-value learning. This approach ensures that even in the presence of conflicting information, our method is able to learn viable skills from the interactions of multiple agents. Comprehensive testing of Double Co-Imitation Learning has been conducted across a variety of challenging scenarios, including a multi-agent predator-prey problem and a multi-goal navigation domain, and has consistently demonstrated its ability to learn skills from peer examples more effectively than traditional imitation learning techniques. Furthermore, we have found that Double Co-Imitation Learning scales naturally to address issues in related fields, such as multi-goal reinforcement learning and peer learning. These findings have significant practical implications, highlighting the potential for our method to be used in these critical areas. One such scenario is in our interpretation of a multi-goal navigation problem as an instance of multi-goal reinforcement learning, and another is in our viewing of the predator-prey problem as an example of learning skills from peers. Ultimately, our Double Co-Imitation Learning approach offers a versatile solution for learning skills in a variety of complex, real-world, and expert-inaccessible applications. This paper investigates the maximum likelihood (ML) performance of nested codes, which comprise a polar code concatenated with a Reed-Solomon code, when decoded sequentially, for various bias parameters introduced through the polarized cutoff rate. The research includes generation rates, error probabilities, and simulation results for specific code combinations, considering several bias parameter values. The study finds that selecting a bias parameter that is half the gap to the maximum achievable rate results in the sequential decoder experiencing an error probability close to its minimum possible value, which is dictated by the minimum of the individual code error probabilities of the polar code and the Reed-Solomon codes. Furthermore, increasing the bias parameter reduces the error probability but also lowers the effective generation rate of the code combination, with tighter error bound approximations possible when the bias parameter is half the gap to the maximum achievable rate, making this value a suitable choice for the bias parameter when balancing error probability and generation rate. The research also offers three distinct approaches for tightly approximating the error probability of the sequential decoder. The first method involves the generation rates of the code combination, the second relates the error probability to the minimum of the individual code error probabilities, and the third involves a tight approximation bound influenced by the bias parameter and generation rates, which becomes tighter when the bias parameter increases. The third method can provide more accurate tight approximations than those previously established, with higher effective generation rates, for long code sequences and high bias parameters. The research further finds that selecting a bias parameter that equals the gap to the maximum achievable rate results in the error probability experiencing a sharp decrease as the generation rate approaches this value, indicating that the error probability goes to zero more rapidly for lower generation rates, which is also observed through simulation results. Current hand tracking models can struggle with challenges like occlusion, hand-object contacts, and complex backgrounds. To address these issues, a novel hand tracking method is proposed that utilizes implicit surface reconstruction to accurately model hand and object appearances under various conditions. By integrating a generative adversarial network, the method efficiently learns high-quality hand and object representations from RGB data, without requiring explicit supervision. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed approach's superior performance in dealing with occlusions, hand-object interactions, and adverse backgrounds, outperforming existing state-of-the-art hand tracking techniques significantly. The proposed method's code and model will be publicly available. The associated video can be found at https://yours3fer.github.io/HandFlow/.

We have achieved a significant classification result concerning linear groups over a finite field that have been reduced. These are groups of the form $G/\mathring{G}$, where $G$ is a linear group over a finite field and $\mathring{G}$ represents a specific subgroup consisting of upper triangular matrices. The main goal behind this work is to address a problem posed by Michael Koch, which revolves around classifying $G/\mathring{G}$ for a given field $\mathbb{F}_q$. Our approach involves developing an efficient strategy to tackle this vast domain by establishing a connection between invariant measures under the action of $G/\mathring{G}$ and a model based on a countable set of integers. Once this connection is established, we can apply existing results from ergodic theory, as demonstrated in an accompanying paper by Li and Tao. Finally, to compute specific group identities, we found it necessary to create a novel database to facilitate rapid identification of corresponding key patterns. As a separate observation, our investigations also reveal that the distinctness of $G/\mathring{G}$ groups is equivalent to a conjecture proposed by Richard Wotling in 2007. This outcome provides further evidence that the latter theory has a profound connection to one involving polynomial normal p-groups, as described in an earlier paper by the current author. Last but not least, our findings have significant implications for the broader domain of group theory, as they relate to the long-standing Alperin's conjecture in the context of finite simple groups. To support this claim, we note that the process of classifying $G/\mathring{G}$ groups has enabled us to derive precise estimates regarding the occurrence of specific $p$-components within these groups, which may be useful in formulating a revised form of Alperin's conjecture. These estimates are modeled after similar findings in the study of polynomial normal $p$-groups, as detailed in an accompanying paper by the current author. However, a comprehensive presentation of this theory is reserved for a future study, which will provide an independent verification of the obtained bounds. Additionally, our study has also led to the formulation of a revised form of Alperin's conjecture, which is more refined and is likely to be true. This new form is hopeful of being resolved, which in turn may lead to a verified form of the original Alperin's conjecture. Recent research has shown that deep learning techniques can effectively tackle end-effector pose estimation challenges, despite these methods typically relying on extensive calibration data. In this study, we explore ways to leverage these models in more practical ways by integrating them with a depth camera during actual calibration procedures. Our proposed approach involves using the depth sensor to impose soft constraints on estimated pose data, thereby improving the robustness of calibration processes affected by factors such as wearable or attachment artifacts. Our results demonstrate that this method can be applied in a variety of calibration problems, leading to more accurate end-effector pose estimations. Additionally, we demonstrate that this approach allows for the effective calibration of articulated objects with a significant number of degrees of freedom, a task previously considered difficult. Our technique has been found to produce favorable outcomes compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, as evidenced by the associated code being available on GitHub at the following repository: https://github.com/Princessess/CalibDepthCamera. Our associated video can be found on YouTube at the following link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J1KbEo2uH9U.

However, pinpointing the most relevant scale at which to analyze this interference proves challenging. We develop methods for determining the most appropriate scale at which to detect interference and demonstrate their utility in detecting interference in experiments involving a linear chain of nodes. We also consider the problem of identifying the source of interference when the scale at which interference occurs is known. We show that identifying the source in such cases amounts to solving a computationally demanding problem, but offer a simplified alternative approach that is applicable in certain situations. We complement our theoretical findings with results from actual experiments, showcasing the effectiveness of our proposed methods. To facilitate replication, we provide an implementation of our methods in an online supplementary document. This approach can also detect interference patterns not previously reported in the literature, as seen in the experiments conducted. In particular, we use our methods to discover a previously unknown form of interference in a Bose-Hubbard system. Our detection of this pattern opens up new avenues of research, including using network approaches to identify multiple-scale network interference in various systems. We believe this strategy can enrich the analysis of experiments, enabling researchers to identify known and unknown patterns of network interference. The methods developed in this study are versatile and can be applied to detect network interference in various systems across various fields. We anticipate that our approach will inspire research in the detection of complex patterns of network interference. We also provide an example of the effective application of our strategy to identify known and unknown patterns of network interference in the context of light systems. The presence of self-annihilating dark matter in a neutron star can be analyzed through a model that incorporates both dark matter injection and its destruction. This process occurs in two phases: initial cooling, which follows the neutron star's formation, and late-time cooling, happening after the initial phase. Utilizing a modified version of the standard neutron star cooling theory, we calculated the effects of dark matter on initial cooling. Subsequently, we determined the late-time cooling behavior, taking into account the neutron star's mass and core density, as well as the properties of dark matter. These calculations were performed for various types of dark matter, including fermions and scalar and vector bosons. Additionally, we estimated the amount of dark matter present within a neutron star, based on the knowledge of its mass and core density, as well as the properties of a specific dark matter candidate called WIMPs. This analysis provided bounds on the WIMP-nucleon scattering cross section, obtained through a thorough examination of the neutron star cooling paradigm in the context of dark matter. This study also yielded neutron star mass constraints, derived from the analysis of the cosmic positron flux. Ultimately, our findings revealed the possibility of having a substantial amount of dark matter, by mass, within a neutron star, with its density ranging from $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ g/cm$^3$, depending on the properties of dark matter. This density is significantly higher than what is typically observed in the solar system. Furthermore, for certain parameters of dark matter, its density within a neutron star could be as high as $10^{18}$ g/cm$^3$, which is two orders of magnitude higher than the observed value. This phenomenon can be attributed to the r-process nucleosynthesis, which doesn't completely eliminate dark matter from forming a neutron star. As a result, the dark matter present in a neutron star can be viewed as a residual product of the r-process. This situation is analogous to the observed situation in the solar system. Therefore, the presence of dark matter within a neutron star, when analyzed in conjunction with the r-process nucleosynthesis, can provide valuable insights into the properties of dark matter. This can be achieved by combining the knowledge of the neutron star cooling with the r-process nuclear interactions, through an effective nuclear interaction, denoted as $f_{\rm np}$. The precise measurement of galaxy shapes is crucial for weak lensing analyses.  ShapePipe is an advanced galaxy shape measurement pipeline that leverages multiple algorithms to boost accuracy.  Originally designed for its comprehensive analysis of sources and performance, this paper highlights key developments since its initial introduction, including incorporating more sophisticated algorithms, expanding its analytical capabilities, and documenting its outcomes in depth.  By assessing its influence on the final weak lensing results using data from the Kilo Degree Survey, this research evaluates the impact of ShapePipe on its associated cosmological findings.  Verification analyses confirmed that ShapePipe maintains high levels of accuracy and reliability, removing systematic errors that could impact its weak lensing measurements.  As a result, the majority of weeks lensing estimates derived from ShapePipe data belonged to a specific tight distribution, this included multiple analysis components which all fell within the same tight distribution.  Furthermore, a comparison between ShapePipe measurements and those derived from other similar analysis pipelines revealed minimal but potential systematic differences between them.  Ultimately, the findings of this research suggest that ShapePipe measurements are essentially impermeable to algorithmic changes, making it an extremely reliable tool for galaxy shape analysis.  This reliability, in turn, makes ShapePipe an ideal choice for analyzing data from upcoming large-scale weak lensing cosmology experiments. The Veech discrete 2-circle problem concerns exchanging circles in a Veech surface's pattern to minimize the hyperbolic volume of the resulting modified surface. Research has demonstrated that key geometric features, particularly geodesic flow on modified surfaces, hold crucial insights into solving this problem. Building upon this finding, we hypothesize that solving the Veech discrete 2-circle problem will provide us with a valuable tool for understanding geodesic flow on these modified surfaces. In turn, we believe that geodesic flow on these surfaces can offer valuable insights into solving the Veech discrete 2-circle problem. By working together, these two concepts may hold the key to providing new insights and making progress on both issues. In this paper, we will delve into the details of geodesic flow on modified surfaces and examine its potential to contribute to solving the Veech discrete 2-circle problem. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of 'twin' surfaces, where corresponding geodesic features allow us to translate between volume properties of the original surface and those of the modified surface. By leveraging these 'twin' surfaces, we show that volume minimization for the Veech discrete 2-circle problem is equivalent to finding a specific geometric configuration on the original surface, which can be approached using concepts from minimal pairs. In turn, we show that minimal pairs, where the hyperbolic volume is close to its ideal value, can be obtained through a different geometric exchange, which raises questions about the existence of such pairs with arbitrarily small hyperbolic volume. In addition, we adapt our findings to contribute to the linear-spectral problem, which involves determining whether certain numbers on the Veech surface can be made arbitrarily close to each other in terms of their distance under a specific geometric transformation. By applying our results to a specific type of surface, which has a complex pattern and has been studied extensively, we find that the linear-spectral problem can be solved positively, which means there exist certain numbers on this surface that can be made arbitrarily close to each other in a specific geometric transformation. In conclusion, we summarize our contributions and future directions, which include finding minimum hyperbolic volumes for the Veech discrete 2-circle problem and determining whether certain numbers on the Veech surface can be made arbitrarily close to each other in a specific geometric transformation. We establish a characterization of k-rationality for hypersurfaces of degree d≥3 and dimension n≥2 through the use of an invariant parameter, specifically the smallest exponent m0, which is 0 if the hypersurface is k-rational and 1 otherwise. Furthermore, it has been found that m0 depends solely on degrees and dimensions, raising the question of whether this is a deliberate choice or an inherent property of k-rationality. Additionally, it is demonstrated that k-rationality can be determined for a specific class of hypersurfaces using m0, but this proves to be insufficient for a broader class of intermediate hypersurfaces. An alternative method for characterizing k-rationality of these intermediate hypersurfaces has been developed. It was also discovered that k-rationality is determined by the type of field and that this property is inherited by hypersurfaces of higher degree and intermediate hypersurfaces. It is speculated that k-rationality is a fundamental property that is inherent to the underlying field, and this theory is supported by findings from related research. Our research provides a clear distinction between two types of k-rationality, namely strong and weak, and it is proposed that these labels be adapted to 'universal' and 'particular', respectively. It is worth noting that many of our conclusions apply not only to hypersurfaces, but also to a broader class of k-rational varieties. It is intriguing to speculate whether the concept of k-rationality is solely a product of the underlying field or an inherent characteristic of the variety itself. As a means of investigating this hypothesis, it is observed how k-rationality interacts with certain subvarieties, specifically their minors. Up until now, it has been widely accepted that k-rationality is an innate property of the field, and this research seeks to verify this notion. As an alternative approach, it is proposed that k-rationality is a fundamental characteristic of the variety itself, and this theory is supported by a wide range of conclusive evidence. To further confirm our findings, it is demonstrated that k-rationality is an invariant property of the variety, unaffected by minor alterations, and this proof is substantiated by a considerable amount of supporting data. Ultimately, it is suggested that k-rationality is an innate characteristic of the field, and this is reflected in the behavior of the variety, as observed through numerous consequences. We present APMSSM, a publicly accessible tool for computing minimal supersymmetry masses, derived from the $a\omega$MSM model which combines QCD axion mechanics with supersymmetric models to resolve the strong CP problem and address the electroweak vacuum's stability. The tool allows users to calculate sparticle masses within the framework of the $a\omega$MSM, taking into account the influence of axions, light pseudoscalars, and MSSM fermions. Users can select from various options for the axion decay constant, $f_a$, and light pseudoscalar mass, $m_{a_\mathrm{light}}$, as well as choices for soft supersymmetry-breaking parameters and higgsino mixing. The tool then produces the masses of bi-doublet gluinos, light flavon fermions, and other supersymmetric particles. Additionally, the code includes implementations of one-loop electroweak symmetry breaking and numerical decay constant derivations. It is accessible through a web interface, where users can input parameters and obtain results, or through a local version that can be run using Python, Python3, or MATLAB. We provide a detailed guide explaining the tool's usage and the underlying physical assumptions. In the appendix, we outline the mathematical formalisms employed by APMSSM. It is worth noting that APMSSM is primarily designed for numerical calculations, but it can also be utilized for analytical studies. We encourage the supersymmetry and early universe cosmology community to use this tool, particularly for investigating the cosmic effects of the $a\omega$MSM model. As such, it is listed on the 'Early Universe Cosmology' software page maintained by the CosmoComputing directory. This research investigates a Tsallis holographic dark energy model with interacting coupling in a universe exhibiting accelerating expansion, constrained by cosmological observations. The study analyzes various cosmological parameters, including deceleration parameter, EoS parameter, energy density, and equation of state graphically. To further examine the model, we calculated the interacting coupling parameter and energy density in a accelerating universe, assuming a Tsallis holographic dark energy model with coupling. The results obtained for the coupling parameter $\gamma$ and energy density $\rho_{TD}$ in terms of the Hubble parameter $H$ show that both increase with $H$, indicating that in a universe undergoing accelerated expansion, the interacting coupling parameter and energy density exhibit direct correlations. Additionally, we compared our model with the non-interacting Tsallis holographic dark energy and found that the inclusion of an interacting coupling parameter leads to differences in the Hubble parameter and energy density. Furthermore, we analyzed the stability of the model by plotting the total energy density and EoS parameter, revealing that the former exhibits two phases: a stable phase with negative energy density and a metastable phase with positive energy density. Notably, these findings demonstrate that the stability of the model is primarily influenced by the EoS parameter rather than the Hubble parameter. Next, we investigated how the constant parameter $c$ affects the EoS parameter and found that for $c<1$, the EoS parameter remains in the metastable region, while for $c\geq 1$, it enters the stable region. Finally, we explored the differences between our model and the non-interacting Tsallis holographic dark energy in terms of the EoS parameter, revealing that the inclusion of an interacting coupling parameter leads to variations, especially at lower Hubble parameters. To validate our findings, we applied the Hubble parameter data from Hubble 2020 and found that the model with interacting coupling parameter results in a better fit than the non-interacting Tsallis holographic dark energy, indicating the importance of considering interacting coupling in cosmological applications. Furthermore, we observed that while the model with interacting coupling predicts a positive energy density, it does not violate the energy conditions, indicating the complexity of the energy spectrum, especially at lower Hubble parameters. This study, one in a series from the LAMOST Time-domain survey, utilizes data collected from SDSS, CRTS, and PTF to establish a binary star catalog based on initial velocity measurements from SDSS and accompanying optical light curve data from SDSS, CRTS, and PTF, as well as semi-manual selections from these sources. A multi-component machine learning algorithm was employed to enhance the accuracy of existing light curves by combining information from various sources and using imputed data to remove missing values. As a result, a binary star data set containing 3497 unique binary candidates was created, comprising systems primarily classified as detached (42%), followed by partially detached (26.8%), overcontact (21.4%), and unknown or undetermined types (10.8%). To reduce discrepancies in photometry, data from SDSS was adjusted using data from CRTS and PTF through an interpolation technique. Although this may introduce minor noise, the revised light curves show improved accuracy and precision, as validated through various statistical measures. A multi-periodogram method was used to determine unknown periods for 1108 binary stars and an automatic fitting approach was employed to solve light curve models for 2997 detached and semi-detached binary stars. Moreover, a cross-correlation technique was applied to calculate orbital elements for 472 binary stars with readily available velocities. We investigated the diffusion of a solute in a solvent with a variable temperature, excluding cases where the solvent molecules interacted in groups. By simulating this process at a molecular level using a model that incorporates the NFTK equation, we discovered that the commonly accepted Einstein relation does not hold when the temperature is unevenly distributed throughout the system. Instead, we found that the diffusion coefficient is directly proportional to the temperature, as opposed to being positively related to the thermal energy. This means that areas with lower temperatures will experience slower diffusion. To confirm our findings, we conducted experiments using a single-component system where we manipulated the temperature gradient and verified that the Einstein relation is indeed invalidated under such non-Uniform temperature conditions. We demonstrated that the gradient of the temperature has a significant impact on the diffusion process, causing the predicted thermal diffusion to be drastically underestimated when the temperature is unevenly distributed. To summarize, our research supports the notion that the Einstein relation will never be accurate in systems that rely on molecular interactions or have uneven temperature distributions. Conversely, the Einstein relation remains relevant and accurate in systems that consist solely of single-component systems with consistent temperatures. A key innovation in cryptocurrency transactions is the use of ring signatures, allowing sources to anonymously transfer funds to a common address.  However, the widespread adoption of ringCT, a ring signature variant, has been hindered by its relatively slow transaction processing speed.  A new delegation-based scheme, Delegated RingCT, has been developed to address this limitation by offering an efficient way for users to delegate their ringCT transactions to a central entity, known as a delegate, for verification.  This removes the need for interactive verification typically required for ringCT transactions.  As a result, Delegated RingCT can increase transaction speed while maintaining the anonymity of users.  Furthermore, Delegated RingCT retains the ability to conceal sensitive information, including transaction amounts and sender information.  Due to its scalability and the ability to protect user privacy, Delegated RingCT is suitable for use in large-scale cryptocurrencies.  The Delegated RingCT scheme consists of four main components: an intuitive proof of knowledge, a modular and efficient delegation of computation, a secure and efficient proof of knowledge, and resistance to linkages.  A formal security analysis of Delegated RingCT, along with its implementation and performance evaluation, is also provided in this paper.  The Delegated RingCT construction is based on a modular approach, combining existing research ideas rather than deriving from a single original source.  Delegated RingCT offers an efficient way to achieve an anonymous and scalable transaction capability, a key requirement for a cryptocurrency. Our research builds upon the foundational work by Datta et al. 2022, adapting their concepts to create a range of reduced solvers for linear systems that can be solved in low-degree multivariate polynomial equations. By leveraging circuit complexity, we demonstrate the feasibility of producing these reduced solvers, which can be derived from each other with minimal additional circuit complexity. Furthermore, we prove the existence of a reduced solver for low-degree resultants with a circuit complexity that is essentially equivalent to solving the resultant itself. Using this reduction framework, we obtain new lower bounds for solving linear systems of various forms, which are consistent with the hardness of solving low-degree multivariate polynomial equations. Notably, our work provides the first known lower bounds for solving linear systems over finite fields in circuit complexity. Additionally, we derive new circuit complexity lower bounds for solving systems of linear equations with restrictions on the rank of the matrix under specific parameters. By applying modular arithmetic, we obtain a range of finite-field linear system solver upper bounds, which are close to our derived lower bounds for certain scenarios, thus nearly closing the gap. These results are also generalized to solve linear systems over other types of rings. Finally, we extend our findings to derive new lower bounds and upper bounds for solving systems of quadratic equations in circuit complexity. These upper bounds are close to our derived lower bounds for specific scenarios, thus nearly closing the gap. These results are also generalized to solve quadratic systems in finite fields and other types of rings. Additionally, we have found that the well-known random projection method does not apply to ell_p spaces when p is not equal to 2. In particular, we illustrate this by calculating the distance preservation ratio for standard ell_p spaces and compare it to the random projection method, which raises the question of whether there are linear dimension reduction operators that approximate the identity transformation. This study introduces a pioneering continual learning technique for neural network models, allowing for effective modeling of complex history-dependent behavior in solid mechanics, like rate-dependent plasticity. By utilizing past experiences to prevent skill loss and adapt new materials without starting from a blank slate, this method significantly enhances model generalization capabilities. Furthermore, it maintains the models' ability to make accurate predictions for previously encountered materials, a crucial feature in industrial settings. The proposed approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations involving multiple materials with varied properties, showing improved performance compared to traditional learning methods. In particular, it outperforms by up to 130% in terms of prediction error when training sequentially on a single material, and by up to 25% when switching between different materials. Therefore, this continuing learning technique has the potential to play a key role in the modeling of history-dependent behavior in solid mechanics. To investigate the impact of radiative cooling with varied thermal conductivity and metal enrichment, we simulated the collective process of conduction and cooling in a 2D array of gas cells. The simulation took place within a static magnetic field, representing the environment of a galaxy cluster. Formulas governing conduction and cooling were adapted from existing literature and implemented in an original code that simulated both processes in a coupled manner. Initially, we set all gas cells to have the same temperature and metallicity parameters. The simulation showed that, in the presence of cold gas islands, a temperature gradient formed perpendicular to the magnetic field direction, causing conduction to occur more slowly in that direction due to reduced efficiency. This led to an increased growth rate of the island's mass, compared to a scenario with usual conduction efficiency, by as much as two times. Furthermore, we observed that a decrease in metal enrichment factors resulted in lower effective cooling rates and consequently allowed cold gas islands to grow more quickly. The contrast between these situations illustrates that both conduction and cooling behave in an anisotropic manner and thus need to be considered together in simulations of galaxy clusters, especially in the presence of magnetic fields. The anisotropic nature of thermal conduction may have a significant impact on the formation of galaxy clusters, particularly through the growth of cold gas islands and the formation of cosmological mini-halos. Conversely, metal line cooling was found to have a smaller effect on these processes.
