We derive exact high-energy strings scattering amplitudes, expressing them in a novel way that connects to the concept of dualities in string theory. Our findings challenge previous theories about string theory's symmetry, particularly the "S-matrix duality" and "emergent S-matrix duality" which suggested a more complex relationship between different strings. Although our results confirm that different strings are not equivalent, we show that there's a more subtle relationship, with the amplitude's form dependent on the specific string being used. Our analysis also raises questions about the existence of a unique "stringy" symmetry. To validate our conclusions, we compare our amplitudes to those obtained from perturbation theory. Our scattering amplitudes align with the conjectured "maximally transcendental" structure of two-loop quantum field theory amplitudes, leading to new hypotheses about the connection between string theory and perturbative quantum field theory. This research introduces a model-driven approach to optimize edge computing energy efficiency by incorporating fine-grained power management and a data center's cooling system. A multi-period linear programming model calculates the optimal configuration for each time period, enabling the adjustment of device settings and data center cooling modes to minimize energy consumption and promote device scalability. A hierarchical division of the timeline into large and small periods facilitates solution simplification and efficient computation. Furthermore, this model addresses constraints related to device loading, temperature stability, and sudden changes in device settings. To address the problem's variability and discontinuities, a two-stage solution strategy is proposed, involving online prediction of period boundaries and offline solution storage. The latter is achieved through chunking, where similar periods are grouped, and an average matrix is created. The model's effectiveness is evaluated using simulated data from a real-edge computing facility. For real-time application, a two-stage decision-making algorithm is implemented, mapping each time period to an indexed chunk and applying the corresponding solution. The model shows promising results, with the entire process taking less than 1 millisecond and yields an optimal energy consumption of 3780 Watts, compared to an average of 4167 Watts when using default settings. The proposed strategy offers a 9% energy consumption reduction and achieves a 31400:1 improvement in solution computation speed, compared to traditional flat power management methods. Follow-up studies using actual facility data yield a 5.8% average energy consumption reduction, along with a 10.4% reduction in cooling energy and a 24100:1 improvement in solution computation speed. Finally, the proposed method achieves a 31400:1 improvement in solution computation speed, along with a 214% increase in scalable devices and a 4% decrease in temperature stability risks. The underlying framework is designed to be adaptable to various scenarios, energy-efficient, and capable of handling multiple constraints. It provides a general solution that can be applied to different practical scenarios, as evidenced by the case study of an edge computing facility. To date, this model remains the first to address power management and cooling optimization in edge computing, facilitating a 9% average energy consumption reduction, a 214% increase in scalable devices, a 4% decrease in temperature stability risks, and a 31400:1 improvement in solution computation speed. The model's efficiency is primarily attributed to its ability to handle fast computations, accurate predictions, and adaptive solution storage. This study develops two novel latent variable models for speech, one transient and the other steady-state, which can capture non-stationary patterns in speech synthesis. By incorporating a time-varying error term into a hidden Markov model framework, the transient model is designed to capture rapid changes in speech characteristics over brief time periods. In contrast, the steady-state model utilizes a stationary error term to capture slower, more gradual patterns in speech. When combined, these two models enable the capture of speech's inherent non-stationarity across various time scales. Experimental results indicate that the combined model outperforms existing speech synthesis models in terms of both naturalness and accuracy in clustering, with clusters identified that are largely consistent across different datasets and evaluation criteria. Furthermore, the model's transient and steady-state clusters display distinct gender-dependent distributions, revealing distinct temporal dynamics in male and female speech. An open-source implementation of the model is available at https://github.com/daniel Field/lvm_nonstationary. Field's thesis, titled "Latent variable models of speech with transient and steady-state components," is based on this work. Optimizing motion planning for multi-limbed robots in complex environments under dynamic constraints is computationally intensive. Current methods often assume valid initial configurations, generate a sequence of poses, and then create a single trajectory, but they don't guarantee joint limits compliance. Additionally, they require significant online adjustments. Our proposed multi-stage optimization framework allows simultaneous generation of a trajectory that meets joint limits, maintains stability, and is easily adaptable to changes in constraints. The framework is composed of multiple stages: initial configuration optimization, trajectory planning, and adjusting the trajectory. The evaluation shows that our method significantly reduces online computation time, eliminates pose adjustment, and yields a more accurate trajectory. The source code is available at https://github.com/saeedagah/multi_limb_motion_planning.

The problem of the cup of coffee has been explored through numerical modeling, 
investigating the influence of pivot placement on cup behavior during horizontal 
movement. When simulated using a mass-scaled model, the observed dynamics differed 
significantly from real-world experiments, where rotating the cup seemed to occur 
around its center. A variable pivot position was introduced in the simulation, 
showing that when positioned off-center, the cup exhibits complex, direction-dependent 
behaviors. When rotated near its edge, the cone shape can become unstable and give 
way to a stationary, off-center equilibrium. A cone model also failed to capture the 
simple rotation seen in early stages of early experiments, where energy was initially 
introduced. These findings highlight the intricacy of this problem, suggesting that 
descriptions of the cup of coffee as a single-degree-of-freedom system are inaccurate. 
Instead, the system's behavior is more accurately represented by considering its 
entire shape and how energy is introduced. This research is part of the 2021 Physics 
competition, where the rotating cup of coffee challenge was posted. All source code 
is accessible at https://github.com/Physics2021/Challenge_4, where further details 
of the model and simulation can also be found. Research was conducted without external funding.

In large-scale machine learning applications, a conventional approach involves dispersing a dataset across multiple devices and training a model in a decentralized environment. This study focuses on improving the convergence rate of Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD) by introducing a simple yet effective process. By allowing devices to take additional model updates, known as "bounces," the convergence rate can be accelerated. More specifically, increasing the number of bounces or iterations proportsally improves convergence while incurring additional communication costs. DR-DSGD can now achieve an asymptotic convergence rate of $O(\sqrt{K} + \sqrt{N/K}\log(T)/\log(\log(T)) + \sigma^2/K)$ for smooth and strongly-convex objectives, surpassing the previous best rate, $O(\sqrt{K} + \sqrt{N/K}\log(K)/\eta + \sigma^2/K)$, found in a prominent paper. Furthermore, the result includes a usable, tight bound for the number of bounces, showing that $O(\sqrt{N}/\eta)$ is the maximum acceptable value, indicating that the number of bounces scales inversely with the step size. In addition to its superior convergence rate, DR-DSGD offers enhanced robustness to hyperparameters, demonstrating its superiority in various numerical experiments. To gain insights into the complex nucleus-nucleus collisions, we introduce a pre-equilibrium period in our thermal model to calculate entropy production. This entropy production is factored into components stemming from quark and gluon degrees of freedom. By incorporating the ratios of final-state hadron yields to entropy production in the pre-equilibrium and equilibrium phases, we refine our thermal model to better replicate the ratios of charged particles observed in experiments. Furthermore, we identify the role of entropy production during the pre-equilibrium phase in enhancing our model's accuracy. Utilizing the simplified Bjorken model, we isolate how factors like geometry and initial conditions influence entropy production. Lastly, we compare the efficacy of our approach to two alternative models. Our findings indicate that, whereas the other models solely rely on equilibrium considerations, our method incorporates essential insights from the pre-equilibrium phase. This work lays the groundwork for future developments in pre-equilibrium hydrodynamics. Additionally, we provide tables summarizing the input parameters for the pre-equilibrium and equilibrium phases, along with calculated quantities for nucleus-nucleus collisions at specific energy levels. Our model outputs align closely with experimental data across multiple energy levels and collision centrality levels. This work ultimately aims to facilitate advancements in the understanding of nucleus-nucleus collisions at lower energy levels. Since it is not always possible to eliminate these factors, which can be seen as system imperfections, a new concept is introduced to address their impact. This paper proposes a new model, which takes into account the role of these factors, to improve system safety by introducing 'compensators' - a type of control mechanism that can mitigate their effects. This safety-enhancing model can serve as a basis for developing more effective safety management policies, ultimately leading to a superior safety culture. This paper demonstrates the efficacy of this new model by applying it to a real-world setting, specifically in the chemical industry. The selected case study investigated the potential safety risks associated with a new technology, known as pressure swing adsorption, which is used to capture carbon dioxide. The study revealed valuable insights into the effectiveness of this technology in minimizing accidents. Our proposed system leverages a graph-theoretic approach to optimize pose and shape estimation, achieving enhanced robustness in the face of data corruption. This robustness is made possible by treating data corruption as node or edge removal/insertion in a graph, where an optimization algorithm determines the most reliable information to utilize. By employing a range-based consensus algorithm after data fusion, we demonstrate considerable resilience to data corruption in various 3D object scenarios. Furthermore, this framework allows for the seamless integration of multiple sensors, such as LiDAR and RGB-D cameras, to estimate objects' 3D shape and pose accurately. By formulating shape and pose estimation as an underlying graph optimization problem, we decouple optimization variables and leverage consensus algorithms to achieve commutative consistency, even with the presence of corruption. Experimental results validate the substantial benefits of our system in maintaining robustness against data corruption. The study of nonlinear control systems with position-dependent dynamics is significant in motion control, where precise tracking is essential. This research investigates how position-dependent dynamics influences motion control, focusing on a nonlinear system of two interacting particles. We develop a trajectory tracking problem, given a reference trajectory, and examine its feasibility and complexity in relation to existing results. Additionally, we explore the stability of an optimal control problem for this system, converting it into a finite-dimensional analysis due to its connections with Scharf's work. This finding highlights the importance of position-dependent dynamics, as two fundamentally different cases arise, depending on how quickly the disturbance term varies with position. This contrasts with linear systems, where a single condition applies. To generalize these results, we utilize a new classification of connected spaces, making the study of topological properties a key aspect. This leads to the definition of a new group, whose classification is essential in distinguishing between stable and unstable optimal control scenarios. This work also finds applications in the study of magnetic nanoparticles under external magnetic fields, an area that has gained significant interest in recent years. Specifically, we consider two types of external fields – a constant field and a time-varying field. By analyzing the characteristics of the disturbance term in the first order approximation, we find that the former corresponds to a position-dependent dynamics with positive topological properties, whereas the latter corresponds to a position-dependent dynamics with negative topological properties. This distinction leads to fundamentally different behaviors in the two cases, as evident from the existence of optimal controls in both scenarios. In fact, we provide a constructive proof for the existence of optimal controls through a series of mathematical transformations that facilitate a direct comparison with a finite-dimensional analysis. This compares nicely with the existing results by Scharf. Furthermore, we extend our findings to a second order approximation, given the presence of viscous forces, by which we establish the existence of optimal controls for both scenarios, accompanied by rigorous estimates. These are the main findings of this research. Additionally, we extend our theoretical analysis to the related area of trajectory equivalence by establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for two trajectory sets to be trajectory equivalent. This evidential analysis is supported through numerous illustrative examples. Lastly, we apply our theoretical findings to the significant scientific problem of controlling magnetic nanoparticles in free space, for which we provide a scientific commentary at the end. Action anticipation in videos has numerous applications in filmmaking and healthcare, and has become a crucial area of study within computer vision. Previous studies have employed spectral models that incorporate kernel-based features, however these models lack the ability to learn from video temporal structures due to the non-parametric nature of existing kernel methods. Our study analyzed flare emissions from the hot plasma and its impact on the surrounding stellar light. We studied high-resolution spectra of 19 flares from K2 IV-V and M V stars, observing significant increases in line broadening and line formation length during the flares. These findings correlate positively with increases in the far-ultraviolet and visible continuum emission. Notably, our data show that line broadening is a more sensitive indicator of the flare's energy influx than other emission measures. Our results also indicate that high-energy particles are inherent in the high-energy photons emitted during the flares, and that line broadening can serve as an indicator of the penetration depth of these flares in the stars' atmospheres. Based on these findings, we developed a new model describing the line broadening caused by flare photons, and established a relationship between line broadening and other emission parameters. This relationship can aid in identifying similar flare emissions in future spectroscopic and photometric observations. Our analysis is applicable to M-dwarf stars, which are expected to exhibit more frequent and intense flares in the upcoming decades. Our research will also contribute to the development of radiation protection strategies for future direct imaging missions searching for exoplanets in the star's vicinity. Recent point cloud models have achieved impressive results, but their susceptibility to image transformations has raised concerns. The TPC framework addresses this limitation by certifying the accuracy of point cloud models against twisting transformations. Previous TPC approaches relied on simplifying assumptions or were only applicable to 1D and 2D data. This paper builds on existing research and proposes an enhanced TPC that can certify 3D point cloud models with complex features and provide accurate predictions on unseen data. The new framework consists of an intermediate feature representation, multiple projection layers, and a prediction head. By introducing a regularizer and carefully selecting model components, we can guarantee the accuracy of the certified predictions. Experimental results demonstrate the success of our TPC framework, with certified 3D object detection accuracy rates exceeding 90% for a range of rotating transformations and point cloud augmentations. Moreover, our approach outperforms traditional 3D object detectors while providing robustness against data augmentation strategies. The source code is available at https://github.com/AttenoTC/TPC-for-3D-Object-Detection.

However, achieving high throughput in these networks is hindered by the limited duration of each packet and the resulting high interference probabilities. To overcome this challenge, we develop a novel transmission technique, called Chirp Packing, which enables multiple radars to transmit and receive information simultaneously, as well as efficiently schedule packet transmissions in high mobility scenarios. By controlling the number of chirps per packet and packet duration, we design a chirp packing strategy that maximizes network throughput, while also reducing interference and packet loss caused by packet timing discrepancies. Our results show that an optimal balance between interference and throughput can be achieved through an appropriate chirp packing configuration, and we propose an iterative algorithm for optimizing chirp packing in FMCW radar networks. Furthermore, we validate our solution by conducting simulations and analyzing the performance of different chirp packing scenarios. Our study indicates that the number of chirps per packet, interference probabilities, and throughput are directly related, as increasing chirps per packet also increases interference, but reduces throughput; on the other hand, high packet duration leads to decreased interference and throughput, but improves packet loss rates. Additionally, we investigate the impact of high mobility on packet loss and demonstrate that using multiple packets for data transmission is a viable solution. However, it also raises concerns about increased interference and throughput efficiency, resulting in a trade-off between packet transmission methods and network throughput. To resolve this trade-off, we examine various packet transmission strategies, such as delaying transmission until successful packet reception, using a retransmission protocol, and combining transmission and retransmission efforts, and evaluate their effects on network performance, specifically interference and throughput. Our analysis indicates that these strategies have distinct impacts on interference and throughput, as delaying transmission until successful packet reception is inefficient, retransmission may not always guarantee successful transmission, and combined transmission and retransmission efforts are optimal in high mobility scenarios. Furthermore, we propose a randomized transmission and retransmission strategy, where radars transmit multiple packets simultaneously and efficiently schedule retransmissions, as a viable solution for improving network throughput in FMCW radar networks. Our results show that this novel transmission and retransmission technique significantly reduces packet loss and increases network throughput, as it accounts for packet timing discrepancies and efficiently utilizes spectral resources, thereby maximizing transmission efficiency. Temporal knowledge graph completion (TKGC) involves predicting unobserved relationships in a temporal knowledge graph. A significant challenge in TKGC is incorporating cycle information, which is often discarded in previous studies due to difficulties in modeling. This paper addresses these difficulties and proposes a novel method using the deep graph encoding of cycle-aware time (DECAT) scheme. By converting cycles into directed graphs and applying node and edge encoding techniques, DECAT leverages cycle information to enhance prediction performance. Experimental results demonstrate that DECAT outperforms current TKGC methods on real-world datasets. Furthermore, DECAT's effectiveness is validated through the discovery of meaningful cycle-embedded temporal relations in various applications. For example, its application in predicting maintenance intervals discovers notable patterns of maintenance activities within the last century. Additionally, its use in understanding historical events reveals new insights into historical battles, particularly that many significant battles took place during times of war characterized by prolonged conflict and little action. Lastly, its application in forecasting solar flares discovers interesting patterns of geospatial distribution and temporal occurrence among reported solar flares. This research ultimately positions cycle information as a vital component in TKGC, which can contribute to practical applications with significant societal impact. By contrast, I argue that infinite sets, characterized by an endless multitude of elements, more accurately correspond to bounded infinity, as they possess a finite conceptuality despite their endlessness. Conversely, I suggest that infinite spacetime, described by Leibniz as both endless and boundless, exemplifies unbounded infinity. Additionally, I contend that infinite possibilities fall somewhere in between, as they are both endless and boundless in their multiplicity. However, I will argue that this objection can be overcome by distinguishing between an endless multiplicity of choices and an endlessness of choices that is not really endless. While the latter would necessitate an endless process of decision-making, the former would simply imply a multitude of choices that can be comprehended within a finite conceptuality. Consequently, the endless multiplicity of choices that are part of an endless world does not necessarily preclude the world from being the best world. under the condition of inverse Gaussian semi-circle distribution.

which corroborate the predicted outcomes.

We develop and investigate a randomized distributed algorithm designed to estimate the size of an unbounded incremental heap-ordered network, where each node maintains a left child and potentially multiple right child nodes, in a random order. We develop an estimation method for the network's overall size by combining individual node views into a compact representation, utilizing spanning trees constructed from this data, which we numerically analyze to derive accurate size estimates, along with associated concentration bounds. We demonstrate that this estimation method yields accurate results, with high probability, whose accuracy approaches the best possible outcome, up to a limited degree of error, in terms of the number of messages exchanged. We investigate the properties of a specific matrix, known as the extended finite impulse response (EFIR) matrix, in the basis pursuit problem. Our results demonstrate how the spectrum of the EFIR matrix affects the number of non-zero components in sparse solutions and ultimately determines whether sparse solutions can be accurately represented in the chosen basis. Our analysis also reveals a fundamental limitation to accurately representing sparse solutions, which arises from the non-normality of the EFIR matrix and the associated instability of the basis pursuit problem. To overcome this limitation, we propose a regularization technique based on the minimum description length principle and provide numerical evidence that supports our findings. Our study focuses on the EFIR matrix due to its relevance in various applications and its distinct properties, which differ significantly from those of the standard Toeplitz matrix. In particular, we show that the spectrum of the EFIR matrix exhibits distinct features, such as non-negativity, non-positivity, and bi-positivity, as well as instability and non-normality, which are uncommon in the spectrum of the standard Toeplitz matrix. Moreover, we illustrate the efficiency of the basis pursuit algorithm in representing sparse solutions at high frequencies, where the EFIR matrix has more desirable properties, such as near-orthogonality and normality. Our work offers novel insights into the properties of the EFIR matrix, which may be of interest in other applications, as well as provides a new direction for future research. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first to thoroughly examine the properties of the EFIR matrix, which has significant implications for the basis pursuit problem and its applications. Our results are supported by numerical experiments, which validate our theoretical findings and highlight the fundamental differences between the properties of the EFIR matrix and those of the standard Toeplitz matrix. A novel mixed finite element method is developed to solve the vector transport equation. By incorporating the conservative variable and the transported vector field as primary and secondary variables, a continuous and discontinuous formulation is created. These components are approximated using a combination of continuous and discontinuous elements, enabling the scheme to overcome issues with standard methods that may encounter difficulties in finding iterative solutions or face convergence problems. A key advantage of this new method is that it yields more accurate vector field representations, which is particularly beneficial in remote regions far from the boundary where the gradient might be low. A thorough convergence analysis is performed, and numerical results confirm that the proposed method 1) achieves optimal convergence rates, 2) produces more accurate conservative approximations, and 3) generates smoother transported vector fields. Furthermore, when the source term is chosen appropriately, the transported vector field retains its $H^1$ smoothness. A comparative study also demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms other approaches, including a non-mixed finite element formulation. This research introduces a novel class of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods tailored to address Hamiltonian ODEs and variational problems. By deriving explicit formulas for the intermediate stages and corresponding flow, it demonstrates that these methods conform to specific well-known constraints. Furthermore, it proves that this new class includes efficient and precise representations of explicit Runge-Kutta methods, such as the Nystrom method. Additionally, it offers a novel interpretation of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods as variations of Neimark-Sacker, Sirlin, and Diagonally inertial methods. Examples and implementations are also provided to validate the findings. The study further provides and tests a continuous adaptation of the Kahan-Nguyen-Quan method. It is also shown that certain continuous-stage RK methods have close connections with implicit methods, as exemplified by the implicit Runge-Kutta methods of Langrishe and Sirlin types. The research specifies that an explicit, multi-stage method can be constructed by truncating a continuous-stage RK method, though not all continuous-stage methods admit valid truncations. A counterexample is presented to illustrate this notion. Last, it is shown that an implicit stage can emerge from a continuous-stage RK method if its polynomial does not have a zero constant term, as illustrated with the implicit Runge-Kutta method of Langrishe type. The research offers a novel understanding of continuous-stage RK methods, providing new insights into the development of efficient numerical methods for solving Hamiltonian ODEs and variational problems. To achieve this goal, it introduces an operator lifting technique that generalizes the concept of solving problems with right-hand side functions to those that require derivative functions as part of their formulation. This operator lifting technique is then applied to explicit, implicit, continuous-stage RK methods in various contexts, such as solving Hamiltonian ODEs, variational problems, and their generalized forms. Recent studies have highlighted the benefits of local critic training (LCT) for
enhancing efficiency in training convolutional and recurrent neural networks.
LCT's effectiveness relies on the localization of errors within smaller network
segments, allowing for more efficient update policies and reduced communication
requirements during distributed training. This paper builds upon previous work by
introducing a new method for error localization in neural networks, which employs
randomness from the backpropagation process to create unique and accurate error
maps. This novel approach is combined with an existing optimization strategy to
form a new learning paradigm, which is found to outperform conventional methods in
terms of efficiency and performance. Experimental results demonstrate the
validity of this new technique, which shows promising potential for
convolutional, recurrent, and fully connected neural networks. Furthermore, this
study also evaluates the efficacy of this new method on distributed training
scenarios, which confirms its ability to significantly reduce communication
overheads. Overall, the proposed technique is found to strike a balance between
efficiency and performance, resulting in a substantial improvement in training
efficiencies while maintaining optimal test accuracies. Based on these findings,
the proposed method is deemed suitable for practical use cases. Details of this
study are presented in an open-source repository: https://github.com/muhoonmoon/LCT_NNSegment.git. The process of star formation (SF) is the foundation for creating new life in the universe, and by comparing formed stars to their surrounding interstellar medium, we can uncover the origins of life itself. To make this comparison, we must have a thorough understanding of both stars and interstellar medium, which requires an extensive, detailed dataset to analyze - a task that's recently become possible through the latest observations and simulations. As a result, it's necessary to standardize these comparisons across different regions of the universe, from nearby to distant. To achieve this, we've developed the Star Formation Benchmark Suite (SFBS), a comprehensive collection of 21 benchmark regions representing diverse SF processes. By applying a well-defined set of physical and chemical measurements, we can ensure consistent comparisons across these regions, allowing us to pinpoint the exact instant when stars begin to form. Furthermore, we've set up a systematic observation program to monitor the evolution of these regions over time, giving us a deeper look into the progression of SF processes. By gathering more data, we can refine our understanding of SF and ultimately gain insight into when and how life emerges in the universe. As a first step, we've presented new findings for 11 benchmark regions from our SFBS dataset, presenting the first-ever standardized comparison of SF and interstellar medium observations. These findings set a benchmark for future research, enabling us to follow the development of SF and life in the universe through a comprehensive set of quantitative measures. To achieve this, we've developed specialized software packages that can accurately reproduce our results, as well as monitor the progression of SF processes in various regions of the universe. By doing so, we can make significant strides in understanding the intricate, interconnected processes of star formation and life in the universe. To view our software packages and access our dataset, visit our website at: https://starformation.github.io/SFBS/.html. Additionally, all research data is available through our website or can be downloaded from the following location: https://smc.astro.uam.es/SFBS/.html. As the primary investigators of this research, we're happy to provide any necessary support to ensure the success of future projects based on our dataset. Conversely, we welcome contributions from other researchers to help expand our dataset, as well as improve our benchmark suite and its associated software. By collaborating, we can accelerate the advancement of star formation research and gain a more in-depth understanding of life in the universe. To get involved, please reach out to us through our website or on GitHub at: https://github.com

The estimated information, or estimated entropy, is a valuable tool that enables the derivation of entropy from noisy, indirectly accessible probability distributions. This study provides a comprehensive overview of estimated information methods, including initial techniques based on entropy estimates through partitioning, nonlinear regression, and scaling. Additional considerations are given to modern approaches rooted in information geometry and machine learning. Specifically, the development is grounded in the quantization problem, which underpins all estimated information methods. A key innovation of this work highlights the universal applicability of these methods to any statistical quantity, not just entropy. The presentation is further characterized by the integration of both fundamental theoretical insights and practical algorithmic implementations. Ultimately, the aim is to make estimated information methods more accessible to researchers, with the hope that they will be more widely utilized in scientific and engineering fields. These methods are demonstrated to be effective in analyzing complex, high-dimensional data sets, which are inseparable from the concept of irreducibility. Consequently, the study also offers a thorough examination of the irreducibility of probability distributions, a notion that can be efficiently quantified through the estimated information framework. As a concrete demonstration, the capacity of information channels is treated as a natural instance of estimated information, which enables the calculation of irreducibility and asymptotic irreducibility to be determined directly from observed data. Additionally, the use of estimated information methods is suggested as a valuable strategy for characterizing the functional properties of nonlinear dynamical systems. The application to sleep patterns in a human population serves as a suitable case study to illustrate the effectiveness of these methods. The analysis is completed by employing machine learning tools to build a sleep prediction model over extended periods of time, which is grounded in the estimated information framework. A related software package is available for download at https://git.io/VDLWm.

Classifying malicious URLs in binary is crucial for protecting connected devices, but creating a lightweight system to support this task is a difficult challenge. The number of training labels required for effective binary classification is excessively high, exceeding what's currently available in labels for URL data. To tackle this issue, we've developed a tool called NBcoded, which uses an advanced encoding technique to tackle the label scarcity problem. By leveraging knowledge from an established URL classifier, NBcoded enhances the performance of lightweight classifiers on resource-constrained devices, while also providing a platform for fine-tuning these classifiers using device-generated data. The effectiveness of NBcoded has been confirmed through experiments, which show improved accuracy when using the encoded classifier over a previously trained classifier without enhancements. Additionally, NBcoded enables the utilization of device data to refine existing knowledge, indicating a potential application in maintaining up-to-date knowledge on malicious patterns with limited scope. The source code for NBcoded is publicly available on GitHub at the URL: https://github.com/advanced-threat-detection/NBcoded. NBcoded supports classification of two types of data: binary URLs and network flows. The tool can be accessed through a command-line interface that's available for download from the NBcoded GitHub page. The steady drift dynamics of objects falling through a fluid are commonly modeled using well-established equations, but unsteady drag forces and measurement inaccuracies can complicate this picture. Researchers have developed a novel data-driven method to identify the dynamic behavior of objects falling through a fluid, despite noisy measurement data. This new approach relies on a state-space representation and an extended Kalman filter to identify the drag coefficient and fluid density from time-series data. Simulation studies have shown that this method accurately determines these key parameters, even in the presence of significant measurement errors. Furthermore, real-world experiments confirming earlier observations of the Goldstein effect, where the drag coefficient can vary based on the object's velocity, are also successfully replicated using the developed state-space model. A special case was considered for objects experiencing a sudden force, resulting in a successful recovery of the parameters influencing this impact. This research has successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of data-driven modeling for describing the complex dynamics of objects falling through a fluid. Additionally, the developed state-space model has potential applications in analyzing data obtained through other means. For instance, this approach could be used to study the influence of a sudden force on the motion of a projectile, which could be applied in airburst fragmentation modeling. Future work will focus on eliminating the requirement for a pre-defined force law and on incorporating partial information, which may be useful in certain practical situations. Deep learning's effectiveness relies heavily on its feature representations, which often serve as the backbone for modeling success. While handcrafted features are efficient, they're inherently bound by their design and can't surpass their creation date. Conversely, deep learning model outputs possess unparalleled potential but suffer from unpredictability in their output quality. We introduce Bonsai, an algorithmic framework allowing us to harness the best aspects of both worlds by converting a trained deep learning model into a set of optimized, highly effective features. Bonsai's feature construction is guided by an iterative, constrained search algorithm that explores a tree of potential feature combinations, evaluating their utility at each node along the way. The process is accelerated through Bonsai's pre-computed feature space, a database of previously constructed features and their corresponding attributes. The algorithm's search process is also adaptable, allowing us to curb computational costs and adjust the trade-off between feature optimization and construction speed. Evaluations across five diverse NLP datasets show Bonsai's capabilities in generating high-quality features, often rivaling state-of-the-art models while requiring significantly fewer model evaluations. Numerical examples demonstrate the efficiency and practicality of this new model. Furthermore, we develop a simulation-based inference framework, which incorporates Markov chain Monte Carlo, for estimating the model's parameters. We apply this new framework to analyze the Nestorn-Uhlenbeck approximate inverse Gaussian model, yielding valuable insights into its theoretical properties. Lastly, we employ the model to price real-world inflation-indexed securities, such as German and Swiss bonds, resulting in precise exact match benchmarks that can be utilized for model selection and efficiency assessment. Our study reveals that the Nestorn-Uhlenbeck approximate inverse Gaussian model outperforms the nested Ornstein-Uhlenbeck and Garch models in European and Bermudan annuity pricing tasks. The Diophantine equation $x^a-1=x^{a+b}$ has a solution for two positive integers $a$ and $b$, which has been previously undiscovered. According to the proof, the values of $a$ and $b$ are specifically 3 and 6, respectively. This equation can be rewritten as $(x^{1/2}-1)(x^{1/2}+1)(x^{1/2^2}-1)\cdots (x^{2^{a-1}}-1)=0$, which illustrates that any solution requires that the first factor, $x^{1/2}-1$, equal zero. Consequently, $x$ must be a perfect square. Furthermore, the set of all possible $x$ values, where $x$ is a perfect square, can be defined using the equation $x=(y+1)^2$, where $y$ is an integer. Substituting this perfect square $x$ into the original equation, it becomes evident that any solution requires that the exponents in the equation $x^{a+b}=x^a\cdot x^b$ both be even, except in the special case where $x=0$. Additionally, it has been discovered that for any given even exponent, there exists a solution for the equation $(x+1)^2=x^a\cdot x^b$, which has significant implications for the original equation and a broader class of similar equations. Consequently, it can be concluded that the number of solutions for the equation $x^{a+b}=x^a\cdot x^_b$ is infinite. This new discovery generalizes a previous finding, which was specifically for the case of equal exponents, and was made possible through an observation of the $x=1$ solution, as well as an evaluation of the graph of functions $f(x)=\log(x)-\log(x^b)-\log(x^{ab})$, which reveals that the equation has a solution for the case of odd exponents $a$ and $b$. Finally, it has been discovered that the number of solutions for the equation $(x+1)^2=x^a\cdot x^b$ is limited to only three, specifically with the exponent pairs of $(2,6)$, $(3,6)$, and $(5,10)$, which has significant implications for the original equation and a broader class of similar equations. Consequently, it can be concluded that the equation has an infinite number of solutions.

This research examines the dynamics of a liquid jet flowing through a channel filled with another liquid, focusing specifically on the regions where the two fluids meet. Unlike most studies, which only consider the interface where the jet meets the surrounding liquid, this study also explores the opposite interface where the jet itself meets another liquid within the channel. Governed by the same Rayleigh-Taylor instability principles as the more commonly studied interface, this interface's behavior is largely influenced by the ratio of its wavenumbers and the difference in fluid densities. However, factors such as wall confinement, viscous effects, and air pockets can alter the instability timescale and cause it to deviate from the expected linear behavior. Moreover, when the jet is considered as the surrounding fluid, the instability growth rates become linear with time rather than exponentially growing, as the air pockets affect the instability dynamics in both cases. In an effort to simplify the complex problem, this study provides analytical solutions for the linear instability phases as well as numerical simulations to model the subsequent non-linear phase, ultimately highlighting the importance of accurately modeling the air pockets to understand the liquid-liquid interface dynamics. These findings are then applied to analyze the geochemical layering instability in oceanic basins during large-scale geochemical mixing events. This study examines how the statistical properties of three-body systems behave in terms of escape dynamics when subjected to various types of non-ideal interactions. Utilizing numerical simulations, we analyzed the escape patterns of systems consisting of three uniformly massive particles, both in scenarios where they followed ideal (Newtonian) physics, as well as when non-ideal interactions were introduced through a universal gravitation constant slightly greater than 6.67 $\times$ 10$^{-8}$ cm^2 g^-1. A comprehensive statistical analysis was conducted to compare the results with predictions based on a previously established three-body collision model. A thorough examination of 100,000 unique three-body systems was performed, yielding substantial findings that include: (1) Both the distribution of escape probabilities and the correlation between escape probabilities and energies in non-ideal systems align closely with their ideal counterparts. (2) However, when the universal gravitation constant is relatively small (less than about 6.85 $\times$ 10$^{-8}$ cm^2 g^-1), a discrepancy is observed in the distribution of escape probabilities, particularly at lower energy levels, where it diverges from the predicted statistical distribution based on the three-body collision model. (3) A comparison of the correlation between escape probabilities and energies in non-ideal systems with the predicted correlation reveals a notable discrepancy, especially at higher energy levels, where it diverges from the predicted statistical distribution based on the three-body collision model. (4) Finally, both types of systems (ideal and non-ideal) share a common feature in their statistical behavior, as both exhibit identical distributions of second escape probabilities, consistent with predictions obtained through analytical methods. A thorough discussion of these findings is provided, along with a brief overview of the three-body collision model used in this study. This model is seen as a useful tool for understanding and describing the statistical properties of three-body systems, with potential applications in astrophysical contexts. Additionally, this work contributes to the broader field of statistical mechanics by investigating general principles governing the statistical behavior of systems consisting of three or more interacting particles. This research may be of interest to researchers working in the fields of statistical mechanics, astrophysics, and general three-body systems. Moreover, the methods employed in this study are versatile and can be adapted to investigate non-ideal systems governed by interactions other than gravity, as illustrated through a discussion of future work. Deep learning sequential models have achieved great success in various applications. However, these models that utilize Bi-LSTM/GRU often struggle with long sequences due to their limitations in handling information over lengthy timelines. To address this limitation, research has focused on designing internal feedback mechanisms or utilizing external attention schemes that help these models capture both long-term and short-term information efficiently. To address these issues, this paper presents the DepAttn bi-LSTM and bi-GRU models that integrate deprioritized attention directly into the cell state and gate update equations, enabling these models to selectively capture information from both short and long sequences effectively. Experimental results on benchmark datasets indicate that DepAttn models outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in sentiment analysis and action recognition tasks. Notably, the DepAttn models can be easily extended to support deep sequential models that incorporate bidirectional and hybrid architectures. This research suggests that deprioritized attention is a useful technique for designing internal feedback mechanisms within deep sequential models. The well-known subset sum problem involves finding distinct subset sums of a specific size within a given range, but only using a portion of available elements. Previously, it was thought that solving this problem required at least O(2^n) time, where n is the number of elements, due to lower bounds. This note presents a denotational and an operational probabilistic semantics for higher-order, imperative programs that utilize mutable references. In contrast to typical operational probabilistic semantics, which focuses on trace reduction, our denotational approach within a trace-based framework adheres strictly to the denotational methodology, abstracting from low-level reduction traces. The operational semantics we introduce merges aspects of trace and abstract operational methodologies, defining a hybrid reduction relation derived directly from a denotational counterpart. Both the denotational and operational semantics we developed are proven equivalent, showing that a program's meaning is unaffected by whether it is described through a denotational or an operational framework. Additionally, our study provides a novel demonstration of the equivalence between trace-based and abstract operational semantics methods. However, the example also reveals limitations of the trace-based method, as it is unable to accommodate program components that examine the history of context-free traces. Finally, we outline a possible remedy for this shortcoming, suggesting an extension of the trace-based framework that incorporates the concept of 'amnesia traces' – a type of trace that forgets past context information. Despite this potential enlargement, the paper still encounters a limitation in expressing program behaviors that involve the analysis of previous traces. For a comprehensive solution to this challenge, see our companion paper, 'Probabilistic Higher-Order Mutually Recursive Procedures: Trace-Based Denotational, Operational, and Hoare Styles'. Both papers were inspired by an idea from Richard Bellud's thesis.

Recent advancements in design mining have yielded impressive results by leveraging large datasets of design documents. However, conclusion stability and cross-project relevance remain significant challenges, particularly due to the inherent variability of design conclusions across different projects. This study presents two novel approaches that contribute to enhancing conclusion stability and increase relevance across projects: first, a pre-valuation method that utilizes an expert's subjective assessment to refine conclusion clustering; second, a cross-project translation technique that translates frequent design conclusions from one domain to another based on semantic similarity. This research offers valuable insights into effectively extracting meaningful conclusions from large design datasets, paving the way for more accurate design knowledge capture and cross-domain design knowledge transfer. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of pre-valuation in boosting conclusion stability, while the cross-project translation method achieves state-of-the-art results comparable to those obtained through in-domain fine-tuning in Natural Language Inference tasks. Furthermore, the study presents an innovative DesignMine benchmark, a large-scale dataset of 315m conclusions from over 140 diverse design projects, complemented by expert-curated valuations for 38 projects. This benchmark facilitates fair evaluation and state-of-the-art baselines for design mining tasks. Based on this benchmark, the proposed methods outperform existing alternatives in conclusion clustering accuracy and cross-project translation performance. Ultimately, this research achieves state-of-the-art results on valuation prediction metrics, specifically achieving a 0.733 F1 score, which represents a notable 0.133 F1 score improvement over previous design mining studies. In the field of machine learning, datasets are frequently partitioned into groups based on their labels or other characteristics, yet standard optimization algorithms fail to exploit these divisions. By detecting the differentiability manifolds within these groups, our method allows for adapting the optimization procedure, effectively reducing the dimensionality of each group and thus facilitating faster convergence. The technique employs a novel check to determine if a dataset is differentiable, along with an efficient split-Atan method for optimizing parameters and estimating gradient directions. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms established baselines across multiple applications. The proposed framework shows promise for detecting differentiability manifolds and offers potential applications beyond data labeling. Furthermore, our research successfully removes the reliance on explicit error bounds in vector extrapolation, making it more versatile. By measuring the lag between the signals in the cross-correlation spectrum, we can determine the direction and distance of a potential source. This technique leverages the symmetry of the cross-correlation, converting the complex geometric relationships between sensors and the source into a simpler, more interpretable format. Using the example of a gamma-ray telescope, the study demonstrates how the proposed method can be applied to lightweight, miniature devices. Furthermore, the proposed technique has the potential to be implemented in multiple disciplines, such as radio astronomy and dark matter research. The results from our experiments confirm the substantial performance gains when agents can simulate multi-agent scenarios, and the introduced limitations successfully mitigate the discrepancies between simulated and real settings.  The observed outcomes align with our theoretical analysis, showing the advantages of our method over baseline imitations.  The proposed technique achieves state-of-the-art results on existing benchmarks, and we provide a new collaborative task for the evaluation of imitation learning. Research suggests that angular momentum plays a crucial role in the formation of planets and stars.  Past theoretical studies indicated that conserving angular momentum in expanding gas clouds resulted in the clouds's radial structure influencing the rate of fragmentation.  However, these studies took into account neither non-uniform density nor radial structure.  A recent numerical simulation by Stephenson and Brocksopp analyzed the radial structure and density of the Angelfish nebula and surrounding molecular cloud.  Their analysis considered data from the Infrared Fundamental Catalogue and submillimeter mapping by the Herschel Space Observatory.  The resulting radial velocity maps and vector plots suggest that the cloud's velocity patterns follow a rotating elliptical shape. Individuals struggling with mental health issues are more likely to engage in criminal behavior.  Various studies have examined the link between mental health treatment and crime reduction, yielding mixed results.  Two key issues have been the accuracy of diagnostic procedures and the potential biases in studying mental health treatments.  A major concern is that certain mental health diagnoses may be selectively applied to repeat offenders, while other diagnoses may be preferentially diagnosed in non-offenders.  Another issue is that mental health treatments are sometimes chosen based on the type of crime committed, rather than being an effective solution for the underlying mental health issue.  To address these concerns, a novel approach was developed by treating each county as a test environment in which to apply statistical models of optimal diagnostic procedures and crime reduction strategies.  This approach was applied to data on individuals diagnosed with mental health issues in Florida.  The research revealed that, while certain mental health diagnoses may be beneficial in reducing specific types of recidivism, the optimal diagnostic procedure and crime reduction strategy varied significantly depending on the county and the type of crime, and were found to have no connection with each other.  The findings suggest that, in order to design an effective mental health treatment policy, the relationship between diagnostic procedures and crime reduction should be broken, and a more impartial approach to diagnosing and prescribing mental health treatments should be explored. This research uses a unified approach to derive key properties of specific polynomials, including those related to Fibonacci, Lucas, central, and Hermite polynomials. A fundamental property of these special polynomials is that they can be expressed using generating functions, which also serve as cumulative generating functions for various other polynomials. By utilizing a generating function approach, many of their important properties can be easily demonstrated. Building on this framework, several key properties of the polynomials can be derived directly from the corresponding generating functions. Notably, this method enables a straightforward derivation of multiple identities for Fibonacci and Lucas polynomials. A key advantage of the generating function method is that it facilitates the easy identification of recurrence relations for central and Hermite polynomials. Furthermore, it enables the direct derivation of numerous other identities, particularly for Fibonacci and Lucas polynomials. In addition, the study of their generating functions provides insight into their connection to exponential generating functions and reveals a general framework for special polynomials, which can be applied to other well-known polynomials, such as the Dickson polynomials. A notable finding is that Fibonacci and Lucas polynomials satisfy the same exponential generating function, which confirms the existing hypothesis that the two sets of polynomials are linearly dependent. In support of this conclusion, it is observed that both Dickson and Hermite polynomials also share the same property. A comprehensive study of their generating functions reveals that the generating functions for central polynomials factor into the product of a Fibonacci generating function and a Lucas generating function, while for Hermite polynomials, they factor into the product of a Dickson generating function and a central generating function. A notable connection is also discovered between the Dickson polynomials of the second kind and the reciprocal zeros of certain Hermite polynomials. A key advantage of the generating function approach is its versatility and the ease with which new properties of special polynomials can be derived from it. As a testament to its utility, this study successfully employs it to derive numerous previously known properties of the polynomials in question. A key distinction of this research is its innovative use of the generating function method to analyze special polynomials, which provides a fresh and unified perspective on their existing properties. A key goal of this study is to demonstrate the potential of the generating function approach, while also contributing new identities to the existing literature on special polynomials. In order to optimize radio map creation through measurement collection, a reliable indicator of map uncertainty is needed. This letter presents a new metric for calculating map uncertainty by comparing actual to simulated radio signal measurements, allowing for the adaptation of radio map models in advance of those measurements. This metric is further utilized to develop an efficient measurement scheduling strategy, in which antenna positions are selected based on the greatest expected reduction in map uncertainty. This method is validated using 20 MHz LTE signal measurements in a 4-room building, in comparison to a random measurement collection approach. Results indicate that this optimized schedule yields a 35% reduction in map uncertainty in under 5 minutes, with little change after that time. Additionally, this method demonstrates superior performance to other existing measurement scheduling strategies. Details regarding the building and used signal information can be found in the appendix. Detecting anomalies in unsupervised learning is a prominent issue without the constraints of labeled data. The goal in anomaly detection is to identify data points that deviate from the normal pattern or contain inconsistencies, often found in self-driving systems, medical diagnostics, network intrusion detection, and manufacturing quality control. The identification of anomalies can be seen as a supervised learning problem if we consider anomaly data as a separate class, but this approach is impractical due to the difficulty and expense of labeling anomalous data. As a result, researchers have developed various unsupervised anomaly detection methods using clustering, support vectors, generative models, and feature scaling. The depth k-means algorithm is a modified version of the traditional clustering technique that uses a determined number of iterations to terminate, but it has limitations in performing unsupervised anomaly detection. To overcome these limitations, a new method based on depth k-means and approximate Bayesian inference is proposed to calculate the probability of anomaly without specifying a distribution or requiring labeling. The approach involves creating clusters from the data and calculating the likelihood of anomalous points having certain data points as their sole cluster members. The performance of this method is compared with other anomaly detection techniques using synthetic and real-life datasets. The results show that, similar to depth k-means, this approach is suitable for verifying the presence of anomalies but may not precisely identify anomalous data points. The main contribution of this research is in approximate Bayesian inference for depth k-means, allowing for the generation of probabilistic representations of normal data and identifying anomalies based on those probabilities. The method is reasonable in its assumptions and efficient in its computational requirements. The code is publicly available on GitHub. Our study evaluates the effectiveness of verification systems designed for natural language inference tasks in two different settings. The first setting features standard sentence pairs used in NLI as test data, while the second setting incorporates artificially introduced flaws in the same data. Notably, the flaws introduced in this study affect both sentences of a pair, whereas real-world NLI data often presents sentence-level noise alone. Our analysis reveals varying levels of verification system performance under clean and noisy conditions, with systems like ofa and COMPLEx exhibiting relative robustness to the introduced flaws. The findings suggest that NLI data enhancement through augmentation can be beneficial but may not always align with the NLI inference task as formulated. Furthermore, this study provides NLI models with a new level of scrutiny by evaluating their performance in a challenging, heavily noisy environment, much like that of real-world data. In machine learning, augmenting data changes the outcome unpredictably. Specifically, advancements gained from this process on natural language processing tasks depend on various factors, including the amount of initial training data and how the data is processed. This research investigates the effect of several variables on the outcome to provide clarity and establish a standard method for effectively using data augmentation in natural language models.

The study examines the impact of data augmentation on 8 distinct tasks drawn from the HLMT (Health, Law, Medicine, and Technology) dataset, which is widely used for studying semantic role labeling. Each task was completed using the Hugging Face Transformers library and the FastAI library, both with and without data augmentation, employing two different augmentation techniques: token substitution and sentence reordering. Additionally, the analysis considers the influence of varying initial training data sizes on the outcome.

The findings indicate that token substitution yields more consistent and notable improvements than sentence reordering. Furthermore, the study shows that data augmentation is highly effective when training on limited data but adds little value to the outcome for models trained on extensive data. These findings are consistent across all examined tasks. Based on these discoveries, the research offers guidelines for implementing an effective data augmentation strategy that is standard, straightforward, and easy to reproduce. This research specifically looks into the augmentation of question formation techniques, leading to a notable improvement of 2 F1 points after 5 hours of training. This outcome serves as a benchmark, demonstrating the value of using data augmentation for enhancing natural language processing models. This study investigates how weakly convergent estimators of parameter functions converge uniformly in probability. Building on this, we establish conditions for the convergence of estimators of smooth functions of parameters. Specifically, we leverage these results to examine the asymptotic behavior of estimators in generalized linear models, mixed effects models, and functional linear regression. Ultimately, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, the estimators of these models are uniformly almost-surely strongly consistent. Furthermore, we extend the findings to obtain the uniform convergence in probability of estimators of functions of parameters in other statistical models, including those with non-ergodic behavior. To achieve this, we draw upon modern tools, such as the use of $\beta$-mixing, coupled with specific bounds on the weighted average of estimator variances. The findings of this work are illustrated through the analysis of real-data examples. Moreover, we apply and contribute to the development of alternative estimators that outperform existing models in terms of efficiency. Specifically, these estimators improve upon those for the functional linear regression, mixed effects models, and the generalized linear models, particularly when the working model is a semiparametric model. The new estimators possess the same asymptotic properties as the original models. The theoretical findings are implemented through numerical simulations that validate the performance of these estimators in practice. The associated software can be found under the repository name 'Estimatortoolbox' on GitHub. The key contributions of this study are the extension of existing asymptotic results to a broader range of statistical models, the development of new estimators with superior efficiency, and the application of modern tools in statistical estimation theory. The new model estimators offer improved efficiency over existing models for various applications, including generalized, mixed effects, and functional linear regression models. The wide applicability of these findings is demonstrated through the analysis of real-data examples. The new estimators also provide better performance, coupled with improved complexity of computational requirements. The rise of data protection regulations such as GDPR and CCPA has sparked significant interest in incorporating data privacy considerations into data management systems. Current research on privacy-preserving data sets overlooks the interconnections between individual data records, failing to consider how these relationships (dependencies) might compromise privacy. Our investigation explores how these dependencies exacerbate privacy breaches, especially in data sets derived from small populations (like those of medical or sporting institutions). Utilizing the framework of information-theoretic privacy, we quantify the level of privacy exposure when data holders request information from data providers, finding that record dependencies indeed increase the risk of privacy breaches. To address this, we devise an algorithm for data collectors to assess the extent of dependencies among data records and propose a method (based on conditional mutual information) for determining the minimum required data set size to guarantee record independence. Our results highlight that data collectors often need larger data sets than those recommended by the standard K-NN approach and that dependencies in data sets with limited sizes (like those of small populations) significantly increase the required data set size. By analyzing C$_2$H emission in 20 GHz channels, we observed the molecule's presence in regions closer to the star compared to CO and [O I], with its column density highly correlated with CO levels. However, in some disks, C$_2$H exceeded CO by a factor of 10 in outer regions. We discovered that C$_2$ H column densities varied significantly with the C/O ratio and found a positive correlation in most disks. Notably, when C/O > 1, there was a positive correlation between C$_2$ H column density and gas mass in inner regions, whereas this relationship flipped in outer regions. This suggests that C$_2$ H acts as an efficient tracer of gas masses in the disk's outer parts when C/O > 1. When C/O < 1, we found a positive correlation between C$_2$ H column density and gas mass in all areas, with C$_2$ H generally offering a more accurate measurement. We propose a model where C$_2$ H column density is influenced by the C/O ratio and gas mass in the disk's surface layers, with C/O's effect diminishing at lower C/O values. Model predictions are highly consistent with observed patterns, suggesting that the disk's surface layers play a significant role in determining the molecule's emission. Model simulations of C$_2$ H also enabled a more accurate calculation of the gas mass in disk CO, with gas masses varying between 1.3 and 4.4 solar masses. In the realm of mean field games, the constant pursuit is on to specify end conditions for differential equations that capture the essence of equilibrium play. Our work focuses on a specific class of mean field games governed by Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations, particularly those with constant coefficients. We find that under fairly standard assumptions - including equilibrium smoothness - the equilibrium equilibrium can be characterized as a smooth function that satisfies a specific partial differential equation. However, when these smoothness assumptions are relaxed, the equilibrium equation is no longer well-defined, revealing a key challenge to the standard mean field games framework. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach based on the use of initial conditions, no longer requiring the equilibrium to be smooth. This new method is compatible with standard existence results for differential equations and allows the construction of equilibrium trajectories that are continuous in time. To illustrate the applicability of this approach, we consider two specific examples - a continuous-time driving game and a planning decision-making model - demonstrating how the equilibrium equations can be explicitly defined and solved. These examples include scenarios in which the equilibrium dynamics are inherently stochastic, a phenomenon not previously observed in mean field games. Ultimately, our work provides a framework for solving a broad class of mean field games involving continuous-time actions, opening up new avenues for application and research. To keep the presentation accessible, we have included an extensive collection of supplementary materials, including an alternative explanation of our approach, a detailed review of key concepts and results, and the formal analysis of two specific counterexamples. These additional resources are intended to facilitate the understanding of our work, addressing potential questions and criticisms from fellow researchers. Individual fashion item creation is an innovative yet error-prone process, leading to outfits that don't quite match. As consumers increasingly expect personalized fashion, the demand for correcting styling mistakes has risen. Current methods rely on expert manual inspection but are expensive, time-consuming, and limited by the expertise and capacity of these inspectors. We introduce a novel approach, introducing a new task type and a corresponding dataset, dubbed MismatchDetect. This dataset is specifically designed to improve detection accuracy when identifying fashion items that don't fit together. We've also developed a range of new models based on state-of-the-art architecture and unsupervised methods that can identify mismatching items in outfits. These models outperform existing alternatives, setting a new benchmark in accuracy. Notably, our unsupervised model performs nearly as well as the supervised method, indicating a significant cost savings in training these models. With these advances, the detection of mismatching items can now be done more efficiently, paving the way for a more automated and fashion industry-changing process. Existing Gibbs sampling-based algorithms for sparse grid Markov chain Monte Carlo have been shown to be ineffective in policy evaluation for large-scale reinforcement learning tasks. In contrast, we introduce the sparse grid polynomial Gauss-Seidel SARSA (SPGP-SARSA) algorithm, a novel approach that accelerates sparse grid Markov chain Monte Carlo using the SARSA-Nash policy. By leveraging the SARSA-Nash policy, the SPGP-SARSA algorithm enhances the efficiency of policy evaluation, allowing for a significant reduction in the computational time required. Experimental simulations of underwater navigation tasks have demonstrated a substantial speedup of the SPGP-SARSA algorithm over previous implementations. Furthermore, the SPGP-SARSA algorithm exhibits superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art algorithms in these tasks. Experimental results suggest that the SPGP-SARSA algorithm is suitable for large-scale reinforcement learning tasks characterized by partial observability, multiple action options, and sparse rewards. In particular, the SPGP-SARSA algorithm is shown to be particularly effective in underwater navigation tasks with partial observability. In addition to its success in these practical domains, the SPGP-SARSA algorithm is found to be one of the most accurate algorithms in theoretical evaluations. The SPGP-SARSA algorithm is implemented in an open-source repository at https://github.com/alecgoodman/spgp-sarsa. The detailed description of algorithms, experimental procedures, and data analysis can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.11522. The associated code for these experiments is available at https://github.com/alecgoodman/spgp-sarsa. By building on connections between kernel regression and Riesz representer theorems, our work develops a unified framework for understanding these projections in an operator-theoretic context. Key advantages of our method include improved convergence and more accurate approximations, achieved through a smoother representation of the underlying operator. A crucial aspect of our approach is the ability to control approximation errors by selecting suitable kernel regularization parameters. To facilitate practical applications, we present a novel, adaptive strategy for choosing these parameters, along with an assessment of its performance. Experimental results confirm that our method surpasses conventional parametric projection methods in terms of convergence, while also demonstrating the effectiveness of its kernel-regularized form. Furthermore, we show that our approach is general enough to be applied to multivariate datasets, illustrated by results from spectral analysis and regression. Furthermore, it establishes relationships between the $	eta$-analogues and other notable combinatorial structures, such as the q-Dowling polynomials and the Dowling numbers. To validate the $	eta$-analogues, the article presents a recursive generating function for these polynomials based on the combinatorial concept of chains in partially ordered sets. Additionally, it provides a theoretical framework for proving the validity of the $	eta$-analogues using the principles of free Lie algebras. Several illustrative examples are included to demonstrate the application of the $	eta$-analogues in mathematics. Overall, the study offers an innovative approach to extending mathematical concepts to the realm of Lie algebras. Recent research has achieved significant progress in modeling temporal knowledge graphs. Nevertheless, current models have several limitations, particularly the assumption that knowledge graph embeddings are static. Real-world knowledge graphs, however, often include time-related attributes like valid-time and duration. These attributes are missing from static embeddings, making it difficult to model them directly. A possible solution is to use time-dependent knowledge graph embeddings, which can effectively capture temporal properties. A notable example is the TimeGKE model. While TimeGKE effectively addresses the issue of valid-time, it overlooks duration's influence on the embedding of the same entity. A new model, called DiS-TimeGKE, addresses this issue by introducing a novel scoring function and an optimized objective function based on the linear layer. A comprehensive comparison between DiS-TimeGKE and TimeGKE on diverse datasets demonstrates the former's superior performance. Additionally, DiS-TimeGKE achieves competitive results on datasets incorporating only valid-time attributes, validating its effectiveness. The source code is available at https://github.com/jfjoffrey/Dis-TimeGKE. The knowledge graph embeddings used in the experiments are available at https://knowledge-graph-embeddings.github.io.

In the quest for more accurate language models, researchers have explored combining existing models with knowledge graphs, which have proven invaluable in addressing questions and performing other tasks. However, incorporating knowledge graphs can be costly in terms of memory and computation, making it difficult to integrate them into pre-trained language models. To tackle this issue, a new model called OREO-LM has been developed, which compacts knowledge graphs into a compact form and incorporates them into the model architecture. Specifically, OREO-LM is designed with an innovative Knowledge Interaction Layer that enables the model to interact with its embedded knowledge, and it is constructed by merging object knowledge with existing BERT-type models. Empirical results have confirms OREO-LM's effectiveness, with the model outperforming other leading language models and knowledge-graph-based models on question-answering tasks. Furthermore, when supplemented with additional training on question-answering tasks, OREO-LM achieved an astonishing 14.44% improvement in accuracy on the Semantic Matching Bank dataset. Given its remarkable performance and compact design, which results in only a 10% increase in model parameters, OREO-LM is an attractive choice for enhancing pre-trained language models.
