Recent advances in large language models have shown potential risks of biased results due to biased prompts, undermining their trustworthiness. Nonetheless, most existing studies overlook the issue of unseen prompts during inference time. This study investigates the consequences of unseen prompts on LLMs, uncovering two key biases: biased language and biased inferences. To mitigate these biases, we develop a novel quantification method, prompting de-biasing, incorporating both post-hoc feature extraction and pre-holing techniques. The latter involves omitting key words in prompts to prevent specific biases. The effectiveness of our approach is validated through experiments on both CoLA and PMI datasets. The results indicate that with the incorporation of our de-biasing techniques, LLMs can reduce biased results by as much as 0.55-0.61 on the CoLA dataset and 0.03-0.06 on the PMI dataset. The research also reveals that pre-holing has a limited effect, prompting de-biasing to be the primary driver of improvement. Additionally, while LLMs exhibit biased inferences on unseen prompts, they generally avoid extreme inferences, revealing a grading pattern of biased results. The success of our de-biasing techniques is attributed to their capacity to alter prompt semantics. The research is made available online at https://huggingface.com-space/biased-prompts. The code is also accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/Space-Eye-Cloud/biased-prompts. The dataset can be found at https://huggingface.com-space/datasets/38. Recent advancements in Neural Networks have led to increased interest in fully connected Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), initially showing superior performance over traditional convolutional neural networks in specific tasks. Nevertheless, training fully connected RNNs proves to be a persistent challenge. Our research introduces an innovative architecture, comprising a combination of attention mechanisms and residual connections, to facilitate the efficient training of fully connected RNNs. By leveraging attention mechanisms, we enable the model to selectively concentrate on relevant data during training, while residual connections empower the network to learn meaningful, end-to-end consistent representations. Our new architecture, named Multi-Head Attention-based Residual Recurrent Neural Networks (MAR-RNNs), effectively stabilizes training for these networks. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of MAR-RNNs in solving large-scale visual recognition problems, outperforming conventional RNNs and convolutional neural networks on benchmark datasets, such as ImageNet. Additionally, our findings highlight the advantages of MAR-RNNs in solving complex synthetic datasets, successfully overcoming the limitations of convolutional neural networks in generative tasks. Our research also involves a comprehensive analysis of the efficacy of MAR-RNNs on various problems, thoroughly evaluating the benefits of using attention mechanisms and residual connections. The COVID-19 pandemic led to a global effort to develop and implement public health interventions through mathematical models to inform policy decisions. However, these models often required rapid updating of parameters, which typically involved a labor-intensive process of retraining an entire network of experts. In this study, a more efficient approach was developed, utilizing an artificial brain and a large, diverse network of 1,200 virtual experts to predict and adapt medical and economic outcomes for vaccine policies, yielding accurate results similar to those obtained by leading pandemic modelers. The application of the artificial brain to pandemic modeling was successfully demonstrated, producing reliable forecasts and policy recommendations for mitigating the impact of COVID-19. This innovative approach can accelerate the adaptation of mathematical models to address emerging health crises, such as new pandemic variants, by automating the expert network training process and reducing it to a few iterations. Moreover, the potential exists to expand the artificial brain to address broader, more complex challenges in policy decision-making. Debugging data processing pipelines has historically relied on a tedious, manual, and time-consuming approach that necessitates individual component inspection in sequence. Recent research has developed data visualization and analysis techniques aimed at facilitating this task, but these methods still require significant human input and have limited potential to reveal the actual causes of errors. In response, we introduce DataScope, an innovative, fully automated data debugging tool that quickly identifies the origin and explanation of data discrepancies. DataScope builds upon the concept of data lineage, but adapts it to support complex, nested data structures and pipeline compositions. By utilizing a new, efficient algorithm, DataScope propagates data types through the pipeline, enabling the tool to accurately explain data inconsistencies and support fine-grained data validation. In our evaluation, we demonstrate that DataScope significantly outperforms existing data debugging approaches, achieving faster diagnosis times and higher precision when compared to traditional methods and a leading data profiling tool. Mn$_3$IX$_6$ compounds, with X equal to Sn, Cr, or V, exhibit unique properties in which molecular-type magnetic ground states are stabilized due to strong covalent bonds and significant spin-orbit interactions. These interactions mediate a strong exchange between nearest-neighbor spins within each molecule, thereby inducing molecular trimerization that stabilizes non-collinear magnetic arrangements. This phenomenon is evident in Mn$_3$Sn, where it causes a significant reduction in magnetic helicity and leads to unusual properties like anomalous N\'{e}el domains and spin-q fluctuations. This review focuses on the theoretical models and experimental findings that describe the trimerization effect in Mn$_3$Sn and explores its potential applications of spin-q materials in generating stable fringe states and efficient thermal conduction. Additionally, we discuss the prospect of extending the concept of trimerization to other Mn$_3$X$_6$ compounds by adjusting molecular exchange constants and investigating the properties of spin-polarized electrons within these systems. Ultimately, this review aims to provide insight into the unique electronic behavior of these materials and encourages further research into their potential for carrying topological currents.

Between 2016 and 2021, the value of cryptocurrencies fluctuated wildly, with some, like Bitcoin, gaining significant value, while others, like Dogecoin, experienced rapid and unpredictable shifts. This study investigated the relationship between holdings of different cryptocurrencies and the daily price movements of each individual cryptocurrency from 2016 to 2021. Analyzing over 8000 trading days, we discovered that the correlation between most cryptocurrencies and their peers was minimal, yet as time progressed, the correlations tended to strengthen. Notably, the Pearson correlations for the period 2020-2021 exceeded those of the 2016-2017 period by approximately 250%. This growing interdependence is likely attributed to the 'Dogecoin Effect,' which sees smaller, lesser-known cryptocurrencies benefiting from community hype and endorsements by influential figures, thereby amplifying the overall volatility of the cryptocurrency market. The findings were consistent when using alternative correlation metrics, and we observed patterns of synchronized price movements across groups of cryptocurrencies. This research provides initial insights into the complex and interconnected nature of the cryptocurrency market. Further study is needed to model the market's dynamics and predict future price movements with greater accuracy. Additionally, the study's methods and findings offer a framework and reference points for conducting similar analyses on other financial markets. This involves deriving the stochastic hydrodynamic equations from a non-linear noise impression of the original dynamical system. Consequently, we obtain an exact relation between the stochastic hydrodynamics and the non-linear noise theory, expressed as an integral equation. Specifically, we demonstrate that the interaction between noise and dynamics leads to a non-linear effect on the system's long-time dynamics, thereby providing a thorough explanation of this interaction's impact. Furthermore, we derive a non-linear noise impression for the direct correlation function of the stochastic hydrodynamic system, and subsequently, derive the structure of the non-linear noise impression for the entire system. Lastly, we verify that our derived non-linear noise impression is in accordance with the previously established relation between the KPZ equation and non-linear noise theory. Additionally, we derive the equation of motion for the fourth direct correlation function and establish the underlying scaling behavior of this function, as well as the others, in the system. Ultimately, our work lays a theoretical framework that can be applied to other dynamical systems in the future. All necessary details of the derivation process are thoroughly discussed in the accompanying notes and appendices. Nonetheless, we anticipate that the primary paper will still provide a concise understanding of the concept for those interested in its application to other systems. The solar wind turbulence characterization is crucial for understanding the fast plasma variations and space weather implications. Measuring solar wind turbulence using the spacecraft potential with a broadband electrostatic analyzer or a plasma spectrometer, such as the Fast Plasma Investigation on NASA's Wind, yields different results for the turbulence spectral index depending on the instrument. Other discrepancies arise due to the varying instruments' capabilities, such as the inability of the spacecraft potential to distinguish between different plasma species and different ion age groups. In contrast, the Fast Plasma Investigation can differentially measure these properties. To resolve the discrepancies, a new algorithm was developed that estimates the plasma species ratios and ion age groups fractions from the Fast Plasma Investigation data. This algorithm uses the least squares method to fit a mixing model to the data and verify its effectiveness with artificially generated data. Additionally, the algorithm was tested in the real data analysis, but the results showed that the ion age groups fractions could not be accurately determined due to the limited data availability. Therefore, the algorithm was limited to calculating the plasma species ratios. Applying this algorithm to the solar wind turbulence data, the ratios of major plasma species, such as protons, alpha particles, and oxygen, were calculated under different turbulence conditions. These ratios showed independence from the frequency, but varied depending on the ion age groups, indicating that the algorithm worked as expected. In order to further improve the estimates, more data from the plasma species and ion age groups are required. Utilizing the Fast Plasma Investigation, these ratios can be calculated continuously, providing valuable information for the ion age groups distribution function as well. Once the algorithm is optimized with more data, it will allow for the simultaneous determination of the plasma species ratios and ion age groups fractions, which will contribute to the understanding of the solar wind composition, space weather, and turbulence characteristics. To test the limitations of the algorithm, its performance was evaluated under different conditions that might affect its effectiveness, such as low signal-to-noise ratio, which was found to impact the spectral index accuracy. Similarly, the algorithm's performance was evaluated under the conditions of varying data sparsity, instrument resolution, and calibration quality. These evaluations not only tested the algorithm but also provided valuable insights into the instrument performance and its limitations. Observing the solar wind turbulence characteristics, a notable variation in the spectral index was found, which showed a dependence on the ion age groups. In order to further understand the solar wind turbulence, these scales can be analyzed separately by different ion age groups, which can be determined continuously using the Fast Plasma Investigation. In the long-wave context, the linearized equations of motion for a rotating, baroclinic, and slowly evolving atmosphere can be simplified to a singular second-order differential equation, whose solution drives a first-order velocity perturbation. This equation can be further simplified to a modified Taylor-Goldstein equation that accounts for the effects of Coriolis force and radiation, and whose solution is based on the eigenvalues of a specific matrix. A new solution to this modified equation is presented, along with an explanation of its derivation by means of a bi-linear transformation. Additionally, an analytical solution to the original differential equation, valid for any velocity perturbation, is also presented and shows that it matches the proposed solution under long-wave conditions. Both of these solutions are analogous to the well-known analytical solutions to the Taylor-Goldstein equation, and it is also demonstrated that they are in agreement with the numerical methods used to solve the equation, such as the Poincare method. Consequently, these new solutions can be used to model and study waves in the atmosphere and ocean. However, it is worth noting that they are limited to the long-wave context only. On the other hand, the proposed solution to the modified Taylor-Goldstein equation, valid for long waves only, has a broad application, extending beyond the inviscid equation with vertical velocity perturbations, and can also be applied to the viscous equation, as well as those that account for variations in the Coriolis parameter. Furthermore, it is expected that the proposed solutions will be useful for understanding and interpreting the behavior of baroclinic waves in the atmosphere, such as those studied using the GEOS-5 model. Some examples of these applications are presented, such as how the new solutions can help explain how the wave amplitude changes over time, and how it relates to the growth rates of the waves. Additionally, it is observed that the wave amplitude reaches its maximum when the imaginary part of the eigenvalue is zero, and not when the real part becomes zero. Consequently, the proposed solutions should be useful for understanding and interpreting the behavior of waves in the ocean, such as those studied using the MODAREBS model. Some examples of these applications are presented, such as how the new solutions can help explain the variation in wave amplitude with latitude. Finally, the proposed solutions are expected to be useful for understanding and explaining various wave phenomena in the atmosphere and ocean. The DistrictP fairness framework evaluates districting plans based on voter equity across multiple dimensions. This concept leverages Simulated Annealing, a global optimization technique that generates a sequence of neighborhood transformations, randomly selecting one to update the current solution. We apply this approach to large-scale districting problems in Manhattan and Brooklyn, employing geographic information to estimate voter characteristics and defining districts by containing at most k voters. The Simulated Annealing algorithm strives to increase the fairness of generated plans, achieving significant improvements within a timely manner. These improvements exceed those from simpler, local search-based methods, demonstrating the value of Simulated Annealing in addressing complex, real-world districting challenges. Moreover, the framework's flexibility allows for easily adjusting parameters to prioritize different fairness metrics or reduce computational costs. As such, Simulated Annealing effectively addresses the inherent trade-offs in creating fair districting plans. Moreover, the results highlight the significance of spatial structure in determining districting plans that balance equity and political influence. Similarly, in Manhattan, the algorithm found districting plans that balanced fairness and political influence, outperforming simpler, district-based approaches that prioritized these criteria over voter equity. A crucial framework is introduced, involving a maximally saturated linear subspace within a complex vector space, which enables the classification of these quadrics. Furthermore, the paper introduces a new diagonal form for a symmetric matrix, which is applicable to all possible quadrics. Consequently, the class of smooth quadrics can be equivalently represented by a symmetric matrix, which is parameterized by a complex vector system, along with specific conditions derived from its minimal representation. Additionally, the paper establishes a connection between the geometric structure of quadrics and algebraic varieties, which are known as Grassmannians or projective spaces, ultimately resulting in the computation of the Hodge numbers of these quadrics. Significant storms spreading across the Atlantic Ocean can cause extensive damage along coastal areas, and recent advances in satellite imaging have enabled researchers to monitor these storms from space.  We've used wind speed data from Metop satellites to study the extremal spatial behavior of wind and wave patterns, and our findings show an exponential decline in extreme wind speed and wave heights over large distances when conditioned on extremely high Metop wind speeds.  This includes a 5000 km drop-off in extreme wind speeds and wave heights of around 25-30%, as well as wave height reductions of around 20% within the same distance range. Furthermore, it's been shown that for complex varieties, hyperbolicity implies an infinite number of rational points, under a slightly different set of conditions, and a corresponding result for integral points also follows. Finally, it's been shown that for certain types of varieties, hyperbolicity implies an infinite number of rational points, and this result is independent of Zariski density. In addition, examples illustrate that the required conditions cannot be weakened and that rational points can be concentrated in a set of logarithmic scale. Similarly, thinness of rational points isn't sufficient to establish the existence of rational points, and an infinite number of rational points can correspond to a finite number of geometric hyperplanes. Lastly, the existence of an infinite number of rational points on certain types of varieties that have a hyperbolic geometry is independent of the generalized Riemann hypothesis. Instead, the required conditions for the existence of rational points on these varieties are equivalent to the generalized Riemann hypothesis. The production of top quark pairs influences the visibility of Higgs boson signals and affects the precision of top quark cross section measurements, in addition to impacting the searches for new physics in events featuring multiple leptons. This research investigates the impacts of several factors on the detection of Higgs boson production via gluon fusion in the mass range of 120-180 GeV: the statistical distribution of background processes, the transverse momentum of top quarks, the direction of momentum of bottom quarks, radiation patterns of gluons and photons, and two-prong fragmentation products of bottom quarks. The results of this research demonstrate that higher statistical events, 13 TeV energy, and two-prong fragmentation of bottom quarks significantly affect the discrimination between signal and background processes. The MATRIX simulation is shown to accurately reproduce the experimental results, whereas the TESTO and SHERPA programs yield different results. Additionally, this research reveals the detection capabilities of the LHC experiments for the Higgs boson production in the mass range of 120-180 GeV, as well as the impact of bottom quark direction on the detection of Higgs boson signals. The research further recommends the potential utilization of these new decay models for the detection of the dark photon in the mass range of 20-100 GeV. A proven approach for estimating 3D objects from 2D images involves using a two-part model. The first part learns features from individual images, while the second part uses these features to predict 3D object poses. However, the learning of canonical poses, essential for feature extraction and classification, is often hindered by being'staged' or delayed in the training process. This often results in sub-optimal canonical representations, which in turn negatively affect feature extraction and performance. This paper addresses this issue by adopting a multi-stage training technique that iteratively refines both feature extraction and classification. The model is trained in stages, starting with preliminary estimates of both features and poses. As training progresses, the model iteratively improves both features and poses, leading to superior performance and more accurate pose estimation. This multi-stage training technique is unique and can be applied to a range of 2D and 3D estimation tasks. When applied to the task of estimating 3D car poses, this model significantly outperformed state-of-the-art alternatives by achieving an average error of 6.75 degrees. Additionally, when integrated into the fully supervised LiDAR object detection (FULO) model, this method reduced 3D object detection error by 12%, resulting in an average error of 0.42 m. This improvement is particularly noticeable in the detection of smaller objects. Consequently, the FULO model detected more objects, resulting in a 9% increase in detection numbers. This multi-stage training technique is unique, easy to implement, and shows promising results when applied to the problem of 3D car pose estimation. Furthermore, this technique may also be applied to a range of other computer vision tasks. Based on these results, we propose that this training method be used for all 3D object estimation tasks. Attosecond pulses, resulting from high-harmonic generation (HHG), can be tuned by adjusting factors like an iris but determining their total energy and exact temporal profile remains challenging. We developed a technique combining HHG and thermally induced gratings in a dichroic beam splitter to create a reference spectrum and an actual spectrum, both measured at different angles. This unique approach enables accurate estimation of pulse energy, duration, and shape without significant temporal dispersion, showcasing its effectiveness with weak signals and minimal modification of the experiment. We obtained reliable results for an iris-controlled attosecond pulse, yielding an 8.8-fs temporal profile and a 0.3-0.5 eV bandwidth, and confirmed the efficacy of our method with deep learning algorithms. Our technique has potential applications in various experiments relying on attosecond physics, as well as in emerging fields like controlling non-linear processes. Additionally, its angular sensitivity and versatility make it a suitable candidate for a parameter-controlled table-top free-electron laser. We envision our method to be integrated in future type-II free-electron lasers, where an x-ray pulse is accompanied by an optical driver pulse generated through HHG. This integration can facilitate the development of novel concepts in x-ray free-electron laser spectroscopy, such as pulse shaping and optimizing far-field spectra. Moreover, our technique can also be adapted for use in single atom spectroscopy, as well as for investigating the atomic origin of the HHG process itself. Furthermore, its high sensitivity makes it a suitable tool for detecting quantum effects in intense laser fields in real-time. Due to its potential for quantum signal enhancement, we propose naming our method the "attosecond on demand" technique. Our study of the Algol-type binary star Algol C has yielded significant findings.  Despite remaining unchanged for over 800 years, as recorded by historical observations, we discovered a slight and recurring change in its orbital period, which emerged from analysis of the available data.  We found that Algol C exhibits a predictable variation in its orbital period every 10.44 years.  Additionally, we identified evidence of a longer orbital period cycle, which seems to be linked with the 220 years cycle found in other binary stars.  Specifically, we determined the orbital period of Algol C to be 42.0 days.  Furthermore, we detected that Algol C's brightness displays a synchronized pattern with its orbital period, but exhibits an irregular change in brightness every 10.44 years.  We attributed these phenomena to the presence of a dwarf star that orbits the inner binary system every 220 years and a hidden third component that may be responsible for the observed variability.  Specifically, we suggested that the 220 years cycle is linked with a tidal interaction between the two inner binary components, which causes the variation in their orbital periods.  Moreover, we proposed that the observed variability in Algol C's brightness is a result of the hidden third component, which causes disturbances in the binary system, resulting in the observed photometric and spectroscopic variations.  Finally, based on our analysis of the available data, we constructed an improved model of the binary star Algol C, which provides a more accurate representation of the system.  Specifically, we revised the mass ratio of the binary star Algol C to be 0.7, which seems to be stable for the next 220 years.  Furthermore, we noted that the area under the HR diagram, which represents the binary star Algol C, is consistent with our improved model.  Specifically, we determined the masses and radii of the binary star components to be approximately 5.0 solar masses for the primary component and 3.5 solar masses for the secondary component.  Moreover, we noted that further spectroscopic observations are required to validate our improved model, which is expected to provide an accurate estimation of the masses and other physical properties of the binary star components.  Finally, based on our improved model, we calculated the distance to the binary star Algol C, which is estimated to be approximately 40 parsecs.  Specifically, we used the parallax method to determine the distance to the binary star Algol C, which is well-known for its significant variability.

A novel deep learning architecture, referred to as the Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation (RANG), enhances the training efficiency of Physics-informed Neural Networks (PINNs) by dynamically creating data points for the network to learn from.  By optimizing node creation in relation to data and using a residual-based strategy for adapting the node generation process, RANG swiftly identifies a suitable subset of data that facilitates efficient PINN training. Notably, RANG does not require a predefined validation set or assumption about data distribution, making it a fully automatic process. Experimental results on both regression and partial differential equation problems confirm the effectiveness of RANG in reducing training time by up to two orders of magnitude compared to traditional PINNs. Furthermore, RANG is found to boost the performance of surrogate-based optimization by incorporating the optimized PINN model, resulting in a significant enhancement in target values prediction accuracy. Our findings indicate that RANG has the potential to significantly improve the scalability of PINN-based methods of solving inverse problems. A significant number of programming languages suffer from notable security issues on popular package repositories. Despite existing patching libraries, many developers remain unaware of potential vulnerabilities in their code, posing a threat to entire ecosystems. Our research provides an in-depth analysis of two extensive repositories: one for Rust, and one for JavaScript. For each repository, we detailed the process of discovering and fixing existing vulnerabilities, maintaining consistency with the original codebases, and evaluating the effectiveness of current security management practices. The findings reveal that a substantial number of libraries in Cargo still exhibit vulnerabilities in their latest versions, amounting to around 28.3%, despite many vulnerabilities having known fixes. A notable issue arises from a limited number of maintainers contributing to library security, with over 40% of vulnerable libraries in Cargo having security issues that could not be resolved due to a lack of involvement. Conversely, JavaScript's npm reveals a lower instance of under-maintained libraries with security issues, amounting to around 17.1% of affected components. Notably, the analysis highlights that a considerable number of libraries in Cargo and npm have security issues that could be resolved if developers addressed corresponding documentation recommendations. These findings emphasize the significance of implementing effective security management techniques that involve both developers and automated tools, highlighting the need for further research into programming language and package maintenance. This study investigates the long-term behavior of the stochastic complex Ginzburg-Laudau equation (CGL) driven by a pure jump L\'evy noise and a deterministic force within a bounded domain. We establish that the CGL reaches a stationary ergodic state and calculate the distribution of this stationary state. Furthermore, we determine the rate at which the CGL converges to its ergodic distribution. Our analysis also evaluates the impact of the jump parameter in the L\'evy noise on the CGL's convergence rate. Additionally, we demonstrate that the CGL can be reduced to a differential equation driven by a Brownian noise with a multiplicative fractional stabilizing force, which helps to understand its long-term behavior. We then use these reductions, among other methods, to demonstrate the well-posedness of the CGL and establish an ergodicity criterion for the CGL in terms of its jump parameter and a parameter representing the strength of its stabilizing force. Our analytical findings are further supported by numerical simulations, which demonstrate the CGL's convergence to an ergodic distribution as time progresses and highlight the effect of the jump parameter on its convergence rate. Finally, based on our analytical results, we investigate the stability of the CGL in the presence of different types of initial data and demonstrate that it can exhibit stable periodic, stable quasi-periodic, and stable chaotic behaviors, as well as stable stationary behaviors, depending on its parameter settings. To the best of our knowledge, our study is one of the first to investigate the ergodic behavior of the CGL in a bounded domain driven by a pure jump L\'evy noise and a deterministic force. Our analytical methods are innovative and may be extended to other types of stochastic partial differential equations in the future. Based on these findings, we also establish the stability of these stable modes in the CGL, which helps to understand their dynamic behavior. Finally, we provide a roadmap for future research on the CGL, which could involve investigating the stability of patterns in the CGL and reducing the CGL to a simpler form, among other topics. For these groups, the algebra of class functions becomes a maximal abelian self-adjoint algebra when the deformation parameter is negative, zero, or specific positive values. Furthermore, we demonstrate the deficiency of a different approach to constructing functional calculi for non-commutative differential operators, which has implications for linear spectra. Additionally, we explore the lack of completeness in these functional calculi, leading to a corresponding issue in spectral projections, which raises questions about the linearity of the spectral measure, particularly in $SU_{\mathpzc{p}}(2)$. Lastly, we apply these results to examine the Weyl functional calculi on these quantum groups, which have previously been proven to be complete. However, for non-compact groups, the completeness of the Weyl functional calculi is contingent upon the group's spectrum, while the linearity of the spectral measure remains a topic of uncertainty. In contrast, the linearity of the spectral measure is proven for $SU_q(2)$. Large Multi-dimensional dynamic systems, such as large MDPs and large geometric games, can significantly hinder the MCTS algorithm's efficiency. Our research focuses on enhancing the MCTS performance in these complex systems by introducing an inexact version of GMRES policy iteration. This inexact iteration enables more rapid convergence by accepting approximate residuals from the environment instead of requiring precise calculations. Our findings demonstrate that the inexact iteration can be nearly as effective as the traditional method in smaller systems, but significantly outperforms it in larger ones. Specifically, in MDPs with 10,000 to 200,000 states, the inexact iteration can be 5 to 15 times faster, while in geometric games with 10,000 to 20,000 states, it can be 10 to 60 times faster. These enhancements enable the Mont-Carlo EM algorithm to solve larger problems, such as more complex Geudoku puzzles and larger Reversi boards, more efficiently. Our most promising results show that the MC-EM algorithm can solve Reversi with 5 to 7 players in the Nash equilibrium of the first-best strategy layer 5 to 15 times faster than the current state-of-the-art algorithm. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexheyer/inexact-gmres-mctsemp. Our research also introduces a new evaluation technique for MCTS in large geometric games that involves a hierarchical Monte-Carlo planning approach with the current-best policies as the base layer, providing a valuable tool for assessing the performance of iterative policy evaluation methods. Moreover, this new evaluation technique can accelerate the Nash equilibrium finding process by approximating the first-best strategy layer, which traditional MC-EM algorithm struggles with. Our research indicates that this two-layer evaluation can account for most of the Nash equilibria's value compared to the deep-layer evaluation, making it a valuable reference for assessing iterative policy evaluation methods' performance in large geometric games. Additionally, a method to parameterize strongly graphic weighted directed graphs is provided, allowing us to classify such graphs for certain specified parameters. Our findings contain multiple theorems, examples, and a open problem. Also, an edge ideal is found to be strongly bicritical if and only if it has a specific property related to its associated monomial ideal in certain circumstances, as shown in Theorem 3.20. Finally, an open problem related to classifying certain classes of graphs is presented in Problem 4.4. All the provided proofs are meticulous and follow a step-by-step reasoning. Researchers have examined the properties of samples from Martian and Lunar regoliths with the goal of evaluating their potential as extraterrestrial building materials. A critical material property for building materials was investigated using Uniaxial Compressive Strength testing on simulated regolith samples, replicating conditions found on the surfaces of Mars and the Moon. Initial results from the Lunar regolith simulations showed a higher UCS value compared to the Martian regolith. Furthermore, the stiffness and failure behavior of these regolith samples were observed and their microstructures analyzed. Ultimately, the goal is to use these findings in simulations to predict the mechanical behavior of regoliths under various extraterrestrial environment conditions. Two types of porous media models will be developed, one inspired by the Micro Model and another using the Finite Element Method. These models will be used to evaluate their ability to predict compressive strength, stiffness, and the failure mode of the regolith samples. The accuracy of these models will be assessed by comparing their predictions to the experimental UCS values. Additionally, the potential for utilizing extraterrestrial building materials will be evaluated by applying the PCM models to the Martian and Lunar regolith simulations, with a view to guide future simulations towards predicting the UCS, stiffness, and failure behavior of these materials. It is anticipated that the predicted UCS values will range from approximately 0.03 MPa to over 0.3 MPa, with the stiffness being influenced by void ratios and the stiffness of the parent rocks. The stiffness and strength of the regolith samples are expected to be primarily affected by moisture content and the presence of ice. The findings from these simulations will guide the selection of Martian and Lunar regolith samples for 3D printing, with a view to establishing their potential as building materials for human settlements on other planets and moons. The ultimate objective is to utilize these materials in constructing habitats and other infrastructure on other planets and moons, marking a significant milestone in the development of extraterrestrial building materials. Traditional methods of modeling duration have severe limitations when dealing with non-proportional, time-dependent, and competing risks. Conventional techniques often assume a single underlying duration process, neglecting prior observations, and result in a single predictor variable (the duration itself) being used in models like the Cox proportional hazards. This paper proposes a new framework for modeling duration, known as multi-component duration modeling (MCDM), which consists of multiple underlying duration processes, can incorporate prior knowledge, and allows for the contribution of prior observations to be modeled. Each component duration process can rely on different sets of predictor variables and have unique proportional hazards models. This framework offers a more comprehensive description of duration data and enables the separation of duration variability into meaningful sub-categories. Additionally, MCDM offers the capability of modeling different phases of a duration process, such as the time taken for a patient to receive treatment after being hospitalized, as having several distinct components (pre-admission, admission process, post-admission), each explained by separate sets of predictor variables. This paper outlines the method for estimating MCDM through maximum likelihood estimation, presents a Monte Carlo Markov chain simulation method for obtaining posterior distributions, and demonstrates the efficacy of MCDM in capturing the complexity of real-world duration data through an actual example. Results show that MCDM is more effective than the conventional Cox proportional hazards model in explaining the variation in duration data. MCDM is available in the R package durationModeling.R.

The formation of strong magnetic fields in slowly rotating, massive stars is better understood thanks to advancements in the study of dynamo theory, particularly the $\Omega$-dynamo and $\alpha$-dynamo. Research suggests that in rapidly rotating stars with strong rotation, magnetic cycles may not occur, whereas in slowly rotating stars with strong internal rotation, magnetic fields can survive and strengthen over time. However, in the latter scenario, the resulting magnetic fields have been shown to exhibit cyclic behavior only if they are generated through a specific dynamo process, whereas other methods of magnetic field generation may lead to non-repeating patterns. A recent study has found that these patterns can persist for centuries, long enough to be observed across an entire magnetic lifetime. This research offers new insights into the long-term behavior of magnetic fields in the atmospheres and winds of O and B-type stars. By studying how these fields evolve, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the dynamics involved, particularly the interaction between winds and the surfaces of these stars. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the $v\sin I$ distribution of O9-B3.5 stars is not solely determined by rotation, but may also be influenced by stellar evolution, which could explain the shape of this distribution and the location of its break point. Finally, the research indicates that the magnetic cycle can provide a possible explanation for the observed variations in the surface magnetic fields of Ap stars, a phenomenon known as the 'Maunder-like cycles'. This phenomenon, characterized by the fluctuations of the surface magnetic fields of Ap stars over different time periods, has been documented in several cases, with the fluctuations occurring around the following timescales: 7-10 years, 20-30 years, 40-60 years, 110 years, 220 years, and 440 years. Notably, the magnetic cycle has been found to be capable of producing variations that align with several of these time periods, suggesting that the magnetic cycle could be the primary process responsible for the observed fluctuations in the surface magnetic fields of Ap stars. This new understanding of the magnetic cycle and its ability to produce variations aligned with several of the listed time periods, combined with the potential for further refinement of the timescales, offers new hope for solving the problem of the missing solar dynamo at the end of the Maunder minimum. Moreover, the research offers the possibility that the $\Delta$-dynamo can produce variations aligned with the longest time period of 440 years, suggesting that this dynasty could be the correct solution to this problem. We demonstrate that any instance of the model produces the same long-term population structure, regardless of the model parameters, with the exception of the mutation rate. This exceptional case aside, the population structure is always unique. Conversely, there exist multiple distinct models, each defined by varying levels of selection pressure, that produce the same long-term population structure. In other words, the model is not uniquely determined by the population structure itself, a phenomenon confirmed by numerous numerical examples. However, we also identify a specific class of models where the population structure becomes fully resolved over time and propose an algorithm to calculate the population structure at any given time in such models. Finally, we provide specific instances of models that are difficult for computers to handle and require significant computational power. These models are identified by extremely low effective population sizes or extremely high mutation rates. These challenging models can hinder our understanding of evolutionary processes and make it difficult for computers to reconstruct the evolutionary history of a species. This reconstruction process is known as phylogenetic inference. Automatic speech recognition-based spoofing countermeasures have gained significant attention in recent years, with various approaches being explored to enhance their effectiveness. While existing methods have achieved notable performance improvements, they still have limitations in detecting speech artifacts, particularly subtle ones found in genuine voices. This paper proposes a novel feature extraction technique to address this limitation, by leveraging attention mechanisms to accurately identify and highlight relevant input segments. Moreover, the paper introduces a new training method to optimize the attention weights, by incorporating a target speaker's voice into the training data. Experimental results on the ASVspoof 2019 challenge data show the proposed system's superiority, with this technique and data combination resulting in a 14.24% enhancement in accuracy compared to the baseline system. Furthermore, the paper evaluates the efficacy of attention mechanisms in deep neural networks through analysis of their robustness and generalization capabilities. The results indicate that the proposed system is more resilient to corruptions and has improved generalization abilities, with the attention weights exhibiting predictable and consistent patterns across different corruption types. Additionally, the paper observes that the attention networks are able to discover and highlight speech artifacts, spoofing voices, and target voices effectively. We investigate nonreciprocal optical interactions within silicon microdisks by generating and controlling photon pairs through a pump-scattering process. To quantify the nonreciprocal properties, we evaluate coherence functions of the photon pairs while reversing the pump's direction of propagation, which demonstrate significantly distinct characteristics. Furthermore, we develop an analytical model to explain our findings, taking into account the nonideal boundary properties of the microdisk and its influence on coherence functions. By varying the coherence function's phase, we successfully achieve complete control of the pump's direction, showcasing its relevance to nonreciprocal optical systems. Additionally, we explore the influence of loss and show that modulating the pump's power can also overcome traditional coherence-time limitations. Our work lays the groundwork for the design of new nonreciprocal optical systems utilizing silicon microdisks and highlights their potential for dynamic control and coherence enhancement. Moreover, the established analytical model can be applied to other microresonator systems, enabling their coherence function management. Leveraging the unique properties of silicon microdisks, we devise a plan to extend nonreciprocal optical interactions to various silicon-based systems, thereby expanding their technological scope. Specifically, we illustrate the implementation of a complete control system of the pump's direction in a silicon microdisk cavity, which can also function as a mode-locked laser to produce ultra-stable, direction-dependent optical pulses. Moreover, we demonstrate that the phase of coherence functions of photon pairs can be employed as a new degree of freedom to enhance or modulate the efficiency of optical transitions, which can be particularly beneficial in quantum optics and coherent population transfer applications. Lastly, we show that directional photon pair generators based on silicon microdisks can serve as efficient sources of single-mode, directionally sensitive, and spectrally stable optical pulses for integrated quantum optics and quantum processing purposes. The carrier concentration of silicon surfaces varies based on the etching process used to create them. This study examines the carrier concentration of silicon etched using different methods, including reactive ion etching in oxygen and fluorine-based plasmas, and compares it to silicon etched in a buffer oxide etch (BOE). Carrier concentration was measured using photoconductivity and contactless techniques. BOE etched silicon exhibited higher carrier concentrations than etched silicon, with carrier concentrations ranging from 1x10^16 to 2x10^17 cm^-3, depending on the etching conditions. Oxygen etched silicon had a carrier concentration of 1x10^17 cm^-3, while silicon etched in a fluorine plasma had a significantly higher carrier concentration of 1x10^18 cm^-3. These measurements were verified using a contactless capacitive method, with results showing good agreement. Evasion attacks on network detection systems are becoming increasingly common. They allow attackers to circumvent Dynamic Protocol Detection mechanisms, rendering these systems ineffective. To counter this issue, researchers are exploring new approaches that can automatically identify and mitigate evasion attacks while maintaining accuracy. In this research, we develop an evolution-based method to detect evasion attacks that modify network traffic patterns. Our method utilizes an unsupervised detection system built from P2 vectors, combining gradient-based optimization and hyperparameter tuning through surrogate-assisted optimization to effectively identify traffic patterns. We evaluate our method on a real-world dataset from the Unpatched NIDS 2006 dataset, comparing it to a leading detection system that uses neural networks and gradient-based optimization. In our evaluation, we find that our method yields higher accuracy and fewer false positives, outperforming the comparison system. Furthermore, we find that our method detects 100% of attacks and 98.5% of anomalies, while both the comparison system and a traditional gradient-based optimization method fail to detect some anomalies. We also find that our method offers a significant performance improvement over the comparison system, reducing false positives by almost 7%. In addition to evaluating the performance of our method, we conduct an assisted optimization case study to analyze the effectiveness of different optimization strategies. The results of this case study confirm that our method is an effective approach to detecting evasion attacks. The proposed method is fully defined and can be replicated by other researchers, who validated its performance through independent experiments. This research investigates the combined effects of superconducting strips and external magnetic fields on the propagation of magnons in a thin film with easy-plane anisotropy. By leveraging the linearized Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, a stochastic system representing small-angle magnon behavior is established. Utilizing the eigenvalue spectrum of the system's Jacobian, the stability of this stochastic system is analyzed via eigenvalues, with stable modes corresponding to stable magnon propagation. A novel method for determining the phase of these stable modes is developed, applied in various scenarios, including a specific case with a unique mode that demonstrates a sharp change in phase near a certain field value. This mode's phase, however, does not match the predictions of a previous model; further study is needed to verify the predicted phase versus field curve for this mode. Additionally, it is found that superconducting strips can support two distinct modes of stable magnon propagation, with different transverse profiles; the phase of these modes remains unchanged. Finally, the research involves numerically solving the full nonlinear Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation to examine the magnon beam propagation in two scenarios, with the results showing good agreement with the predictions based on the linearized system. This study paves the way for exploring magnonic devices utilizing superconducting strips and external magnetic fields. The emergence of the Metaverse demands interactive 3D content at an impressive scale. To overcome the limitations of traditional fully connected models, which struggle with processing complex, high-resolution 3D data, our zero-shot federated learning framework has been designed to efficiently categorize 3D shapes from a variety of distributional sources. The framework achieves this by leveraging a pre-trained, autoencoder-based model to map inputs to a common latent space, followed by the implementation of a metric learning system that reduces within-distribution discrepancies and increases cross-distribution distinctions. The framework's metric learning component is further enhanced by introducing a set of prototype points that represent the various 3D shape distributions, and whose optimization can be jointly shared across different data providers to save communication resources. The efficacy of our framework has been demonstrated through experiments on multiple datasets, and the results show that it outperforms several baseline models, including non-adversarial and federated learning-based approaches. Furthermore, the framework's performance has been shown to improve significantly with the addition of new 3D shape categories. The quantum Fourier transform is a crucial quantum algorithm with significant applications in both computation and communication. Its execution, however, poses significant technical challenges on near-term quantum devices due to the extensive number of gates required. Our research demonstrates that these problems can be tackled by mapping the SISW problem onto the standard SWAP basis, resulting in a reduced number of gates needed to perform the quantum Fourier transform, particularly on high-dimensional multi-photon systems. This advancement is anticipated to have a significant positive impact on the near-term quantum devices' efficiency. Our experiment implemented the transformed quantum Fourier transform on four qubits using superconducting quantum processors. The resulting accuracy of our execution exceeded 90 percent, achieving a considerable 45 percent reduction in the total number of gates compared to the standard SWAP basis implementation. This breakthrough sets the stage for the quantum Fourier transform to be applied in multiple-photon systems. Furthermore, our findings also contribute to the growing understanding of the SISW problem, showing its potential to bridge near-term quantum computing and the long-term goal of universal quantum computers. The improved quantum Fourier transform we developed will likely have a broad range of applications in both computational and communicative tasks. Its potential benefits extend to various domains such as cryptography (particularly in OWL strategy for ATOP), optimal solution searches, and random number generation. In addition, its potential for applying the Fourier transform to multiple photons may accelerate the standard quantum Fourier transform. This study analyzed the daily updates from local newspapers in Germany regarding COVID-19 from January to April 2020. A randomly selected sample of 40 publications provided a total of 3,960 articles, which were examined to understand the impact of article type, section, and editor decisions on the volume and content of local news coverage. Additionally, the study looked into how editorial decisions affected the coverage of specific COVID-19 topics, such as government policies, economic issues, and personal health matters. Our findings show that news volume correlated with a region's COVID-19 infection rate but declined in areas experiencing high mortality rates. Furthermore, qualitative content analysis revealed significant variations in the style of local COVID-19 coverage influenced by the region, article type, and editorial decisions. To better comprehend these patterns, the study established two COVID-19 news style profiles, characterized by a "pragmatic" and "solidary" orientation towards mitigating the crisis. Our results are set to inform data-driven strategies for navigating the interplay between editorial decisions, news content, and the ongoing pandemic. This research is based on a collaboration between academic scientists and journalists from Westdeutscher Zeitung and WDR. Due to data privacy constraints, the full dataset cannot be shared publicly, although replication materials are available upon request. Based on our analysis, two potential approaches to enhance public health communication can be identified. Firstly, different news organizations are characterized by distinct COVID-19 news styles that stem from varying infection rates, resulting in a need for increased awareness of reliable information norms in areas experiencing high infection rates. Secondly, the profile of a "solidary" news style presents a model for effective newsroom practices, emphasizing the potential for media outlets to foster a united response to the pandemic through their reporting. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to increased interest in systematic
extrapolation, allowing models to make accurate predictions outside their initial
training scope. The potential for systematic extrapolation is closely tied to the
model's ability to accurately predict its own performance beyond its training
bounds, essentially predicting its own limits. In this study, the relationship between
a model's performance on its own training data and its ability to extrapolate is
investigated. Specifically, we look at whether a model can successfully train on
subset datasets, predict its own performance on untrained data, and whether these
performance predictions are influenced by hyperparameters and dataset properties.
We test this on both the MNIST and Fashion-MNST datasets using a simple neural
network, and our results indicate that models are generally capable of
self-prediction, but are limited in their ability to accommodate additional
training data, leading to constrained behavior. Furthermore, we find that models are
more versatile in their prediction capabilities, suggesting that their predictive
capabilities extend beyond their training limits, and we discuss the implications
these findings have on the study of systematic extrapolation. Finally, we examine
the connection between self-prediction, extrapolation, and generalization, and how
these related concepts impact our understanding of model performance. Specifically, we
find that model performance on self-prediction and extrapolation are influenced by
the same factors, but require unique hyperparameter settings, and that generalization
may not be the primary driver of either self-prediction or extrapolation. These findings
suggest that the study of self-prediction and extrapolation may provide insights
into the limits of model performance, and could potentially become more important
 factors in model evaluation. The full text is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.10623. The code for this project can be found at https://github.com/alexrame/alexrame.github.io. Recent research introduces xor filters as a highly efficient alternative to traditional Bloom filters, boasting significant speed and memory advantages. This work delves into the fundamental principles of xor filters, examining their fundamental characteristics and developing a comprehensive mathematical framework to evaluate their performance. Additionally, experiments are conducted to compare the created implementation with state-of-the-art Bloom filters, revealing that xor filters consistently require substantially less memory to achieve comparable speeds. Furthermore, this research introduces a novel variant of xor filters, dubbed xor filters with initialization, designed to offer enhanced resilience to adversarial attacks at a minimal cost in memory usage. Extensive simulations are carried out to verify the proposed algorithm's efficacy and to establish a mathematical formula for estimating its performance. Experimental results indicate that this new variant is capable of withstanding roughly $e^{98.6n^{\frac{2}{3}p}}$ adversarial attacks before experiencing a slight decrease in performance. This new type of xor filter is designed to provide highly secure membership testing, requiring minimal additional memory and operation overhead. Moreover, this research develops various optimization strategies for enhancing the performance of xor filters. Notably, an implementation is created using binary vectors, demonstrating speed and memory improvements of 2x and 5-6%, respectively, over existing high-performance solutions. This new implementation is made available under the Apache 2.0 license at https://github.com/alegrosjohn/xor-float. This research investigates the temporal framework for market directional insights in exchange-traded funds, with particular focus on the NASDAQ Technology Full Index ETF. Past price data is insufficient for this analysis, as it is concerned with how market participants utilize the information available to them at various time intervals. Instead, this study explores the ability of various time-based models to capture market directional insights, using both fundamental and technical indicators as comparative benchmarks. Recent advancements in the stock market, driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, are also examined to establish whether the information environment has impacted the time-based framework for directional insights. Similarity measures are utilized to model the behavior of similar time-based frameworks, while the reliability of these models is ensured through the application of unit roots and vector autoregression tests. The findings of this study reveal that the time-based framework for directional insights in ETFs typically ranges from hourly to daily, with differences arising based on the specific methodology employed, market conditions, and information availability. Nonetheless, the evidence suggests that market participants utilize market directional insights on a scale of minutes to days, with hours and days being the most prevalent intervals. The research further demonstrates that the hour and day time-based frameworks offer the best balance of accuracy and simplicity. Furthermore, the study shows that the information environment has undergone significant changes since March 2020, with the pandemic causing rapid stock market fluctuations and changes in market participant behavior. As a result, the pre-pandemic hour time-based framework is no longer applicable, with the post-pandemic framework exhibiting only slight differences from the day time-based model. Finally, the research reveals that combining fundamental and technical indicators in the time-based framework is the most accurate approach, with single-type models (either fundamental or technical) being less effective. Our proposed solution, FLVoogd, is the first federated vocal synthesis system capable of generating benign data for a specific task while simultaneously protecting sensitive personal information. FLVoogd employs a customized, adaptive clustering technique to organize clients into groups based on the uniqueness of their voice identities. Using these clusters, an optimized model is created through distributed training, while a data augmentation module ensures that the model avoids overfitting to specific voices within each group. Our experiments, conducted with the CVSSR dataset, demonstrate that FLVoogd successfully protects personal information and prevents overfitting, while maintaining the model's accuracy in synthesizing speech segments. Furthermore, FLVoogd's accuracy surpasses that of a single-tenant approach and is comparable to a baseline federal learning system. Additionally, FLVoogd's protection capabilities outperform those of a vanilla federated learning system. Our findings also indicate that FLVoogd's data utilization can reach 90% of the model's maximum performance with only 10% and 20% of the data, respectively. Our results show that FLVoogd achieves a data efficiency of three to four times that of a vanilla federated learning system. Our analysis on the effectiveness of our adaptive clustering strategy and data augmentation module further validates the robustness of FLVoogd. The growing sophistication of deepfakes is sparking serious concerns about the authenticity of media. As their production becomes more accessible, it's likely that additional false videos will be created and disseminated, potentially harming individuals and social relationships. To mitigate this risk, it's essential to develop effective methods for reliably identifying deepfakes. Although numerous studies have explored deepfake detection, the field remains largely isolated from other computer vision communities, hindering the exchange of knowledge. This paper aims to bridge this gap by providing an overview of the deepfake detection landscape, discussing key research findings, potential future directions, and potential roadblocks for community participation. The abstract presents an introduction to the topic, while a companion paper delves into specific techniques and applications. Together, these documents seek to foster a unified and informed community working to address the pressing issue of deepfake detection.

Numerical methods can help compute individual solution branches in parameter-dependent systems, but it's crucial to ensure their validity. In this study, we introduce a validated numerically-assisted continuation method that can accurately calculate isolated solution branches without relying on specific starting points. This method utilizes high-accuracy numerical techniques to generate valid solutions and incorporates an inexact linear solver to correct perturbations that might arise during the continuation process. A companion software implementation is also provided to illustrate the method's effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that our method successfully calculates valid solution branches in various systems, including cubic eigenvalue problems, linear operators with nonlinear constraints, and autonomous differential equations. These results include both initial and intermediate solutions, and the method has been modified to extend its applicability to problems that meet specific criteria. Future plans include applying and refining the approach in relevant application domains. Detecting abrupt changes in data and pinpointing the cause can be critical in maintaining performance and preventing losses. However, identifying these changes and isolating the root cause in real-time can be impractical due to limited processing capabilities. This work develops efficient online algorithms for detecting changes and tracking the mean and variance in a stream of data. Following the initial detection, we utilize these values to pinpoint the exact time of the change. Subsequently, we employ a Markov model to accurately determine the probability distribution of the process at the detected time point. Finally, we isolate the failure mode by identifying the state that is most likely out of sync with the current data point. This procedure is repeated continuously to monitor and adapt to shifting patterns. We evaluate the effectiveness of the algorithm through simulations and real-world data sets, and find that it outperforms other methods. However, we recognize that our algorithm may struggle when the variations in the process are similar to potential false alarms. To mitigate this issue, we require that the differences between successive detected time points vary significantly before registering a new change. This modification proves to be an effective way to prevent unnecessary isolations while reducing false positives. We observe this improvement through simulations and real-world data sets, and propose a method for automatically determining the desired level of variation. We successfully apply this technique to a current best algorithm for detecting changes in a stream of data, and observe a significant reduction in false positives while retaining the ability to detect the original variations efficiently. This modified algorithm is then utilized to isolate the failure mode, and we find that it outperforms other methods in detecting the cause of changes and tracking the probability distribution of the process. We evaluate the effectiveness of the algorithm by comparing it to other published methods, and find that it surpasses their performance. Notably, we successfully apply this approach to detect and isolate the failure mode in a real-world data set of flight arrivals. This reveals the potential for this algorithm to detect the cause of changes in a practical scenario. Finally, we consider the resource constraints of the algorithm, which could impact its effectiveness. This work provides efficient online algorithms for detecting changes and isolating the failure mode, and improves their performance while reducing false positives. Furthermore, we propose a new approach to detect the cause of changes and track the probability distribution of the process, which outperforms other methods. We evaluate the effectiveness of the algorithm by comparing it to other published methods, and find that it surpasses their performance. Additionally, we consider the resource constraints of the algorithm, which could impact its effectiveness.

We've used a cluster-mass function to determine the formation and dissolution times of two ultra-faint star clusters, Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (or GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1. Our analysis of these clusters reveals the likelihood of them being associated with two specific dwarf galaxies, both of which share molecular gas observations. We found the formation of GSE to have lasted around 2 billion years, while the formation of Wukong/LMS-1 is more uncertain but is estimated to have lasted around anywhere from 1 to 4 billion years. Both of these clusters' lifespans are consistent with, but also slightly longer than, previously estimated times for their respective galaxies, thereby increasing the likelihood of a connection between these clusters and their associated galaxies. We discuss our results in relation to existing knowledge about the chemistry within these galaxies. Our analysis suggests that both clusters likely underwent metal enrichment within their respective galaxies, whereas the tight correlation between mass and the formation/dissolution of these clusters and the galaxies requires further confirmation through additional analysis. We suggest several potential targets that could help achieve this goal. We propose the use of RGB stars to help identify these new candidates. We also discuss potential connections between these clusters and other ultra-faint stars that share similar properties, such as Nemesis/LMS-1 and Nekazna 2, both of which are thought to belong to the Cassiopeia 3 galaxy. Our analysis implies that both Nemesis/LMS-1 and Nekazna 2 are likely to have formed at different times from GSE and Wukong/LMS-1. Our estimates for the formation of Nemesis/LMS-1 is uncertain, but is estimated to have lasted around anywhere from 1 to 3 billion years. On the other hand, we estimate the formation of Nekazna 2 to have lasted around 3 billion years. Our analysis implies that all of these clusters formed at different times from each other, thereby increasing the likelihood of a connection between these clusters and their associated galaxies. Our study is the first to use RGB stellar luminosity to help identify potential new candidates for these galaxies. Our analysis implies that both Enceladus and Wukong/LMS-1 are likely to have metal-rich, SN- enriched rich dwarf galaxies that are rich in metal and are enriched by supernovae, whereas Cassiopeia 3 is likely to have a more uncertain composition of both energy and metal. This proof draws on concepts from minimal pairs and learning principles, which are explored in a companion paper focusing on their theoretical implications and potential applications. Recent studies on model pruning have yielded notable gains, particularly in reducing computation costs for inference. Yet, current approaches often compromise model accuracy. To address this issue, this research introduces ClickTrain, a novel scheme that accurately retrains pruned models in an end-to-end manner. ClickTrain leverages two key components: 1) a customized backpropagation algorithm and 2) an optimal gradient estimation technique, ensuring that pruned models can be effectively updated. Furthermore, ClickTrain's end-to-end structure allows for the simultaneous adaptation of multiple pruning types. To evaluate its effectiveness, this study conducted extensive experiments on various architectures, datasets, and pruning methods. The results reveal that ClickTrain achieves superior accuracy compared to existing pruning techniques, yielding up to a 10% improvement. Moreover, ClickTrain enables the successful retraining of models pruned using different methods, such as weakly-pruned structures obtained by strategically combining multiple types of pruning. The experiments also demonstrate that ClickTrain's customizable nature enables the seamless integration of diverse pruning types, such as different head and tail prunings, which can be challenging to combine directly. The study finds that ClickTrain enables the successful retraining of models combining weakly-pruned structures obtained from pruning the network up to certain layers. Consequently, ClickTrain offers a flexible and powerful tool for efficiently pruning large models, while accurately preserving the original representation. In large-scale complex decision problems, finding an optimal operating policy or approximate solution under specific criteria such as expected reward or constraint satisfaction, often proves challenging. Currently used methods are generally limited to smaller problem sizes or compute approximate solutions with little guarantee of quality. In this paper, we present a new sampling-based algorithm inspired by the primal-dual method that generates operating policies. This approach, though initially designed for M-dynamic convex optimization problems, also yields viable solutions for more practical applications like Markov decision processes and graph-based planning. Our results demonstrate substantial reductions in computational time while maintaining low solution quality errors, even for problems beyond the algorithm's original scope. We complement these findings with theoretical analysis of solution quality and convergence rates. Ultimately, this algorithm offers a valuable solution for complex decision problems, especially those involving multi-objective optimization criteria. For instance, this methodology proves particularly useful in solving planning and control problems for autonomous robots with multi-objective criteria, yielding satisfactory results in test cases. We've developed a novel approach to recognizing hand-drawn mathematical symbols, 
utilizing a kNN classifier trained with a comprehensive dataset of 7,942 symbols 
from the LaTeX and Metafont formats. To enhance generalization, our method incorporates 
a regularization technique that enforces the classification of unseen symbols as unknown. 
The proposed system achieves high accuracy rates of 98.2% and 97.2% for LaTeX and Metafont 
symbols, respectively, and showcases its potential as an intelligent math editor tool. 
Additionally, we've set the stage for future research applications in mathematical symbol 
classification, encompassing topics like augmented input and formula suggestion.

Network scientists seek to identify highly connected nodes that contribute to information dissemination and disease propagation. In this study, we examine the predictability of spreading processes on random networks based on their structural characteristics. Our results show that spread predictability is influenced by network density, with higher predictability in dense networks. We also find a correlation between network cliqueness and spread predictability. In particular, the predictability of spreading processes in networks with high cliqueness is similar to that in small-world networks. Therefore, reducing connections within clusters may aid in predicting and controlling spread propagation. This study provides structural characteristics that can aid in selecting target nodes for intervention strategies. Additionally, we introduce a novel metric for evaluating the effectiveness of node removal interventions. Our results are validated through simulations of epidemic models on various networks, including a real-world transportation network. This study's findings can inform strategies for information dissemination and disease control based on network structure. Furthermore, we analyze the properties of a novel, growing network model that is characterized by high spread predictability, strong clustering, and interplay between small-world and cliqueness properties. This model is distinguished from other network models by the diversity of node ages and is parameterized by the variance of node ages. Our results demonstrate that there is a correlation between the variance of node ages and network cliqueness, as well as a correlation between the average node age and network density. Therefore, reducing the variance of node ages may aid in predicting spread propagation. Notably, the properties of this growing network model are similar to those of a network of human proteins, as revealed by a comparison with a dataset on human protein networks. This study's findings highlight the importance of considering the diversity of node ages in network models, as well as the potential for age-related factors to influence the spread of diseases and information. Furthermore, we identify a novel, effective strategy for controlling spread propagation by removing nodes that are no longer present, which are easily targetable due to their older age. We introduce an innovative way to enforce general safety rules in reinforcement learning by converting them into reachable constraints. Our method ensures that an efficient path to achieving rewards in a safe manner is prioritized over violating safety standards, which remains difficult to achieve with current techniques. By formulating reachability conditions as convex constraints, our method becomes scalable for complex systems, effectively reducing the likelihood of violating safety constraints. This approach is general and adaptable to various reinforcement learning frameworks, though we demonstrate its effectiveness through TensorFlow agents. Moreover, we show that using our method, agents can learn safe policies for challenging tasks without sacrificing performance. Specifically, in the continuous domain, our method succeeds in finding safe policies for tasks like Mountain Car, where traditional methods struggle, and achieves comparable results to the optimal safe policy. Moreover, for tasks like OpenAI Biped, our method enables learning both a safe walking motion and a safe falling response, reducing the likelihood of severe impacts by 91.2%. These results indicate that our method is an essential tool for creating reinforcement learning agents that adhere to safe standards. By connecting the homology classes of X_1(n) and X_1(2n), we create a procedure to detect prime twins beyond the range that the Riemann hypothesis covers. This paper proposes a modular control system consisting of multiple layers for the navigation of mobile platforms equipped with sensors. The system utilizes a hierarchical control structure, dividing functions into individual layers to optimize performance and simplify software design. Each layer operates independently, relying on local sensor data and previous control outputs to make decisions. We implemented a proof-of-concept system using a Raspberry Pi and sonar sensors, verifying its effectiveness through experimental validation. The resulting control system enables mobile robots to navigate their surroundings successfully, even in the presence of obstacles. Our work demonstrates the benefits of a layered control system for sensor-based navigation, offering a novel approach that can be applied to a range of mobile platforms and sensors. Additionally, the project serves as a valuable learning resource for robotics enthusiasts and beginners.
