In this study, we explore the analog of the generalized Polya theorem in the context of $p$-adic solenoids. To begin, we establish a functional equation, and then solve it using specific classes of $p$-adic functions, particularly those involving power series with coefficients in the set of $p$-adic integers. Our findings hold significant value in number theory, as demonstrated by various non-trivial examples. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an analog of the Lerch formula also exists in this context, and establish relationships between some special values of this function and other notable $p$-adic zeta type functions. To facilitate our analysis, we develop an alternative representation of power series with coefficients in the set of $p$-adic integers, and establish some necessary properties of the Haagerup tensor product in this context. Additionally, in the process of solving the functional equation, we develop an analog of the functional equation satisfied by the Gauss sum, and investigate some properties of the $p$-adic extension of the algebra of continuous functions on a compact discrete valuation ring. To conclude, we observe that our method is versatile and can be extended to solve similar problems in more complex settings. Our analysis used a set of artificially generated datasets with varying levels of error introduction, as well as real-world species presence-absence data from six different habitats. We assessed the performance of each algorithm using several metrics, such as silhouette score, Calinski-Harabasz index, and cluster-assignment error rate. Our results suggest that the choice of clustering method depends on the specific characteristics of the data, while general approaches, such as evaluating the number of non-overlapping clusters and searching for local maxima in the graph-theoretic index, may be applicable to any graph. We also found that cross-validation can provide unbiased estimates of the indices and perform well on the artificial datasets, but may not consistently identify the optimal number of clusters in the real-world species data. Furthermore, we found that the partitioning version of CC and GC tended to perform better than their original forms, as well as in combination with fuzzy extensions. Our study indicates that fuzzy-set algorithms can be effective even when the presence-absence data is error-free, but may not consistently outperform their crisp counterparts. The model is optimized using an adversarial learning approach, allowing it to learn essential features from the interactions with both the conditional image synthesis GAN and the salient object detection GAN. A novel iterative image restoration method is introduced to enhance low-dose CT images affected by beam hardening and noise. This is achieved through a two-stage process involving a deep learning-based network and a constrained maximum a posteriori estimation method using an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model for noise modeling. The OU model can effectively handle various noise types by adapting to the image's intensity-dependent characteristics. A penalty term is incorporated into the optimization process to maintain the sparsity of the image and its derivatives, which helps to regularize the image and produce a cleaner output. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method yields a significant improvement in image quality compared to standard low-dose CT reconstruction methods and a commonly used OU-based regularization approach. Further analysis reveals that the proposed method is robust to different types of noise and can produce accurate quantitative results even in low-dose settings. Additionally, it is shown that the proposed method can accurately recover smooth and homogeneous images with low residual error. Our work indicates that the OU-based deep learning and regularization method is a promising approach for low-dose CT imaging and can potentially expand to other medical imaging modalities affected by noise. We suggest a storage structure that efficiently allows for the retrieval of three-nucleon interaction matrix elements, where each element is referenced through a set of single-nucleon momenta and intrinsic quantum numbers. This novel approach reduces memory usage by nearly eliminating unused elements in conventional, fully-permutated arithmetic representations. For example, calculations involving the three-nucleon interaction in the intermediate energy range require a substantial $3! = 6$ factor increase in memory to account for all possible element permutations. In contrast, our proposed method accommodates the unique elements arising from six distinct nucleon configurations without extra overhead. We demonstrate that, using our storage scheme, the total memory required to store three-nucleon interaction elements for a specific energy range and momentum transfer range can be reduced from around 257 GB to approximately 6.5 GB. Furthermore, this improved structure does not introduce computational complexity when switching between the various element permutations. Lastly, we note that our storage method does not affect the form of the three-nucleon interaction elements themselves but rather how their associated matrix elements are stored and accessed. In addition to this improved storage structure, we also provide a C++ implementation of a generalized three-nucleon interaction class that includes multiple arithmetic representations, along with a demonstration of its effectiveness in reducing memory usage. This class has been successfully applied in calculations involving ab initio calculations using the Monte Carlo wave function methods. In particular, we show that using our storage method in calculations with the Birmingham Monte Carlo group yields significant memory savings, allowing the calculations to proceed to completion where they previously ran out of memory. We provide detailed documentation, including a detailed overview of the proposed storage structure and its associated code, in a specially created manual and associated code repository found at https://manuals.lms.cam.ac.uk/manual/storage_for_three_body_interactions. This comprehensive guide and code repository are made freely available under the permissive MIT license. This research investigates the properties of composition operators within the Bergman space of a bounded convex domain in its Euclidean or hyperbolic representation.  The study particularly focuses on the effects of non-zero analytic discs in the domain's boundary on composition operator properties, revealing that the presence of such discs renders the composition operator non-bounded or non-compact in both the Euclidean and hyperbolic scenarios.  Additionally, the findings establish sufficient conditions in the form of weighted integration conditions on the boundary for the boundedness or compactness of composition operators, and an essential criterion for the compactness of these operators is identified in terms of the domain's boundary functions.  In the case of the hyperbolic Poincaré model of a ball, specific boundary functions are pinpointed whose composition operator fails to be bounded or compact, and a detailed classification of bounded and compact composition operators is provided, along with a characterization of the maximal ideal space of the domain's C*-algebra in terms of the Bergman space's orthogonal projections.  Finally, the study considers the properties of multiplication operators within the boundary function space of the domain and identifies both necessary and sufficient conditions for the compactness of these operators.  Specifically, the presence of non-trivial analytic discs in the boundary is shown to preclude the boundedness or compactness of these operators.  The study concludes by examining the properties of weighted composition operators within the Bergman space of the domain, drawing parallels with the results obtained for the compactness of composition operators and identifying necessary and sufficient conditions for the compactness of these operators that generalize those obtained for the Poincaré model of the ball.  Additionally, the results demonstrate that the compactness of composition operators is preserved under the transformation from the Bergman space of the domain to its Poincaré model.  The study further extends its findings to the Bergman space of the extended domain by establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for the compactness of composition and multiplication operators, and identifying pivotal roles for the domain's boundary functions in this context.  Finally, the results are applied to specific examples of bounded convex domains, including the hyperbolic type II Salamanca domain, for which the compactness of composition operators is shown to be influenced by the domain's 'thinness' at infinity.  The study concludes by posing corresponding questions for the compactness of multiplication operators within the boundary function space of the domain. In these models, the Isospin Violation can be attributed to the interaction terms influenced by the $U(1)_X$ gauge boson. Our findings demonstrate that, in general, the Isospin Violation is attributable to the difference in coupling constants between dark currents and their respective interactions with nucleons. This study also establishes a criterion for neighbour-transitive codes in quadrangles and provides implications for the neighbourhood of their elements. Additionally, an analysis of the neighbourhood of elements in the quadrangle W2(3) provided new neighbour-transitive codes. This research offers a valuable pathway for the exploration of entangled photonic states through experimental realization. Current one-sided online spanner algorithms for geometric graphs assume the elimination of Steiner points, making them suboptimal in cost-efficiency. This paper addresses this issue by presenting more efficient one-sided online spanner algorithms that directly utilize Steiner points in three-dimensional geometric graphs. A preliminary algorithm is developed, which achieves a competitive ratio of $\frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon$ with $O\left(\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$ hop count, while a second algorithm has a competitive ratio of $1.5+\varepsilon$ with $O\left(\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\vepsilon^3}\right)$ hop count. By slightly altering these algorithms, two new competitive ratios are attained: $\frac{3}{2}+\varepsilon$ with $O\left(\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$ hop count and $2+\varepsilon$ with $O\left(\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3}+\frac{\log^2(1/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\right)$ hop counts. These improvements are almost optimal, as it is proven that any one-sided online spanner algorithm for three-dimensional geometric graphs with competitive ratio at most $3+\varepsilon$ must have a hop count of $O(\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^2}+\frac{\log^2(1/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon})$. Additionally, this paper introduces new offline spanner algorithms, which are then applied to analyze the online algorithms' worst-case scenarios. These findings reveal nearly optimal results for one-sided online spanners and set a new standard for two-sided online spanners. Based on these discoveries, almost optimal bounds are achieved for online spanners with different constraints. Furthermore, this paper presents new bounds for the k-spanner problem, which involves connecting every pair of nodes with at least k connections. The findings provide close to optimal results for one-sided and two-sided k-spanners, set a new standard for the k-vertex spanner problem with the restriction of allowing Steiner points, and achieved almost optimal results for the restricted k-vertex spanner problem without the use of Steiner points. This research investigates the difficulties in accurately identifying IoT devices across diverse industries, considering factors such as device availability and operational nuances. We observe that existing classification methods are often limited by their inability to account for uncertainty and device dynamics, leading to inaccurate identifications and false positives. We propose a new approach, risk-aware classification, which takes into account the likelihood of false positives and negatives based on predefined risk thresholds. This method allows organizations to balance the trade-off between accurate identifications and reduced false positives. We apply this approach to an actual industrial setting, using real-time IoT data and financial rewards for accurate classifications. We evaluate the performance of this method through both theoretical and practical analyses, demonstrating its capability to adapt to changing device deployments and provide personalized accuracy and false positive rates. We also conduct an experimental study to validate the effectiveness of this method, using real-world IoT data and industrial devices. The results indicate that risk-aware classification offers more accurate identifications and flexible adaptability, while reducing false positives and aligning costs with organizational risk tolerance. This method can serve as a valuable tool for industrial identification, providing actionable insights into IoT device management. Furthermore, this approach can contribute to the advancement of transparent and explainable AI algorithms. This extension enables the analysis of correlation relationships between functions defined on different domains, while taking into account the functions' values at specific points. The theoretical outcomes are validated through the inclusion of relevant examples. One such example concerns the correlation between radial power functions and their derivatives. Another example demonstrates the positive definiteness of a specific function, which arises in the context of interdomain correlation analysis when one domain is compact and the other is non-compact. The study also presents an example of a positive definite function that belongs to a specific class, which cannot be positive definite relative to a different set of functions. The preparation of liquid foams with specifically designed rough bubble surfaces can significantly influence their flow characteristics. A dimensionless parameter, referred to as the roughness factor, quantifies the effect of surface roughness on the foam's rheological properties. In this study, we present a novel, numerical method to determine the roughness factor for polydisperse foams composed of spheres with varying sizes. The proposed approach utilizes finite element analysis to simulate the elastic response of individual spheres and spheres in contact, allowing for the calculation of the roughness factor through energy-based considerations. Additionally, we demonstrate how the roughness factor contributes to the yield stress of polydisperse foams, verifying that the proposed method yields accurate results, consistent with existing observations. Furthermore, we explore the impact of roughness on foam dynamics via batch simulations, revealing how the roughness factor influences the foam's rheological properties and overall appearance. Ultimately, we discuss potential applications of the proposed method across a broad range of bubble sizes and shapes. Due to the complexity of such systems, we also provide a thorough review of the theoretical foundations of liquid foams, facilitating the interpretation of results for polydisperse spheres. Furthermore, we outline the scope and limitations of the proposed method, suggesting possible enhancements to its accuracy. From a broader perspective, we believe that the proposed method can be adapted for use with more complex geometries, such as those encountered in medical imaging or chemical engineering, for example in the production of extracellular matrix mimics or catalysts. Therefore, the underlying principles of the proposed method may be applicable to a wider range of geometries than those considered here. Additionally, we provide support for future research, citing a need for investigating how the surface roughness affects the foam's auditory characteristics, such as its sound production. Consequently, we anticipate that the proposed method, based on the relationship between energy and roughness, can be utilized for determining the roughness factor for various liquid foam applications across a broad spectrum of scales. In the context of scaling, we observe that the characteristics of the foam can be adjusted by modifying a single parameter - the size of the rough bubbles - which facilitates the exploration of general liquid foam behaviors. Therefore, the liquid foams presented here can be applicable to a range of real-life situations, such as the distribution of pesticides, carbon capture, and medical imaging, as these examples illustrate the potential for scaling from microscopic to macroscopic. To reduce costs while maintaining performance, researchers have found that ensemble classifiers can effectively improve results while minimizing the number of models required. This study uses an ensemble of modified convolutional neural networks with varied architecture and learning rates to achieve a top classification accuracy of 92.43% for distinguishing normal and abnormal lung images. The research evaluates the importance of multiple factors in the ensemble's performance using a permutation test, revealing that ensemble size has the greatest impact. Notably, the team achieved an accuracy of 91.95% using half the originally required ensemble size, demonstrating the efficacy of their approach. This model has the potential to lower the computational costs of classification tasks, making it more efficient for physicians to use our system in clinical settings. The system also shows great promise for classifying various types of lung diseases when supplemented with additional training data. The research hopes to expand this capability in the future. Specifically, we demonstrate that any smooth, compactly supported initial velocity will result in a non-smooth, singular solution. Notably, this finding contrasts with the well-known solution uniqueness in two-dimensional Euler equations, highlighting the difference between smooth and general solutions. We introduce Stable Artist, an innovative tool allowing artists to guide image creation and modify generated images easily, even without expertise in imaging physics or coding. This user-friendly platform bridges the gap between existing artistic tools and state-of-the-art image generation techniques, such as text-to-image models. By utilizing artist-generated data and image embeddings, Stable Artist empowers artists to control image generation and make meaningful changes. The effectiveness of this tool was demonstrated in two workshops where artists used it to create new images based on prompts developed in collaboration. The results showcased artists' ability to produce unique, high-quality images that reflected their intended visions. Following the successful deployment of Stable Artist, artists reported increased confidence in using the tool and expressed a desire to use it in their creative work. Artist feedback highlighted the tool's limitations, primarily due to its current inability to efficiently revisit and adjust previous artistic endeavors. Incorporating multi-step brush strokes and improved support for color mixing were other areas identified for improvement to further enhance the artistic experience. These insights have guided the development of future updates for Stable Artist and have influenced the exploration of new artistic tools and generated content. The potential of these tools lies in expanding artistic mediums and the possibilities of using generated content in professional settings. Magnetic bright points, associated with extremely intense magnetic fields, are crucial for understanding the maintenance of solar surface magnetic fragmentation. Analyzing the properties of these features is essential for grasping the dynamics of the solar surface. In this study, we investigate the velocity vectors of magnetic bright points using the magnetic field measurements obtained from the HELIOS IIA satellite, and their corresponding adaptations through the use of the Moffat function. Our findings indicate that, upon correction, the statistical distributions of the x and y components of the velocity vectors are approximately symmetrical, whereas prior research revealed a biased distribution of velocities, especially during the rise of magnetic bright points. Furthermore, examining the correlations between the velocity vectors and the sizes of magnetic bright points, we discover negative relationships, implying that both faster-moving features and those with higher surface coverage are generally observed at lower latitudes. Additionally, we find evidence suggesting a positive correlation between the sizes of magnetic bright points and their mean x-component velocities at higher latitudes. To further explore these findings, we draw upon the observational and theoretical insights provided by the global convective modeling of the AASTAR project. Our study offers a thorough characterization of the statistical properties of magnetic bright points, and their implications for the understanding of the dynamic behavior of these features, thereby contributing to the advancement of solar surface dynamics research. Human movement and behavior are influenced by various visual cues, yet current datasets focused on human dynamics often rely on artificial stimuli, underselling the potential of human body language and eye movements in understanding social behavior and human dynamics. To bridge this gap, our research introduces minimal video tools for generating realistic, naturally-looking human behavior and eye movements, utilizing these patterns in composition to create more immersive and socially informative videos. This revised structure also allows us to analyze the optimal PPT forms for full positivity on partial trace and positivity on global trace in the partial local max mixed state, leading to a new method of obtaining optimal PPT forms for full separability in low dimensions. The revised PPT cloning structure is also shown to be strongly optimal for full separability in low dimensions. Additionally, we provide a computational protocol for finding optimal PPT forms for any bipartite mixed state. The results obtained via this protocol match the previously known forms for certain full separable states and positivity on global trace states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that optimal PPT forms for full separability in high dimensions often exhibit specific structural properties. We also provide examples of full separable states with specific characteristics and show that positive partial trace states can have multiple optimal PPT forms. Banks incur significant losses due to fraud, which can be linked to unauthorized transactions on accounts. To enhance account security, banks monitor accounts for potential fraud by detecting unusual transactions. Current methods involve verifying transactions one by one, which hinders the analysis of large accounts due to the increasing number of transactions. To overcome this limitation, this research introduces a new approach that treats account operations as a network called banking graphs, which are validated and analyzed using the properties of oriented homogeneous multipartite graphs. This method combines transaction verification and graph analysis, allowing for the efficient detection of invalid account operations and the scalability of analyzing large accounts. Furthermore, this research introduces a new algorithm called the HPP+ algorithm, which generates valid banking graphs by removing edges from the HPP extrema. This algorithm enables fast generation of valid banking graphs and detects account fraud quickly. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches, which were tested using real data from the Rdatasets package and the BDDLib library. This research achieves a higher accuracy rate (99.8%) in detecting invalid transactions compared to the best existing approach (97.5%), with a significantly faster HPP+ algorithm at a computationally complex level of O(n^2.5) compared to the best existing approach (O(n^3.1)). Furthermore, this research achieves a higher accuracy rate (98.2%) in detecting account fraud compared to the best existing approach (96.5%), with a faster HPP+ algorithm at a computationally complex level of O( n^2.7) compared to the best existing approach (O(n^3.7)). To ensure the reliability of this research, the code and data used in this study are made available for reproduction and further research purposes. The reliability of this research was verified by reproducing the results, which showed an accuracy rate of 98.8 for the original approach and 98.8 for the modified approach, closely aligning with the expected results. Additionally, the proposed method effectively detects invalid transactions on accounts 001 (98.8%), 002 (99.7%), and 003 (100%), as verified by an independent expert. Furthermore, the proposed method effectively detects account fraud for accounts 001 (99.7%), 002 (99.7%), and 003 (100%), as verified by an independent expert. We show that conventional CNNs and fully connected NNs are specifically instances of Graph Convolutional Networks, where the underlying graph structure is either explicitly defined or assumed to be fully connected. By recognizing these networks as Graph Convolutional Networks, we can apply established theoretical frameworks for analyzing representation learning in graphs to interpret the representation learning process in CNNs and fully connected NNs. Furthermore, this graph perspective enables us to address a critical limitation in the existing literature on Graph Convolutional Networks, where the learned representations are expressed as linear combinations of preprocessed node features, neglecting initial node feature transformations, thus leading to suboptimal performance. To overcome this limitation, we propose an approach that optimizes both the graph structure and the node feature transformation components, where the graph structure is selected to maximize the performance and the node feature transformations are optimized through regression. By combining these graph structure optimization and node feature transformation approaches, we can uncover more effective graph structures that underpin existing state-of-the-art CNNs and fully connected NNs, as demonstrated through extensive experiments. The recent successes of parsing tasks using self-training on large-scale datasets have been noteworthy. Nonetheless, this approach is hampered by inaccuracies resulting from false positives, which necessitate a more effective strategy. An alternative method, Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST), addresses these limitations by incorporating false negative reduction, a novel training technique. By contextualizing self-training, DCST mitigates the propagation of errors and enables the model to leverage contextual information. This innovation involves merging the current model's predictions with self-training, utilizing contextualized knowledge to refine false positives. DCST's contextual awareness is achieved through attention mechanisms, encompassing both self-attention and cross-attention. This design contextualizes knowledge, encapsulating the model's state, which is found to be essential for parsing tasks. DCST's context-aware mechanism empowers the model to contextualize knowledge, merging it with self-training, which is found to outperform existing self-training methods. Moreover, DCST's context-aware mechanism demonstrates an added benefit of improving non-contextualized parsing systems. Experimental evaluations on well-known datasets for English, German, and Chinese demonstrate the superior performance of DCST, which is found to be an effective approach for enhancing parsing systems. Furthermore, the analysis of contextualized knowledge, visualized through t-SNE, highlights the significance of context-aware mechanisms, underscoring the importance of contextualized knowledge in parsing tasks. Lastly, the source code and datasets for this study are accessible on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/InfMin/DCST.

We develop a general method for finding the fusion tables of non-trivial, invertible symmetries in field theory and quantum systems, providing specific results for the Ising and Kitaev models. To achieve this, we use modular techniques, specifically applying the modular homomorphisms $G \to \mathbb{Z}\otimes G$ and $\mathbb{Z}[1/2]\otimes G$ relevant to the Ising and Kitaev models, respectively. We derive the modular group associated with the Ising model and calculate the fusion tables for the toric code and Kitaev models. We also apply our method to other systems, determining the fusion tables for the free fermion and double free fermion symmetries, and providing explicit results for systems with non-invertible symmetries, such as the sum-state symmetry of the Moore-Read and kitaev models. In contrast to the real number system, we find that finite fields exhibit a significant yet intuitive difference in complexity. Specifically, we establish that any solution set for an unordered system of linear equations over a finite field is definable within the confines of a tractable first-order theory. Moreover, we refine this finding further, discovering that even individual solutions to linear equations can be precisely captured using a tractable first-order framework, albeit under a specific condition regarding the rank of the equation's coefficient matrix. In contrast, we find that this rank condition plays a crucial role in determining the tractability of defining solution sets for ordered linear equations. Building on these findings, we explore how these complexities affect the solution counts for linear equations and establish a definitive boundary for the tractability of counting solutions. In particular, we find that this rank condition becomes the pivotal factor, allowing for the precise counting of solutions under certain conditions, whereas an additional restriction is necessary for the tractable counting of solutions over ordered systems. In addition to these theoretical discoveries, we validate our results through a study of low-rank linear equations, demonstrating precise bounds on the tractable rank condition for various equation types and field characteristics. Our findings are further substantiated by an investigation into the complexity of linear equations containing a significant number of variables, revealing a profound impact of variable count on the complexity of solution sets and solution counting. The proliferation of software features has contributed to their success in both
commercial and open-source domains. However, this growth also poses challenges,
notably resulting in considerable system complexity and the consumption of storage
space. Removing options that are no longer executed during run-time can help
streamline system configuration and minimize storage requirements. Identifying and
removing these options, though, can be labor-intensive for large systems. To date,
existing approaches rely on performance counters gathered during the configuration
process or require modifications to the system's source code to determine
unused options. In this paper, we introduce a new approach that leverages dynamic
reconfigurations combined with performance monitoring to accurately pinpoint and
remove unused run-time options. By doing so, we differentiate from existing
methods, while also illustrating their shortcomings and limitations. Using two
real-world applications as case studies, we demonstrate the efficacy of our
approach in identifying and disposing of unused options without relying on
source code access or premature system configuration. Specifically, we show that
our approach enabled the removal of over 90% of the options in the Eclipse platform
and eliminated 100% of the unused options in the Wildermuth benchmark. To support
replicability, the source code of our method is available on GitHub. Furthermore,
we developed a dynamic reconfiguration framework, dubbed DRCO, to facilitate the
reconfiguration of systems lacking a built-in mechanism. By open-sourcing this
framework, we aim to promote the use of dynamic reconfigurations in various
software systems. The source code of DRCO can be accessed at https://github.com/
jubisch/DRCO. Based on this framework, we further propose an instance of the
problem aimed at identifying and disposing of unused options, dubbed the OUNP
problem. By formulating this problem, we contribute to advancing theoretical aspects
of reconfiguration through the creation of benchmark instances. One such instance,
based on Wildermuth, is provided as a benchmark demonstration. All other benchmark
instances are inaccessible due to intellectual property restrictions. To showcase
the feasibility of our approach, we successfully solved the OUNP instance for the
Eclipse platform and Wildermuth benchmark using our method, thereby highlighting
its potential as a solution for this problem. To facilitate future research on
reconfiguration, we provide benchmark instances for the ECP problem based on the
Eclipse platform. Moreover, we outline possible investigations into the
reconfiguration of system calls, network sockets, and shared libraries.

ECG signal analysis is crucial for identifying cardiovascular disorders and inter-beat intervals (IBIs). However, typical T-wave interference severely degrades traditional time-domain IBI estimation methods. To overcome this limitation, a novel deep learning-based approach is presented, combining a T-wave removal filter with an improved IBI estimation algorithm. The proposed method utilizes a conditional generative adversarial network to create a noise-free surrogate signal, which is then analyzed using a modified respiration-synchronized time-warping algorithm. This unique hybrid excels in IBI estimation accuracy, particularly when compared to existing deep learning and traditional methods. Notably, while other studies have integrated data augmentation and domain generalization techniques, the proposed approach surpasses them in performance. Implemented as an open-source Python plugin for Adobe Illustrator, this method can be utilized to accurately determine IBIs from ECG images, with data augmentation and visualization capabilities included. The detailed analysis of human faces is crucial for creating realistic, three-dimensional models of expression, which is essential for various applications such as filmmaking and gaming. However, modeling all aspects of the human face from a few views is extremely challenging due to the complex spatial relationships involved. In recent years, super-resolution has received significant attention, and super-resolution models based on convolution have been widely adopted due to their effectiveness and efficiency across various benchmarks. Notably, BasicVSR, a simple yet efficient framework, has achieved impressive results on world-wide jetification datasets. Building upon BasicVSR, we introduce BasicVSR++, a refined version with improved performance and efficiency. By optimizing key components, such as the temporal models and loss functions, BasicVSR++ surpasses BasicVSR by 0.3-0.8 dB in terms of PSNR while reducing the computational cost by 2-5 times. Furthermore, BasicVSR++ exhibits superior results on PMO4D and RDTSB, demonstrating its robustness and generalization capabilities. The source code will be publicly available soon.

In our research, we investigate how multi-task reinforcement learning agents learn task-specific models and how these models can be utilized for efficient learning of novel tasks. Our findings indicate that employing a single dynamics model trained on multiple tasks often results in 'contamination,' where the model becomes biased towards a dominant task, hindering its ability to adapt to new tasks. We identify two primary challenges in leveraging learned dynamics models for new tasks: (1) the models frequently fail to generalize across multiple tasks due to differing dynamics, and (2) even when the models are trained on multiple tasks, they tend to minimize effort required for future tasks, leading to data efficiency. We aim to address these challenges by proposing an efficient new-task learning protocol, Dynamical Multi-Task Learning, which learns a task-specific model, a high-level state representation, and a state initializer using a collection of past demonstrations. Our model is capable of generalizing across various tasks and can initialize future state sequences effectively. Moreover, when provided with interactive access to new tasks, our model is able to learn both the dynamics and policy functions simultaneously using transfer learning. Our model's performance is validated through successful application to two complex real-world AtBat games and one MRL benchmark, where it surpasses existing benchmark models in performance. Our model's potential to increase data efficiency and performance in interactive multi-task reinforcement learning is thus demonstrated. Lastly, our model's code and evaluations can be accessed via our repository, https://github/DMRL.

Recent years have seen a surge in interest in Collaborative Filtering techniques that employ biclustering for personalization in Recommender Systems. While these methods can learn complex patterns in user-item data, they often struggle to account for user and item factors separately. To address this limitation, a novel method called USBFC has been developed, which combines unsupervised biclustering with separable data factorization. By doing so, USBFC captures the underlying patterns in data while keeping user and item factors distinct. To evaluate its effectiveness, experiments were conducted on real-world datasets and compared with leading biclustering-based CF methods. Results reveal that USBFC surpasses the baseline performance by a significant margin of 25.65% on average, with further gains achievable through model ensemble. Our method introduces a unique approach to learning image representations by leveraging the principles of contrastive learning. Unlike conventional methods that rely on hand-designed similarity functions, our contrastive loss encourages the encoder to distinguish between identical image duplicates, fostering more effective image encoding. We compare the efficacy of our method to established techniques such as PCA and VAE on various image datasets and find that our method surpasses them in terms of encoding style consistency. Furthermore, our contrastive loss can be combined with Generative Adversarial Networks without compromising their performance. We further develop an iterative enhancement of our encoder-decoder model by iterating between contrastive learning and generative adversarial training, ultimately achieving state-of-the-art performance in semantic segmentation. Deep generative models have significant practical value due to their ability to learn high-level representations of real-world data. Despite initial success with independent identically distributed data, a major challenge in machine learning is handling structured, real-world sensory data with inherent correlations. Recent breakthroughs, specifically with variants of the Gaussian Mixture model and combinatorial models, have shown great potential in modeling dependent data. However, these models often fall short in dealing with complex, high-dimensional data due to their limitations in parameter space and likelihood assumptions. This paper proposes a novel, generative model capable of efficiently modeling large datasets with significant interactions by combining sparse, directed graphical models and combinatorial neural networks. A solid geometric structure, known as a convex geometric hypergraph, can be constructed within a higher-dimensional space by gathering multiple-dimensional subgraphs along a single linear path. Researchers have recently studied this concept, initially introduced by Tóthmérész in 2019, and its corresponding saturation problems. In this article, we address two specific saturation issues for convex geometric n-hypergraphs containing k-sets, and provide an exact determination of the saturation number when k equals two in a two-dimensional space. Additionally, we present a general lower-bound solution applicable to all values of k. Furthermore, we explore a particular subclass of convex geometric k-hypergraphs where the presented geometric structure possesses unique properties and explore the associated saturation problems. In particular, we identify the saturation number for a particular 4-hypergraph in a two-dimensional space. Our findings also extend the research by Tóthmérész on saturated geometric 2-hypergraphs, and provide new insights for convex geometric n-hypergraphs. In the process of our research, we introduce a method to generate a large number of unsaturated structures, thus significantly expanding the known family of saturated structures. Ultimately, we conclude with some open problems and possible directions for future investigation.

This technology has potential applications in robots that can operate on uneven surfaces in a variety of environments. We outline a method to use the Guderley problem - a highly compressed, rapidly expanding shockwave phenomenon - as a standard test case for validating complex hydrodynamic simulation models. To achieve this, a nonlinear direct numerical simulation approach is employed, where an initial perturbation in an otherwise uniformly accelerating flow is introduced and allowed to evolve numerically. To apply this method in practice, a specific flow setup and domain size are chosen and various numerical methods for solving the Navier-Stokes equations are utilized to reproduce the shockwave dynamics. The resulting solutions are then compared to each other and to established experimental data for validation, allowing for a assessment of how well different hydrodynamic simulation models perform in capturing the complex dynamics of this high-aspect-ratio flow. One such comparison is made with an experimental study using laser shadowgraphy and a simulation model based on a cluster of computing cores; the results show excellent agreement between the non-local Navier-Stocks model and the experimental findings, highlighting the effectiveness of this test case in validating hydrodynamic simulation models. Furthermore, the lack of a fixed solution structure in the Guderley problem and the ability to resolve the entire flow domain make the Guderley problem an ideal candidate for validating simulation models across a wide range of scales. To achieve this, a method is employed where the flow solution at a particular instant is utilized as the initial condition for the experimental study, thereby covering a broader range of lengthscales. The resulting solutions show excellent agreement with the experimental findings, demonstrating the effectiveness of this test case in validating hydrodynamic simulation models across a wide range of lengthscales. To make the test case accessible to a broader hydrodynamic community, a detailed description of the simulation approach is provided, along with recommendations for implementing the method in practical applications. Learning detailed image generation is beneficial for multiple applications, but its high-resolution output often appears less realistic than its lower-resolution counterparts. This discrepancy makes high-resolution image synthesis an underutilized capability. This paper proposes a hierarchical deep-generative model called MrSARP, composed of multiple stacked Variational Autoencoders, that synthesizes images across various resolutions using a shared set of learned representations. MrSARP's conditional variant is demonstrated in medical segmentation, where it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models on multi-scale radiology tasks, such as synthesizing complete chest X-rays from inputs of simpler complexity. Additionally, MrSARP showcases promising results in synthetic image generation and organized image analysis. Source code is available at https://github.com/sandipanbanerjee/MrSARP.

This approach employs a lighter model of the Bayesian optimization framework that doesn't require full data reuse or high computational resources, making it suitable for near-term quantum devices. Our results show that Bayesian optimization can significantly enhance the QAOA's performance, outweighing the costs of running additional experiments. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal solutions obtained using Bayesian optimization are comparable to those achieved by full data reuse. We then assessed the model's performance on normal-dose CT scans and achieved comparable results with an 88 alignment score. This note provides more detailed, explicit, and complementary calculations to a previous paper, specifically examining relative I-functions for smooth toric complete intersections with regular boundaries in projective varieties over a field of characteristic zero. To simplify the computations, we utilize logarithmic geometry and the formal geometry of arcs as described in the works of K. L\"ubke and M. Kerz, as well as other associated theories. Furthermore, we apply the concept of fiber products of arc spaces to represent the relative I-functions in question, thereby incorporating toric Tutte polynomials and inductively recovering I-functions for more complex geometric configurations, such as those involving hyperplane arrangements and certain Segre varieties. Additionally, these formulas are applied to calculate specific I-functions for five exceptional smooth toric complete intersections in projective three-dimensional and four-dimensional spaces. Lastly, we connect our findings to the broader context of varieties with regular boundaries, as discussed in the works of L\"ubke, as well as to the realm of elliptic geometry and the study of elliptic curves, as exemplified by certain examples in dimensions two and three. We establish a classification system for the space of degree d homogeneous polynomials in n variables, categorized by the type of their Milnor fibration's topological structure, specifically the space of oriented fibers. This classification is based on a specific invariant, $\mathcal{F}_d^n$, which consists of the topological type of the oriented fiber space. This results in a group action that mirrors the polynomial's algebraic properties, allowing us to calculate the polynomial's Hilbert pair, a crucial invariant in combinatorial geometry, as well as determining the topological structure of the oriented fiber space, $\mathcal{F}_{d,n}$. Furthermore, this classification enables us to compute the polynomial's Hilbert pair and the oriented fiber space's topological structure for specific cases. Additionally, this classification provides a key application in solving the polynomial's equisingularity problem for the fibering structure. M. Biggs, M. Kapovich, and K. Schefter for the case of degree 2 and n = 2k being even. This paper maintains that Galileo's scientific strengths lie in his mathematical skills rather than his observational abilities. While acknowledging the importance of data collection in scientific inquiry, the analysis suggests that Galileo's reliance on empirical methods was somewhat limited. This in turn may have constrained his potential to make significant breakthroughs in the natural sciences. The study also explores how Galileo's focus on mathematical reasoning allowed him to achieve major scientific achievements, particularly in the areas of kinematics and dynamics. However, this mathematical emphasis came at the cost of engaging less intensively with the natural world, which the authors argue may have had a broader impact on the development of 17th-century science. Overall, the analysis suggests that Galileo's scientific contributions were exceptional yet uneven in scope, favoring the mathematical sciences over empirical research in the natural sciences. This dualistic profile of Galileo's scientific work is exemplified by his priorities as evident from his correspondence, which often reveals an inherent tension between his artistic training, which gave greater value to observation, and his growing expertise in mathematics, which gradually led him to place more emphasis on abstract reasoning. The same correspondence also highlights the difficulties Galileo encountered in his interactions with scientists, philosophers, and state officials, which sometimes created discord by misunderstanding his scientific strengths and priorities. The analysis concludes with an examination of how Galileo's scientific legacy has been perceived by three prominent historians, Valerio Provenzani, Stillman Drake, and J. R. Marr, who variously emphasized different aspects of his multifaceted personality and intellectual abilities. The study suggests that any appraisal of Galileo's scientific character must be grounded in a nuanced recognition of his complex and sometimes contradictory traits. Ultimately, the research seeks to humanize Galileo, the historical figure, by rescinding his status as "the father of modern science," which was originally conferred by Augustus De Morgan and later reinforced by subsequent historians, in favor of a more accurate portrayal as a brilliant, if imperfect, scientist. The final chapter reflects on the broader implications of these findings for our understanding of scientific methodology and the natural world, which are found to be inextricably linked with an appropriate humanistic appreciation for the historical context and the personalities involved in the evolution of science. The conclusion emphasizes the necessity for a more empathetic and historically grounded approach in scientific interpretation, which should strive to uncover the unique perspectives and experiences of scientists like Galileo, rather than fitting them into predetermined modern templates. leveraging existing heuristics and developing innovative new approaches.  While
human learning may follow a established pattern, the potential for similar
progress in artificial intelligence remains poorly understood.  This study uses
joint problem-solving with human human and human-computer partnerships to
investigate how cooperative partners refine their strategies over time.  By
initially limiting their AI partner to pre-defined heuristics, the researchers
observed visible progress in their cooperative partnership, as well as their
joint problem-solving performance.  Interestingly, this progress was not only
reflected in their joint decision-making, but also in their individual decision-
making, as well as their joint problem-solving performance.  This study, the
first of its kind, indicates the existence of learning in collaborative AI
systems and suggests the potential for further exploration.  A number of open
questions remain, such as whether similar learning patterns can be observed in
more complex systems, as well as whether these systems are capable of displaying
